docs.title: Day 3 — EDR, Threat Emulation and Host Firewalls
Day 3 — EDR, Threat Emulation and Host Firewalls
docs.text:
Course: Information Security Core Skills · Instructor: John Strand (BHIS) · Day 3 scope: Sysmon lab review → Pass-the-Hash → EDR & defence in depth → threat emulation & Atomic Red Team → AI-written detections → BloodHound → gap-analysis lab → host firewalls

Day 3 at a glance

Day 3 opens with the Sysmon lab walkthrough deferred from Day 2, then shows how Pass-the-Hash (logging in with only a hash) looks in the logs. It then argues that EDR is powerful but not enough on its own — overlapping controls multiply — and that you shouldn't trust vendor claims but verify with tools like Atomic Red Team (gap analysis). It closes with host firewalls: blocking workstation-to-workstation traffic to remove the whole lateral-movement category.

Conventions

💡 Note (added) = my own addition beyond the lecture. (reconstructed) = something the instructor only showed on screen, written out generically. Labs that use offensive tooling are summarised by what they demonstrate and the defensive / detection takeaways; offensive command detail is omitted.

docs.title: Lab recap
docs.text:
1. Windows (victim): disable real-time protection and the firewall, set the admin password to password1234 (for the remote-logon part).
  2. Kali (attacker): build a test payload trustme.exe, move it to the victim, wait for the callback.
  3. Install Sysmon on Windows, then run trustme.exe → the attacker gets a remote session, dumps hashes and demonstrates a keylogger.

Building the file prints "No encoder specified" — meaning no encoding was done to evade AV, on purpose. The goal here isn't AV bypass; it's reading Sysmon logs.

John's numbers: the payload is 354 bytes but the final file is ~73 KB. That's Day 1's stager: the 354-byte piece just fetches the real body (the stage) from the attacker, and it's been stuffed inside a legitimate program, Apache Bench (ab.exe), so the file is the size of that program.

docs.title: What Sysmon recorded
docs.text:
Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational

Sysmon event What it showed Meaning 1 process create trustme.exe ran; description Apache Bench; OriginalFileName ab.exe; run by administrator; hashes; parent cmd.exe file name ≠ original name = a strong clue; launched directly from a command prompt 22 DNS query DNS lookups by trustme.exe where it tried to call home 8 CreateRemoteThread trustme.exe created a remote thread in LSASS the hash-dump signal — the moment hashes were pulled 1 process create notepad.exe, the Event Viewer snap-in, … even the keylogger demo and analysis steps appear in time order

LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) handles logons and credentials and holds sensitive material such as password hashes in memory. Ordinary programs almost never create threads in it.

💡 Note (added)

The classic credential-dumping detections are Sysmon 8 (remote thread into LSASS) and 10 (process access to LSASS). In event 10, the GrantedAccess value (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1410) shows whether memory-read access was requested. Detection queries: LSASS dumping.

docs.title: 2. Pass-the-Hash — logging in without the password
Setup
docs.text:
John changes the admin password from password1234 to a very long one — "uncrackable short of a quantum computer." Dumping hashes again shows the admin hash has changed.

Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:<NT hash>:::
  • aad3b4… (first part) = the LM (LAN Manager) hash. Long obsolete and unused, so it's the blank value — identical for every account. Ignore it.
  • Second part = the NT hash. Changing the password produced a completely different value.

docs.title: The key point — the hash is enough
docs.text:
Even assuming the hash can never be cracked, the attacker can authenticate by presenting the hash itself instead of the password. John uses the same remote-execution approach (PsExec) as Day 1's spray lab, with the hash in place of the password, and opens a new session without knowing the password at all.

However long and strong the password, if an attacker gets the hash they can log in as that user.

Day 1's NT-hash weakness — no salt — is why the hash effectively becomes "a key equivalent to the password."

💡 Note (added) — the defence isn't a stronger password

  • Unique local admin passwords per host — with LAPS, a hash taken from one PC doesn't work on another.
  • Block lateral-movement paths — the host firewalls section below (block SMB 445 between workstations).
  • Credential protection — Credential Guard, the Protected Users group, admin-account tiering.

Artifacts and detection: Pass-the-Hash.

docs.title: What Pass-the-Hash looks like in Sysmon
docs.text:
The earlier attack was a file execution (trustme.exe); this remote one shows heavily obfuscated PowerShell authenticating, uploading and running the payload. The same attacker leaves different log shapes depending on how they get in — detection that only watches file execution would miss this.

💡 Note (added) — traces of remote execution

  • Security log 4624 — logon type 3 (network), authentication package NTLM
  • System log 7045 — new service installed (PsExec-style execution creates a service)
  • Sysmon 1 — PowerShell spawned by a service (parent services.exe) with a long encoded command line
  • PowerShell 4104 — the de-obfuscated script content

Related: PsExec & SMB · PowerShell cradles

docs.title: Is Metasploit used in real engagements?
docs.text:
Not much in professional pentests — many teams use Cobalt Strike, Brute Ratel, Nighthawk. But for breadth of functionality nothing matches Metasploit; its weakness is team collaboration (commercial tools are better at teamwork, AV evasion, BOF extensions).

For an internal team doing day-to-day security work, Metasploit is free — and that's a huge advantage.

docs.title: 3. EDR — the most powerful control, but not one to rely on alone
docs.text:
EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) continuously watches process, file, network and registry activity on hosts and responds. In Back Doors & Breaches the "Endpoint Security Protection Analysis" card neutralises social engineering, compromised web servers, accessibility-feature abuse, logon scripts, lateral movement, privilege escalation, AD weaponisation, C2 and exfil — hence 4 resource points. In real life EDR is also among the most expensive tools. (Moving into this section John also briefly name-checked Velociraptor as a tool BHIS loves.)

The problem is that many organisations now rely almost 100% on EDR.

"To be completely honest with you, a lot of vendors lie" — guaranteeing they stop every attack with zero false positives.

docs.title: Defence in depth multiplies, it doesn't add
docs.text:
"We spent this much" or "we have EDR on 100,000 nodes" isn't defence in depth. Controls that don't overlap are merely additive; controls that overlap on the same asset are multiplicative.

If one host is covered by AV/EDR + network security monitoring (Day 2's Zeek/RITA) + SIEM + UEBA, one failing still leaves the others, and the attacker must evade all of them at once — the cost rises steeply.

From nation-state work — landing on a system defended like that meant asking the command chain for permission to continue, and most of the time the answer was "stop." The risk of exposing very expensive TTPs was too high.

Make the attacker decide "this is too expensive" — that's the goal.

Traditional deny-list AV is "pretty much garbage"; EDR finally lets you see systems holistically. A headline feature is the process tree (which process begat which), which matters again in memory analysis.

💡 Note (added)

A chain like WINWORD.EXE → cmd.exe → powershell.exe → rundll32.exe is the classic "Word macro ran a command" phishing compromise. Sysmon event 1's ParentImage is the raw material for this tree; memory forensics uses the same idea (Volatility pstree).

docs.title: Choosing an EDR — AI is only as good as its data
docs.text:
"We're a brand-new, scrappy EDR company with a completely proprietary AI no one has seen before." → John: odds are it's crap, because its training data just isn't big enough.

CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender (+ Sentinel) and SentinelOne train on billions of endpoints and have the compute to crunch it — very hard for newcomers to match. John's recommendations: CrowdStrike and Windows Defender + Sentinel (the good tier costs money).

docs.title: Blue Spawn — an EDR stand-in for the lab
docs.text: An open-source tool built by Virginia students for the CCDC collegiate cyber-defence competition when AV wasn't allowed in — they asked to write their own, and it worked. But its MITRE coverage is low, so don't use it as a real EDR. The lab's point is to learn how you should test your EDR.

docs.title: 4. Trust but verify — threat emulation
docs.text:
Don't just trust vendor marketing — but it's not all the vendor's fault. Configuration can cripple a product:

  • A rule that globally allows PowerShell everywhere — dumb, but common
  • EDR deployed on 90% of the environment — the remaining 10% is a big 10%

The answer is continuous validation of security controls — BHIS's SOC constantly checks its detection stack is executing as expected with the coverage expected.

docs.title: Emulation vs simulation
docs.text:
Simulation Emulation How a series of scripts imitating attack behaviour one binary + a C2 server behaving like real malware Example Atomic Red Team Caldera agents, Metasploit, … Level entry further down the pipeline

John: "honestly it doesn't make that much difference — do both."

Tools: Caldera (MITRE's adversary-simulation environment — deploy agents and exercise ATT&CK techniques), Infection Monkey, Atomic Red Team (Red Canary — small per-technique tests showing what got detected; this course's main lab tool).

Test in alert-only, non-blocking mode

Caldera publishes the AV signatures for its own binaries to prevent abuse, so any AV nails it. And most simulation tooling reproduces attacks with PowerShell scripts — if your EDR blocks PowerShell outright, none of the remaining tests run. Evaluate EDR in alerting, non-blocking mode so you learn exactly what it detects and misses.

docs.title: Don't write detections too specifically
docs.text:
Atomic Red Team shows each test's general command form and the concrete command with inputs (e.g. a regsvr32 test). A lazy detection engineer who pastes the entire command string — including the full Atomic Red Team path — gets a rule that:

  • fires every time someone runs Atomic Red Team, but
  • never fires on a real attack or pentest, because no attacker uses that exact path.

Instead, turn the variable parts into variables and match the invariant combination — here, "regsvr32 used together with /s /u /i: and scrobj.dll," case-insensitive.

💡 Note (added)

This technique is the well-known Squiblydoo (MITRE T1218.010, Regsvr32) — using the signed regsvr32.exe to run a remote scriptlet. See LOLBins.

docs.title: Using AI to write detections — and what humans must do
docs.text:
John asks free ChatGPT: "please create a Sigma alert based on the following detect." Sigma is the shared detection-rule language you write once and convert to many SIEMs.

title: Suspicious Regsvr32 Scriptlet DLL Execution
status: experimental
description: Detects suspicious use of regsvr32 with scrobj.dll
references:
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/010/
author: OpenAI
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\regsvr32.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'scrobj'
      - '/i:'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate administrator software registration activity
level: high

(reconstructed — the on-screen rule written out generically)

  • status: experimental — still being trialled.
  • references — the ATT&CK technique it's based on.
  • author: OpenAI — the AI credited itself, which made John laugh.
  • logsource — Windows process creation (Sysmon 1 or Security 4688).
  • Image|endswith: '\regsvr32.exe' — path ends with regsvr32.exe, so it matches wherever it's run from.
  • CommandLine|contains|all — the command line contains all listed values.
  • condition: selection — alert when the above matches.
  • falsepositives — "legitimate admin software registration"; John has seen legitimate software use this same technique.

ChatGPT avoided the over-specific trap and wrote a generalised rule; John also had it produce Elastic and LimaCharlie versions.

So what do humans do? Someone answers "tune" — John: "before we tune, we have to test." BHIS's order:

  1. Draft — AI or an analyst writes the rule.
  2. Back-test on historical data — BHIS's Detection Forge asks "how many times would this have fired?" If it's 100,000, you have tuning to do; rules that spew false positives make people dislike you.
  3. Tune — bring the volume down.
  4. Test against a live attack — fire it with Atomic Red Team in a sandbox and confirm it triggers.

Test both directions: history ("not too noisy?") and a current attack ("does it actually fire?").

💡 Note (added) — the back-test idea in Splunk

Translate the rule into SPL and run it over a past window to count hits:

index=* EventCode=1 Image="*\\regsvr32.exe" CommandLine="*scrobj*" CommandLine="*/i:*"
| timechart span=1d count

EventCode=1 is Sysmon process creation; Image="*\\regsvr32.exe" keeps paths ending in regsvr32.exe; the two CommandLine terms keep only command lines containing both scrobj and /i: (space-separated terms are ANDed). timechart span=1d count counts per day as a time chart — hundreds a day means the rule needs tuning.

Nervous about running these tools? Metasploit and Atomic Red Team don't run rampant through your environment — they run specific test cases on a specific host.

docs.title: 5. BloodHound — paths to Domain Admin
docs.text:
BloodHound (SpecterOps) enumerates every path from a standard user to Domain Admin, for free.

  1. The attacker lands on my PC (I opened a bad Word doc) — they are effectively me.
  2. In many AD environments any user can log on to any workstation with their domain credentials.
  3. The tool authenticates to thousands of hosts asking "am I admin here?" — no, no, no …
  4. On the 15,000th host, it finds admin rights.

Why that host? An accounting PC with a flatbed scanner whose software, for some stupid reason, needs local admin to run. So the help desk says "everyone on this team needs the scanner — add Domain Users to local Administrators. Who's ever going to find out?"

BloodHound answers that question — and attackers find out very quickly with automated tools.

From there the attacker escalates, grabs domain-level credentials for services and other accounts, and moves to Domain Admin. Defenders should run this kind of testing too — looking at the whole AD environment through an attacker's eyes, not just one workstation.

💡 Note (added)

BloodHound's collector (SharpHound) generates bulk LDAP queries to domain controllers and SMB session / local-group enumeration across hosts. On the detection side look for one account making network logons (4624, type 3) to very many hosts in a short window, and bulk LDAP from one client (e.g. Zeek ldap.log). The key defence: never put Domain Users in a local Administrators group.

docs.title: John on commercial tools and AI
docs.text:
Commercial emulation tools — Scythe, AttackIQ, XM Cyber — are good, but many pitch themselves as full pentest replacements ("you don't need pentests anymore"). John sees this as the wrong way to apply AI: bolting it onto the status quo and concluding "we need fewer pentesters and SOC analysts, we save money."

The industry was drowning — in vulnerabilities, detections, SIEM and log analysis. Then AI arrived — a chance to finally get ahead of attackers. Instead, vendors immediately saw it as "we can save money."

The right frame is the 80/20 rule — tools and AI cover 80% of the vulnerabilities with 20% of the effort, so humans focus on what humans are good at: business context and attack paths unique to that environment. AI augments; it doesn't replace.

"The attackers have a vote." — they use the same tools, asymmetrically faster.

The author of a recent Windows privilege-escalation zero-day (BlueHammer) has released more, Linux privesc bugs are piling up, and one vendor said it found them with AI. Vulnerabilities will scale very fast; organisations need to realise what's coming down the wire now.

MITRE evaluations — "everyone's a winner": after MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations, nearly every vendor claims victory. Josh Lemon built his own scoring and early results showed wide variation — e.g. McAfee 268, Carbon Black 259, RSA 78 — and he also tallied each product's misses.

💡 Note (added)

The raw MITRE ATT&CK Evaluations results are public. Reading misses and "detections after configuration change" in the raw data beats vendor press releases.

docs.title: 6. Lab — Blue Spawn + Atomic Red Team and gap analysis
docs.text:
Really two labs in one: ① run set techniques with Atomic Red Team and see what Blue Spawn catches, ② hand-reproduce a new attack that has no test yet.

Blue Spawn won't detect everything — that's the point. The goal is gap analysis: find where the holes are.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Blue Spawn on the right (detections stream in live), PowerShell on the left; real-time protection off.

# (reconstructed) install the Invoke-AtomicRedTeam framework plus the atomics test library
IEX (IWR 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redcanaryco/invoke-atomicredteam/master/install-atomicredteam.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)
Install-AtomicRedTeam -getAtomics

# load the module
Import-Module "C:\AtomicRedTeam\invoke-atomicredteam\Invoke-AtomicRedTeam.psd1" -Force
  • IWR (Invoke-WebRequest) — fetch the install script.
  • IEX (Invoke-Expression) — run it. The same command Day 2's Deep Blue CLI flagged in obfuscated payloads — used by legitimate installers and attackers alike.
  • Install-AtomicRedTeam -getAtomics — framework plus the test definitions (atomics).
  • Import-Module ... .psd1 — load it so Invoke-AtomicTest is available.

Answer "Yes to All" to the PowerShell YAML module prompts. (One Atomic Red Team maintainer is Carrie Roberts, ex-BHIS and now an Antisyphon instructor.)

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
Invoke-AtomicTest T1547.004
  • Invoke-AtomicTest — run the tests for a technique.
  • T1547.004 — boot/logon autostart → Winlogon Helper DLL (persistence via the Winlogon registry values run at logon).

💡 Note (added) — useful flags

  • -ShowDetailsBrief — list the tests for a technique
  • -CheckPrereqs — verify prerequisites
  • -Cleanup — revert the test's changes (always run afterwards)
Test Blue Spawn result Lesson T1547.004 (Winlogon Helper DLL) detected immediately we now know this detection works T1543 (create/modify system process — services) 8 technique detections (with the matched string) / generic "modifying a service" item: 0 when activity doesn't match a known pattern, EDRs raise a medium "something happened" alert → focus on classified, technique-specific detections registry-key test nothing at first, then a burst a few seconds later the lag itself is part of the test command-prompt test registry detections "raining" in —

Why the lag? It's very common:

  • Many EDRs store and forward endpoint events; under load the pipeline stalls, then catches up.
  • WEC/WEF and Elastic collectors have been seen to get overwhelmed and pause.
  • Cloud services are worse — Microsoft logs in particular can take up to an hour from event to your analysis platform.

When judging "is our detection effective?", factor in not just whether it fires but how late it arrives.

💡 Note (added) — measuring ingest lag in Splunk

index=* earliest=-24h
| eval lag_sec = _indextime - _time
| stats avg(lag_sec) AS avg_lag max(lag_sec) AS max_lag BY sourcetype

_time is when the event happened; _indextime is when Splunk indexed it. eval lag_sec = _indextime - _time makes a new field with the difference in seconds, and stats ... BY sourcetype tabulates average and maximum lag per data type. A max_lag near 3600 means that source can arrive up to an hour late.

ATT&CK technique IDs change between versions, so the course provides a crosswalk JSON mapping old numbers to new.

docs.title: Ad-hoc emulation — what if there's no test yet?
docs.text:
A new attack drops. Atomic Red Team has no test for it. Management wants to know now whether you'd detect it; CISA has issued a warning.

You need the ability to do custom ad-hoc adversary simulation — reproduce the behaviour by hand. John reopens a remote session on the test VM (the same steps as before, done quickly) and tries behaviours one by one:

Behaviour tested Blue Spawn result Keystroke logging (typing into Notepad) not detected — a clear failed detect Registry persistence ① (autorun key added) not detected Registry persistence ② (a different registry method) detected

(Keystrokes weren't captured because the payload ran via the PowerShell method this time — how you run it can change results.)

What does our EDR detect, and what does it miss? — now you know where to add detections.

💡 Note (added) — log sources to close the gaps

  • Registry autorun persistence (MITRE T1547.001, Run keys etc.) — watch Sysmon 13 (registry value set) for \CurrentVersion\Run, \RunOnce. Persistence
  • Keylogging (MITRE T1056.001) — keyboard-hooking APIs rarely show in default logs, so it leans on EDR behavioural detection or memory analysis — a common blind spot.

The VM ends up "brutalised," so John destroys the lab and restarts it — the surest way back to clean.

docs.title: 7. Host firewalls and stopping lateral movement
docs.text:
Locking down host-based firewalls addresses essentially the whole Lateral Movement column of MITRE ATT&CK. The course philosophy again:

Don't chase individual techniques — take out whole categories of attack.

The core concept is segmentation — down to the host level if at all possible — and the reason is the Pass-the-Hash shown earlier.

docs.title: "Getting compromised is acceptable. But…"
docs.text:
Getting compromised is acceptable — it's going to happen. Like death, taxes and brushing your teeth.

What's not acceptable: an attacker persisting for months, or pivoting from one host to the whole environment in minutes. Host firewalls (or private VLANs) can stop that.

How attackers spread: a client-side exploit or drive-by compromises one host → they want lateral movement, not one box → preferably using built-in Windows protocols (PsExec, pass-the-token, Remote Desktop, Pass-the-Hash) → take over the whole domain.

docs.title: Treat the internal network as hostile
docs.text:
Turning on host firewalls means treating the internal network as hostile — "because it is." Set internal hosts' firewalls as you would at a coffee shop.

It's absolutely insane that your systems are more secure at a Starbucks than on their own network.

You can go further and segment between business units too (host firewalls plus inter-unit segmentation).

From To Allowed? servers, help desk, jump hosts workstations yes (needed for admin / support) workstations workstations no (no reason to talk)

Now a compromised host can't reach its peers, and you get overlapping fields of visibility — if AV, EDR, NSM, UEBA or SIEM fails, two or three others pick up the slack. Use your commercial AV's built-in firewall, or Windows' own netsh advfirewall ("awful, but free," and configurable via Group Policy).

💡 Note (added)

In practice, build inbound rules in GPO under Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Typical ports to block between workstations: SMB 445, RPC 135 (+ dynamic RPC), NetBIOS 139, WinRM 5985/5986, RDP 3389. "Deny all, then allow only the management / jump-host ranges" is the clean pattern.

docs.title: Lab — Nmap before and after the firewall
docs.text:
Run in the new lab environment (antilab). Get the Windows VM's IP, then scan it from the attacker VM.

① Firewall off

nmap 10.10.222.41
  • nmap — a scanner that shows which ports are open on a target.
  • 10.10.222.41 — the lab Windows VM (varies per environment).
PORT     STATE SERVICE
135/tcp  open  msrpc
139/tcp  open  netbios-ssn
445/tcp  open  microsoft-ds
3389/tcp open  ms-wbt-server
5985/tcp open  wsman

135 RPC · 139 NetBIOS session · 445 SMB file sharing · 3389 Remote Desktop · 5985 WinRM

② Firewall on, scan again

netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state on
  • netsh advfirewall — command-line control of Windows Firewall.
  • set allprofiles — apply to all profiles (domain, private, public).
  • state on — enable (state off disables).

The RPC ports disappear (the lab keeps allow rules for Terminal Services and WSMan to stay connected). John: with those ports open, lateral movement is possible and Pass-the-Hash works very well.

③ Confirm with Pass-the-Hash

  • Firewall off → the remote session succeeds; dumping the hash and re-authenticating with the hash also works. "It doesn't matter how strong someone's password is — if I've got your hash, I can authenticate as you."
  • Firewall on → the same attack tries port 445 and is dead in the water.

Shutting down port 445 alone severely restricts lateral movement from that host — specifically Pass-the-Hash-style movement.

💡 Note (added)

With Windows Firewall auditing on, blocked connections log Security 5157 (Windows Filtering Platform blocked a connection). But as John said on Day 2, firewall logging is noisy — in practice log only meaningful rules (e.g. workstation-to-workstation 445/135) or watch from the network side (internal↔internal SMB in Zeek conn.log). Related: Pass-the-Hash · PsExec & SMB.

docs.title: Firewalls aren't the end — preparing the Responder lab
docs.text:
On the same network an attacker can redirect a target's traffic with ARP cache poisoning, LLMNR or WPAD and capture its authentication — Day 1's Responder. That long-dead lab is back thanks to the new environment.

  • MetaCTF → Cloud Labs → code antilab → Submit. Two free lab hours every week (the first "Free Lab Friday").
  • The attacker VM moved from Kali to Ubuntu (more flexible for Docker / honeypot labs ahead; Kali's tools install easily on it). The Windows VM is Windows Server 2025 (AD capable; nested virtualisation and Docker planned).
  • Flow: run Responder on Ubuntu on interface ens5 → in Windows File Explorer browse to \\<Linux IP> and enter password (lower-case) → Responder shows the captured credentials → then crack them.

The walkthrough was deferred to Day 4 morning, and John reposted an updated handout that includes the cracking step.

💡 Note (added)

The fix is Day 1's: disable LLMNR / NBT-NS, enforce SMB signing, plus this section's workstation-to-workstation blocking. LLMNR & NTLM relay

docs.title: 8. From the AMA
docs.text:
• Does the old trick of swapping a logon-screen accessibility tool (Utilman, Sticky Keys sethc, Magnifier) for a command prompt still work? → Yes — and notably you come in as SYSTEM. (This is the "accessibility features" item on the EDR card.)
  • Still using Kali? → John is "old school" and likes purpose-built Kali, but BHIS testers increasingly use a home-grown build.
  • What next after this course? → the next in the cycle, Active Defense and Cyber Deception.
  • Go-to cyber news? → BHIS's internal team that constantly shares news (and a Teams room), plus Simply Cyber's (Jerry) Daily Cyber Threat Brief.
  • Best home antivirus? → "Believe it or not, straight-up Windows Defender is about as good as you'll get."

💡 Note (added) — detecting / preventing accessibility-feature abuse

MITRE T1546.008, typically used with direct disk access (physical access, boot media).

  • Check C:\Windows\System32\ sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, Magnify.exe hashes against originals (an original name of cmd.exe is conclusive)
  • Watch Image File Execution Options for a new Debugger value on those binaries (Sysmon 13)
  • Full-disk encryption (BitLocker) prevents offline file swaps
  • cmd.exe spawned as a child of winlogon.exe at the logon screen (Sysmon 1) is a strong signal

docs.title: Day 3 summary
docs.text:
Topic Key point Sysmon lab review name ≠ original name (1), DNS query (22), remote thread into LSASS (8 = hash-dump signal) Pass-the-Hash a hash is enough to log in — defend with LAPS, lateral-movement blocking, credential protection EDR & defence in depth overlapping controls multiply; AI is only as good as its data Threat emulation trust but verify; test in alert-only, non-blocking mode; don't over-specify rules AI-written detections AI drafts; humans back-test on history and test against a live attack BloodHound standard user → Domain Admin paths; never make Domain Users local admins Atomic Red Team lab technique-specific vs generic alerts; factor in log lag; gap analysis Host firewalls block workstation-to-workstation → remove the lateral-movement category

EDR is powerful but not enough alone — multiply the attacker's cost with overlapping controls, and keep finding and closing detection gaps with Atomic Red Team and hand-built emulation. And stop hash-fuelled lateral movement as a whole category with host firewalls that block workstation-to-workstation traffic.

docs.title: Blue Team Essentials
docs.text:
What this section is

The data a SOC analyst looks at every day (DNS, HTTP, email, endpoint logs, …), each explained as why it matters → what it is → what it actually looks like → when a SOC uses it. Anything that changed recently is marked [Changed], anything that is commonly stated wrongly or is risky if done the old way is marked [Caution] / [Correction], and practical must-knows are marked [Added].

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• DNS

    DNS structure and record types, log collection and safe investigation, domain signals, unauthorised DNS, tunnelling, blockchain DNS, IDNs, encrypted DNS, and a suspicious-DNS triage sheet.

    DNS

Next topic

HTTP will follow.

About these pages

Personal study notes. Not official guidance of any organisation.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
In one line

Almost every attack passes through DNS at least once, and a well-filtered, well-enriched DNS log catches a surprising amount of evil from the domain name alone. In 2026, though, encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT/DoQ) and ECH mean the network shows less and less — company DNS server logs + endpoint logs (Sysmon 22, EDR) are now the centre of gravity.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text: # Page Key points 1 Understanding DNS — structure and records Four server roles, recursion, TTL, A/AAAA/PTR/TXT/CNAME/MX/SRV/NS/HTTPS, subdomain takeover, domain hijacking, reading packets 2 DNS log collection and safe investigation Sensor placement, pivoting to firewall logs, OPSEC-ordered lookups, the four detection steps 3 Domain signals TLD, reputation, age, randomness (DGA), ASN, geolocation, rank 4 DNS abuse Unauthorised DNS and its six traces, shared hosting, record tampering, DNS tunnelling 5 Blockchain DNS and IDNs EmerDNS, ENS, gateways, EtherHiding, Punycode, homoglyphs, IDNs inside apps 6 Encrypted DNS DoT/DoH/DoQ/DNSSEC, responding to DoH, DoH in Wireshark, 2026 collection strategy 7 Suspicious DNS triage sheet Principles, per-field signals, workflow, false positives, corrections, common confusions

docs.title: Ten things to remember
docs.text:
1. DNS only hands out addresses; the connection happens separately — read DNS logs together with firewall logs.
  2. A forwarding server replaces the client IP with its own. Sensor placement decides what you can see.
  3. The IP owner can put any name in a PTR record. It is a hint, not evidence.
  4. Domains and IPs are many-to-many and change at any time. Don't block shared (CDN) IPs — block the domain.
  5. Judge ownership from the right, by registered domain.
  6. Bad reputation is evidence; good reputation is not.
  7. Lookup order: our own logs → passive DNS → (from a non-attributable environment) a fresh lookup. Never nslookup a suspicious domain from a corporate host.
  8. Blocking outbound 53 does not stop tunnelling that rides the company resolver. The firewall blocks the path; the DNS server blocks the destination.
  9. Always decode xn--. Mixed scripts + brand similarity.
  10. Never conclude from one signal. Add who · what · where · what next before you judge.

docs.title: Blockchain DNS and IDNs (Punycode)
docs.text:
What this page covers

Blockchain DNS used to escape domain seizure (EmerDNS, ENS, gateways, EtherHiding) and the detection opportunities it creates; fake domains built from foreign letters (IDN homoglyphs) and how to read Punycode; IDNs inside mail and mobile apps, and real attack examples.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview and the triage sheet.

docs.title: Blockchain DNS
docs.text: Attackers use blockchain DNS to avoid domain seizure. The price is that ordinary DNS can't resolve it — and that weakness is the detection opportunity.

docs.title: The attacker–defender back-and-forth
docs.text: Stage What goes in the malware Defender response Result 1 IP address (hard-coded) Block IP / take server down Infected hosts don't know a new address — attacker loses everything 2 Domain name Block IP Attacker just changes the A record and every infected host follows (fast, with short TTL) → whack-a-mole 3 Domain name Seize / sinkhole the domain The name itself is gone → defender wins 4 Blockchain domain Can't be seized Detect the "doesn't resolve in ordinary DNS" weakness

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Blockchain DNS stores records on a public blockchain → no central authority, so no takedown or seizure. But only the name → IP mapping is unseizable; the server still sits on the ordinary internet, so takedown and IP blocking still work.
  • EmerDNS TLDs: .coin, .emc, .lib, .bazar (widely reported as used by BazarLoader/BazarBackdoor for C2).
  • Outside the ICANN root, so company DNS and 8.8.8.8 both return NXDOMAIN. Using it needs special software, the malware's own resolver, or an alternative DNS (OpenNIC) → which means unauthorised DNS and unusual traces.
  • Detection: lookups of blockchain TLDs, lookups of TLDs not on the IANA list (exceptions: internal names .local/.corp, typos, Chrome hijacking test), unauthorised DNS, software and protocol control.
Review Q&A
  • What it avoids: domain suspension, seizure, sinkholing. What it can't avoid: server takedown, IP blocking — and the "doesn't resolve in ordinary DNS" trace.
  • Don't close node3.bazar NXDOMAIN as "failed, so no problem": the lookup itself is evidence of malware on the host, and it may have retried another way (alternative DNS, DoH, direct IP) → check the same host for unauthorised DNS, 853, DoH and direct-IP connections, the process (Sysmon 22), whether other hosts asked, when it started, then isolate.
  • Legitimate false positives for "TLD not on the IANA list": internal names (.local, .corp, .lan; .home.arpa is official), typos, dot-less single words (Chrome test, NetBIOS-style short names), some VPN and dev tools. What it misses: gateway access (.eth.limo, ipfs.io), EtherHiding (blockchain node APIs over ordinary HTTPS), lookups wrapped in DoH, blockchain services that use official TLDs.

2026 view

  • OpenNIC reportedly dropped its EmerDNS link around 2019 because of abuse (older descriptions may be dated).
  • New main players: ENS (.eth), Unstoppable Domains (.crypto etc.), Handshake + IPFS.
  • Gateways: intermediate sites that turn blockchain names into ordinary web addresses (vitalik.eth.limo, ipfs.io/ipfs/Qm...). They resolve normally through company DNS on official TLDs, bypassing the "unknown TLD" rule. Abused for hard-to-take-down phishing → maintain a gateway-domain list, block if there's no business need, watch for connections right after an email click.
  • EtherHiding (Guardio, 2023): C2 addresses or malicious code stored in a smart contract (an undeletable public notice board) and read via blockchain node APIs over ordinary HTTPS. It passes almost the entire DNS triage sheet → context and behaviour detection: who, which process, and what next (a direct-IP connection with no DNS right after the API call).

docs.title: IDNs and Punycode
docs.text: Fake domains built from foreign letters that look identical to English can't be told apart by eye — but in DNS logs they always appear as Punycode starting with xn--.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• yоutube.com looks identical even on hover, but the second "o" is Cyrillic (U+043E) → "hover over the link" training doesn't catch it.
  • DNS originally allows only lowercase ASCII letters, digits and hyphens → other characters are converted to Punycode (IDN). E.g. Καλημέρα.gr = xn--ixahbwnhi5b.gr, 한국.kr = xn--3e0b707e.kr.
  • Deceiving with identical-looking characters (Cyrillic О, Latin O, Greek Ο) = a homoglyph (homograph) attack. Unlike typo-squats (micros0ft) or letter pairs (rnicrosoft), even close inspection may not reveal it.
  • Punycode structure: xn-- + the ASCII letters + - + encoded info for the non-ASCII letters, e.g. xn--yutube-wqf.com. Every IDN label starts with xn-- (any label — subdomain or TLD) → search logs for xn--.
  • Compare the second part with the real brand: the missing letter is the swapped position. xn--pypal-4ve.com → pypal is paypal minus the first "a" → pаypal.com (Cyrillic а U+0430). Swapping the second "a" gives xn--paypl-7ve.com.
  • Decode locally rather than on an external site: python3 -c "print(b'xn--yutube-wqf.com'.decode('idna'))"; find non-ASCII characters with ord(c) > 127.
  • xn-- is not automatically malicious: a natural name in a single script (한국.kr, münchen.de) is usually fine. The strong signal is imitating an English name + mixed scripts (аррӏе.com has a·p·p·l·e all in Cyrillic).
Review Q&A
  • Why "hover over the link" training fails: the link text and the real address are the same fake address, rendered just like the genuine one. The problem is not Punycode but that it displays as the original characters. Defender measures: alert on xn-- lookups, monitor IDN variants of your brands (crt.sh), mail security that shows Punycode and warns on IDN links, passkeys and security keys (the machine compares the domain exactly).
  • "Block all xn--" blocks legitimate multilingual sites. A better rule: block or alert on IDNs with mixed scripts; allow single-script IDNs but alert if the decoded name resembles a famous brand or our domain. Caution: look-alikes within the Latin script itself such as ɡ (U+0261) don't trip the mixed-script rule → brand comparison is also required. Conversely, blocking every "English + non-English letter" name blocks münchen.de.

2026 view

  • After the 2017 аррӏе.com demonstration, browsers show mixed-script and imitating names as Punycode in the address bar; Chrome also has a look-alike warning page (exact conditions vary by version).
  • [Caution] Mail, chat and documents still show the original characters, so the pre-click stage remains vulnerable. In-app browsers may follow different rules.
  • TLD operators have registration limits such as "no script mixing", but they vary. ᏚĖCUREBANK.com = xn--curebank-3db3419b.com (Cherokee Ꮪ U+13DA + ė U+0117).
  • The real fix: passkeys and FIDO2 security keys.

docs.title: IDNs inside apps, and real attacks
docs.text: The browser shows Punycode only after the page has opened; mail, documents and phone screens show the original characters, so stopping it before the click is hard. Many real attacks also swap characters within the Latin script.

docs.title: IDNs inside apps
docs.text:
• Timeline: shown as original characters in the email → click → page opens (now the address bar shows Punycode) → user gets suspicious. Browser protection works after the page opens, so a malicious download or exploit may already be under way.
  • The same IDN renders differently per app: Outlook desktop, Gmail web, Outlook and Gmail mobile, iOS notifications. How convincing it is depends on the font, and the app or device picks the font.
  • Phones are especially weak: small text, hidden URLs, no hover, tap straight from the notification.
  • Defences sit before the user's screen: mail security (show Punycode, warn, quarantine), link rewriting and time-of-click checks, DNS-layer blocking, passkeys and security keys.

docs.title: Real attacks
docs.text:
Displayed as In DNS logs Swapped character Mixed scripts? ᏚĖCUREBANK.com (illustrative) xn--curebank-3db3419b.com Ꮪ U+13DA (Cherokee), ė U+0117 Yes (Latin + Cherokee) ḟacebook.com xn--acebook-js3c.com ḟ U+1E1F No (Latin only) morɡanstanley.com xn--moranstanley-0df.com ɡ U+0261 No (Latin only) lloydsbankingɡroup.com xn--lloydsbankingroup-0ch.com ɡ U+0261 No (Latin only)
  • Targets: Facebook, Morgan Stanley, Lloyds, UnitedHealth — firms tied directly to money and personal data.
  • Same-script swaps don't trip the mixed-script rule → brand-similarity comparison (map confusable characters to plain Latin, then compare against your brand list — UTS #39 confusables). A Punycode second part that is the brand minus one or two letters (moranstanley) is a strong signal.
  • Slash look-alikes: in bankofamerica.com∕index.jp the real registered domain is com∕index.jp and bankofamerica is a subdomain. With U+2215 it appears in DNS as bankofamerica.xn--comindex-0f7d.jp. The extreme case of "read from the right" (owned by a researcher).
Review Q&A
  • Trap: something like xn--micrsoft-07a.com may look plausible but actually decodes to miăcrsoft.com (ă U+0103). Cyrillic-o examples: micrоsoft.com (first o Cyrillic) = xn--micrsoft-qbh.com, microsоft.com (second o) = xn--microsft-sbh.com. The second part lets you guess the brand and missing letter, but which script it is only shows when you decode it and look at the code point (Cyrillic о or Latin ö?).
  • "The browser shows Punycode, so why not relax?": mail (original characters) → click → page opens → only then Punycode in the address bar. Measures: Punycode display and quarantine at the mail layer, time-of-click checks, DNS blocking, passkeys.
  • paypal.com/login.secure-check.co: if the / is a fake slash, the whole thing is a domain → registered domain secure-check.co (subdomain paypal.com∕login). If it's a real slash, the registered domain is paypal.com and the rest is a path. Same on screen, completely different owner.

2026 view

  • Slash trick: the old rules (IDNA2003) convert it, but current rules (IDNA2008 / UTS #46) reject U+2215 and U+2044 (verified locally) → mostly blocked now. Same-script swaps (ɡ, ḟ) are still allowed under current rules → more important in practice.
  • Time-of-click checking (Safe Links etc.) is standard, but weak against cloaking.
  • SMS and messenger phishing are growing — outside mail security. MDM and mobile Protective DNS.
  • Awareness training is shifting from "check the address carefully" to "don't log in from message links — use passkeys".

docs.title: DNS Log Collection and Safe Investigation
DNS Log Collection and Safe Investigation
docs.text:
What this page covers

What sensor placement lets you see, how to pivot to firewall logs when the client has been lost, the OPSEC-safe order for looking things up, and the four steps of DNS detection (parse · enrich · decide · act).

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview and the triage sheet.

docs.title: Checking your logs and pivoting
docs.text: To catch an attack you first have to be able to see it. Sensor placement and log type decide what is visible and what isn't.

docs.title: Two ways attackers use DNS
docs.text:
Kind Example What gives it away How to catch it Normal DNS to find a bad place Phishing link click → ordinary A query The name itself (blocklists, free TLD, newly registered, look-alike spelling) Compare with lists Using DNS itself abnormally TXT commands, DNS tunnelling, NS hijack Behaviour (TXT ratio, long/random names, NXDOMAIN spikes) Compare with baseline

List comparison alone misses new attacks; behaviour comparison alone misses known ones — you need both.

docs.title: Five checks on your DNS logging
docs.text:
• Where is the sensor? If only above the company DNS server, every client looks like the DNS server's IP
  • Do you use both server logs and network extraction? Each fills the other's gaps
  • Are answers (response IPs) logged? Without them the link to firewall logs is broken
  • Are answers retained? That is your own passive DNS (which IP did that domain have back then?)
  • Can you see queries that bypass company DNS — direct external resolvers, DoH?
Setup Visible Not visible Fill the gap with Company DNS server logs only The real client Queries that bypass company DNS (straight to 8.8.8.8, DoH) Egress sensor (inside NAT), block outbound 53 + alert on attempts, browser DoH policy Egress network sensor only Bypass queries (if on 53) The real client, cache hits that never left, internal-domain queries Collect DNS server logs, firewall pivot, endpoint logs
  • Put the egress sensor inside the NAT, or every client collapses into the company's public IP.
  • DoH looks like ordinary HTTPS to the egress sensor and isn't caught by a port-53 block. Browser-native DoH bypasses the OS resolver and may not appear in Sysmon 22 either — policy is the reliable control.

docs.title: When the client is lost — pivot
docs.text:
Take the response IP from the DNS log, search firewall logs for it, and the real PC appears (using a value from one log to search another = pivoting).

  • Upside: PCs hidden by caching also connect to the same IP, so they turn up too. Widen the time window by the TTL.
  • Limit: with a shared IP (CDN) you get hundreds of hosts. Narrow to new connections in a tight window, use proxy logs (site name), SNI (not with ECH), endpoint logs (Sysmon, EDR) — and fundamentally, collect DNS server logs.

2026 view

  • DoH went from "a question" to reality: blocking 53 is not the end of it.
  • The more traffic is encrypted, the less the network shows — endpoint logs (Sysmon, EDR) become the third pillar.
  • [Caution] Auto-alerts built only on upstream logs will flag the company DNS server as "the infected host". Add an "is this IP a DNS server?" step to alert logic.
  • [Caution] Check whether your logging tool throws away the TTL field.

docs.title: Safe investigation and the detection formula
docs.text: When you need a domain ↔ IP answer, weigh accuracy (is it the answer from that time?) against defensive OPSEC (does the attacker notice?). If the attack is targeted, or you aren't sure, default to quiet.

docs.title: Why your lookups must not be noticed
docs.text: A direct nslookup travels to the attacker's authoritative server and leaves your organisation's IP (or your DNS server's IP) there. The attacker can respond by swapping infrastructure, wiping traces, going dormant, or rushing to the objective. For commodity malware this matters less — sharing even helps other defenders.

docs.title: Three-tier priority
docs.text:
Tier Method Seen by attacker? Answer from that time? When 1 Our own logs: DNS, proxy, Sysmon, EDR, firewall No Yes Always first 2 External passive DNS lookup Doesn't reach the attacker; the service may log your search Yes (has a timeline) When we have no logs 3A Ask an online service to do a fresh lookup Our IP isn't left; VirusTotal publishes, CentralOps doesn't No (today's answer) When 1 and 2 are empty 3B Direct dig/nslookup Our IP is left on the attacker's server No (today's answer) Only if not targeted
  • On the same website, "view historical records" (tier 2) and "run a new lookup" (tier 3) are different features.
  • A direct lookup also creates a fresh "malicious domain lookup" in our own DNS logs, muddying which hosts are infected.

docs.title: The four detection steps
docs.text:
1. Parse: raw log → fields. "Logs are arriving" ≠ "every field you need is there" (watch for missing TTL, response code).
  2. Enrich: ask a question of every field → host name, department, criticality, user, reputation, registration date, ASN, process. Use the time of the incident, not now (check DHCP).
  3. Decide: one strong signal (exact threat-intel match) ≈ conclusive; several weak signals together (newly registered, cheap TLD, short TTL, no reputation, 3 a.m., process in Temp) = strong suspicion.
  4. Act: faster, more accurate verdicts — designed so the system adds enrichment automatically, not an analyst by hand.

docs.title: Enrichment in four directions
docs.text:
Split the alert into fields and ask "what is this?" of each one: who (host) · what (domain) · where (IP) · why / what next (context).

Direction What to add Why Who (host) Asset inventory (name, department, criticality), DHCP at incident time, logons (user) Decides risk and who to contact What (domain) Threat-intel match, registration date (WHOIS), reputation/category, passive DNS history Turns weak signals like TLD into strong ones Where (response IP) Threat intel, WHOIS/ASN (shared?), response code (NXDOMAIN?), TTL On a shared IP, IP reputation weakens Why / what next (context) The process that asked (Sysmon 22), lookups in the preceding seconds (originating site), how many other hosts asked, the actual connection and bytes afterwards, time of day Most often missed by beginners, most often decisive

The same "host looked up a .top domain" alert can end in opposite conclusions:

  • Scenario A: office hours, marketing PC, chrome.exe, news site just before, two-year-old ad domain, 30 other PCs did the same → ad traffic, close as low priority.
  • Scenario B: 3 a.m., critical finance PC, Temp\update.exe, registered three days ago, no reputation, TTL 60 s, response IP listed as C2, six hours of traffic, the only host to ask → isolate now.
Review Q&A — \"Why not just nslookup it from my laptop?\"

Looking up the domain from a targeted incident two weeks ago has three problems:

  1. Noticed: the query reaches the attacker's authoritative server with our IP (OPSEC).
  2. Wrong: you get today's answer. If it differs from two weeks ago, the firewall shows no connection and you wrongly conclude "safe".
  3. Polluted: our DNS logs gain a new "corporate PC looked up a malicious domain" line, confusing which hosts are infected.

Instead: our DNS logs → proxy, Sysmon, EDR, firewall → external passive DNS history → (only if still nothing) a fresh lookup from a non-attributable environment, noting in the record that it is today's answer.

2026 view

  • Mature teams keep a non-attributable investigation environment as standard kit.
  • Uploading a suspicious file to VirusTotal effectively publishes it. "No uploads, hash search only" is a common rule.
  • Some long-standing lookup services have changed (e.g. RiskIQ → Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence).
  • [Caution] Short DNS log retention empties tier 1 and pushes you to tiers 2–3. Keep at least a "domain · time · IP" summary for a long time.

docs.title: DNS Abuse — Unauthorised DNS, Shared Hosting, Record Tampering, Tunnelling
DNS Abuse — Unauthorised DNS, Shared Hosting, Record Tampering, Tunnelling
docs.text:
What this page covers

Unauthorised DNS servers that bypass company DNS and the six places they leave traces, the blocking dilemma of shared hosting, tampering with our own DNS records (domain shadowing, record swaps), and how DNS tunnelling works and how to tell it from legitimate traffic.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview and the triage sheet.

docs.title: Unauthorised DNS servers
docs.text: From here on the attacks use DNS itself abnormally. To dodge logging and blocking, attackers skip the company resolver.

docs.title: The attack list
docs.text: Unauthorised DNS servers / malicious sites on shared hosting / tampering with our records / DNS tunnelling / blockchain DNS / IDNs. They appear at every stage — recon (SRV, TXT), initial access (look-alikes, subdomain takeover), C2 (DGA, TXT commands, bypass DNS), exfiltration (tunnelling).

docs.title: Principle and remedy
docs.text:
• A PC's DNS setting is a request, not enforcement. A program can build DNS packets itself and send them anywhere → the firewall is where you stop it.
  • Legitimate software does it too: browser DoH, IoT and streaming devices with hard-coded DNS, some VPNs, games and dev tools → either malware or a "disobedient program or user" — investigate either way.
  • Remedy: ① allow outbound 53 only from company DNS ② make all DNS visible (server logs alone don't show bypass) ③ alert on the blocked attempts too ④ for DoH, TLS decryption.
  • [Added] Instead of blocking, the firewall can intercept outbound 53 and redirect it to company DNS (hard-coded devices keep working). Log the original destination separately.

docs.title: Discussion: find the suspicious query
docs.text:
Almost everything goes to company DNS (192.168.42.2), but packet 708 alone goes to 8.8.8.8. External DNS use shows up in the destination IP field, not in the name asked (www.google.com). Malware does a connectivity check against Google and the like before contacting C2, so a perfectly ordinary name comes first → look at what happens next. The same log shows different attacks in different fields (name: phishing/DGA; destination: bypass; response: NXDOMAIN/dormant; type: TXT/SRV).

Review Q&A
  • 2 a.m., three queries to 1.1.1.1: www.microsoft.com, www.google.com, a8kq2vx.duckdns.org → time of day, company-DNS bypass and "connectivity check then connect" all line up. The decisive one is the last: a random subdomain on a free dynamic DNS service = C2 candidate. On DDNS and hosting platforms each subdomain has a different owner, so the subdomain is effectively the registration unit — an exception to "only the subdomain is random, so it's fine".
  • Why "we block outbound 53, so bypass is solved" is wrong: ① encrypted DNS (DoH 443, DoT/DoQ 853) ② not using DNS at all, or another path: hard-coded IPs, DNS on a non-53 port, an attacker-run DoH server ③ tunnelling that legitimately goes through company DNS (the question travels via the company resolver to the attacker's authoritative server → unaffected by the 53 block). Response: block 853, block known DoH, browser policy, internal DoH, alert on blocked attempts, default-deny egress, monitor company-DNS query patterns (tunnelling detection), EDR and behavioural detection.

2026 view

  • DoH response in layers rather than TLS decryption (cost/performance, breaks pinned apps, privacy/legal issues, ECH): browser policy, Firefox canary domain use-application-dns.net → NXDOMAIN, block known DoH servers, block 853 (TCP/UDP), offer internal DoH, endpoint logs.
  • An attacker's own DoH server isn't on any list → behavioural detection.
  • Before blocking 53, log-only for a few days to find devices that would break — and infected ones.
  • Correction: DoQ is UDP 853; UDP 443 is DoH over HTTP/3.

docs.title: Traces of external DNS, and blocking on shared hosting
docs.text: External DNS use leaves traces in six places, and any of them should lead to an alert. Shared hosting is not an attack technique but a blocking dilemma: what do you block when one IP hosts thousands of sites?

docs.title: Traces of external DNS use
docs.text:
Source Where Name? Process? Before traffic? Notes ① Firewall Network ✗ ✗ ✗ Both allowed and denied. Outside NAT, sources collapse ② Flow / network sensor Network Flow ✗ / Zeek ○ ✗ ✗ Dest 53 + internal source + external dest + source ≠ DNS server ③ Host firewall Host ✗ ○ ✗ Windows Security Event ID 5156 (Filtering Platform permitted a connection), 5157 (blocked). Needs audit policy; 5156 is high-volume. pfirewall.log ④ IDS Network Rule-dependent ✗ ✗ Past alerts help date the start (infection time) ⑤ Host integrity monitoring Host — ○ ○ Watch DNS settings and hosts file ⑥ EDR Host ○ ○ ✗ (○ if it records config changes) "Any DNS that isn't company DNS" — the most comprehensive

The two places to watch with host integrity monitoring:

  • DNS server setting: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters\Interfaces\{ID}\NameServer → watch with Sysmon Event ID 13 (registry value set). If changed, every program on the host uses the attacker's DNS (e.g. DNSChanger).
  • hosts file: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts → Sysmon Event ID 11 (file create) / FIM. It is consulted before DNS, so no DNS query happens at all and nothing appears in network or DNS logs.

docs.title: Shared hosting
docs.text:
• Around $3 a month, thousands of small sites per IP (one apartment block, thousands of flats). Example: cuzb.com → 91.195.240.79 → 5,857 other sites.
  • Reverse IP lookup ≠ PTR: PTR is the single name the IP owner chose (custip-1079.sedoparking.com); a reverse IP lookup is every domain that passive DNS has seen pointing at the IP.
  • Parking services (sedoparking.com) serve many unused domains from a few IPs — sometimes tied to malvertising and to waiting or abandoned attack domains.
  • The usual answer: business sites rarely live on shared hosting, so blocking both domain and IP is usually OK. Better answer: before blocking, check logs for traffic volume to that IP and the related domains.
Review Q&A
  • A suspected-infected host with no trace at all in network logs → ⑤ host integrity: the DNS server setting (registry) and the hosts file. EDR helps if it records configuration changes. Other candidates: home router DNS, browser DoH or proxy settings.
  • Reverse IP lookup returns 3,000 domains: small hosting ASN + two of our hosts + all malicious domains → IP block is possible (also block the domains, set an expiry, investigate both hosts). Cloudflare ASN + 400 hosts + varied domains → don't block the IP. Block domains instead (DNS, proxy), identify which of the 400 actually went to the malicious domain via DNS/proxy/EDR, report abuse to the CDN if needed.

2026 view

  • "Thousands per IP" isn't only classic shared hosting (CDNs, cloud platforms). The reverse-IP count alone can't tell them apart → check the ASN first, then apply the judgement above.
  • Work from home: home router DNS hijacking → force company DNS on corporate laptops anywhere (VPN or cloud Protective DNS).
  • EDR is standard now, but depending on the product, browser-native DoH may show only as an HTTPS connection, not as DNS.
  • [Caution] Six sources alerting on the same event = alert fatigue. One primary alert, the rest as enrichment; pre-register known exceptions.

docs.title: Record tampering and DNS tunnelling
docs.text: If attackers compromise our DNS admin account, our own domain becomes their tool. DNS tunnelling uses DNS as a data channel — hard to block, but easy to find.

docs.title: Tampering with DNS records
docs.text:
• Domain shadowing: add new subdomains under our domain (blog.example.com → attacker server). They borrow our reputation, age and TLD and pass every name-based check.
  • Record swap (the "really bad" one): clone the VPN login page and point the vpn. A record at it. The captured password is passed through to the real page, the login succeeds, and nobody notices.
  • With DNS control the attacker proves ownership via TXT and gets a genuine HTTPS certificate. Address bar (real domain) and padlock (real certificate) both look right, so user awareness rules fail.
  • Difference from subdomain takeover: takeover uses the empty slot of a neglected CNAME; shadowing compromises the account and adds records directly.
  • Defence: MFA + change detection. Added: keep a record inventory and alert on new records, watch crt.sh for certificates we didn't issue, alert on admin-account logins and changes.

docs.title: DNS tunnelling
docs.text:
• Principle: DNS sends text and receives text → encode data (files, command output) in subdomains; tunnelling software on the attacker's authoritative server (iodine: IP tunnel; dnscat2: C2) decodes it and returns commands in responses (TXT, CNAME).
  • "It almost always works": DNS must be able to leave from at least one place (the company resolver).
  • Two paths: ① straight to the attacker's DNS (stopped by blocking outbound 53) ② recursively through company DNS (unaffected by the outbound 53 block).
  • The outbound 53 rule is "allow only the company DNS server, deny the rest". The company resolver's recursion must stay open or the internet breaks → the firewall doesn't inspect question content, so tunnel queries pass as normal recursion. Forwarding to an upstream Protective DNS delivers them the same way (though the upstream can detect them).
  • The firewall blocks the path; the DNS server blocks the destination: detect the pattern at the company DNS server → block the registered domain (Protective DNS / RPZ) → isolate the infected host.
  • Signals: subdomains padded to the length limit (253 per name, 63 per label), random/encoded strings, a flood of queries to one domain, high TXT/CNAME share, an odd process (Sysmon 22), abnormal data volume.
  • It may look like hex yet not decode because it is encrypted — that doesn't affect the verdict.
Review Q&A
  • Detecting a record swap: A-record change detection, rogue certificates on crt.sh, admin-account login monitoring, response IPs seen internally that aren't our servers.
  • Hundreds of 60-character random-subdomain TXT queries a minute → suspect tunnelling. If it went through company DNS, blocking outbound 53 won't stop it. Check the registered domain first (filter out legitimate AV/anti-spam lookups such as sophosxl.net) → reputation and age → process → other hosts.

2026 view

  • Low-and-slow evasion (small, slow chunks) → ML detection combining length, entropy, frequency, unique-subdomain count and data ratio (Protective DNS, NDR).
  • Tunnelling over DoH defeats DNS-log detection → EDR/NDR behaviour and connection patterns.
  • Bulk exfiltration has moved to legitimate cloud (Google Drive, Telegram, …); DNS tunnelling is for low-volume C2 and locked-down environments.
  • [Caution] False positives from legitimate services that use long random names (AV reputation lookups, CDNs).

docs.title: Telling tunnels apart, and a detection checklist
docs.text: "Long random name = tunnel" is wrong. Judge on two axes: ① the registered domain ② the volume.

docs.title: Discussion: three "possible tunnelling" alerts
docs.text:
Looks like Type Registered domain Volume Verdict ① Very long random name TXT sophosxl.net (Sophos AV Live Protection) Low Benign — technically tunnelling, for a good purpose ② Very long name with non-standard characters NULL (almost never used) pirate.sea (unknown; hack.lu CTF) High Malicious (iodine) ③ Random subdomain A cloudfront.net (AWS CDN) Low Benign
  • AV uses DNS for the same reason attackers do: DNS is open almost everywhere.
  • NULL records can carry arbitrary binary, so they are iodine's default — their mere appearance is a strong signal.
  • An A answer holds only 4 bytes of IP, so it is an inefficient return channel (though the query side can still exfiltrate).
  • Allow-list confirmed legitimate DNS-data services by registered domain — and occasionally check that the process making the lookups really is that product.

docs.title: Detection checklist
docs.text:
• A spike in unique subdomains under one registered domain — each name is new, so it never hits cache and always recurses → it shows up fully in both company DNS logs and the egress sensor (the opposite of "caching means you only see the first lookup").
  • High query volume from one source (1 MB exfiltrated = tens of thousands of queries).
  • Excess TXT, CNAME, MX, NULL.
  • Long random subdomains + an odd registered domain.
  • TXT responses carrying unreadable encoded data (legitimate TXT reads like v=spf1).
  • Use of unauthorised DNS servers.
  • False positives: CDNs, AV lookups, the DNS hijacking test (Chrome looks up a few random dot-less single words at start-up → NXDOMAIN).
  • Heavy querying to an unknown or malicious registered domain may be exfiltration in progress — investigate first.
Review Q&A
  • 4.3.2.1.zen.spamhaus.org (mail server, on every message) = DNSBL spam-reputation lookup, reversed-IP format / k8x2m9q4v7.data.update-svc.online NULL, one host, 300 a minute = malicious tunnelling / qwzxkplmrt on several hosts just after boot, three queries, NXDOMAIN = Chrome hijacking test.
  • Clues that survive low-and-slow (A type, short names, one query per 10 minutes): the registered domain (new, no reputation, new to us), unique subdomain count accumulated over a long period, regular intervals (beacon), continuing when nobody is at the keyboard, the process (Sysmon 22), no other hosts going there. How: group by source host × registered domain and aggregate over days to weeks; check interval regularity.

2026 view

  • More false positives: DNS lookups by security products in general, DNSBLs (zen.spamhaus.org), cloud and telemetry → a documented allow list.
  • Evasion: low-and-slow, A/AAAA (AAAA answers carry 16 bytes), short names, well-reputed domains (shadowing, DDNS) → composite scoring, ML, long-term accumulation.
  • Keep allow lists narrow, by registered domain. Exclude them from the tunnelling rule only; keep them visible to every other detection.

docs.title: Domain Signals — TLD, Reputation, Age, Randomness, ASN, Geolocation
Domain Signals — TLD, Reputation, Age, Randomness, ASN, Geolocation
docs.text:
What this page covers

Signals that estimate risk from the domain name and the response IP alone: TLDs and the Public Suffix List, the traps in domain reputation, domain age and "new to us", DGAs and randomness, ASN and geolocation, and popularity rank.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview and the triage sheet.

docs.title: TLDs and domain reputation
docs.text: TLD and reputation are weak signals from the name alone. A bad verdict is fairly reliable; a good one guarantees nothing.

docs.title: TLD
docs.text:
• TLD = the rightmost label. Generic (.com), country-code (.au, .tk), new generic (.top, .xyz, .zip — over 1,000 of them).
  • Why attackers favour certain TLDs: free or cheap, the names they want are still available, easy look-alikes, lax abuse handling.
  • What to do: block/alert on TLDs with a high malicious ratio that the business doesn't use; split TLD into its own field and watch the distribution (TLDs that spike against baseline).
  • [Added] Split using the Public Suffix List. Naively cutting at the last dot turns www.example.com.au into a single com.au blob.
  • [Added] Read ownership from the right, up to the label just before the public suffix. login.microsoftonline.com.account-review.top → TLD .top, registered domain account-review.top; everything in front is attacker decoration. It has nothing to do with Microsoft's login domain (microsoftonline.com).

docs.title: Domain reputation
docs.text:
• Category (what kind of site) + reputation (how risky).
  • Match automatically against every log where a domain appears — DNS, proxy, mail.
  • What to do: block malicious and medium-risk and above; for Uncategorized, block or show a splash page (make the user pause); watch hosts that frequently visit risky or uncategorised sites; don't trust it blindly.
Verdict Meaning Malicious Reliable — a quick win Safe Not a guarantee; judge with other signals None / uncategorised Itself a weak signal (new or barely visited)

Ways a well-reputed domain can still be phishing:

  • Classified safe, then the content is flipped to malicious.
  • A compromised legitimate site (phishing page inside an old restaurant website).
  • Abuse of a well-reputed platform (SharePoint, Google Drive, pages.dev, netlify.app) — domain reputation ≠ URL reputation.
  • An expired, well-reputed domain re-registered to inherit its reputation.
  • Cloaking: security crawlers see a clean page, targets see the phishing page.

In one line: bad reputation is evidence; good reputation is not. Attackers earn it (flip), steal it (compromise), borrow it (platforms), buy it (expired domains) and fake it (cloaking).

docs.title: Reputation says "safe" but a user reported phishing — checks
docs.text:
• The full URL, not just the domain (an odd path like /wp-content/... inside a good domain?)
  • Open it safely: isolated environment or urlscan.io private mode. Cloaking may mean you need the exact mail link, but its token carries employee data — no public scans
  • Domain info: recent owner change in WHOIS, recent IP change in passive DNS
  • Impact: who clicked (proxy logs), was a password entered → if so, reset immediately and revoke sessions
  • The email itself: SPF/DKIM/DMARC, sender. "An unexpected login link arrived by email" is a stronger signal than reputation

docs.title: Report wording: be certain about what is certain
docs.text:
What follows from domain structure is fact, not guesswork. For login.microsoftonline.com.account-review.top, don't write "probably not Microsoft" — write "this is not Microsoft's login site (microsoftonline.com)". Conversely, don't assert who owns account-review.top until WHOIS says so. Separating what you know from what you don't is what makes a report credible.

2026 view

  • The once-popular free TLDs (.tk, .ml) effectively disappeared after Freenom stopped new registrations in 2023; attackers moved to cheap new gTLDs (.top, .xyz, .shop … check current reports for rankings).
  • .zip and .mov (2023 on) are confused with file extensions; many organisations block them outright.
  • Free hosting platforms are the "new free TLD". Split by public suffix so a subdomain isn't buried under the platform's reputation.
  • Some long-standing reputation services have changed: RiskIQ → Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence; threatcrowd reportedly discontinued; trustedsource changed with the Trellix/Skyhigh split (verify the current address). Alternatives: urlscan.io, URLhaus.
  • [Caution] Reputation lookups leave traces too — a public urlscan.io scan is visible to anyone and can expose the employee email embedded in the URL.
  • [Added] Reputation blocking now mostly happens at the DNS layer (Protective DNS) — which assumes browser policy stops DoH bypass.

docs.title: Domain age and randomness
docs.text: A new domain is "one vote towards malicious"; a registered domain that is itself random is nearly always bad. Subdomains of legitimate services are random too, so judge by the registered domain.

docs.title: Domain age
docs.text:
• Attackers buy domains just before an attack (buy early and you get noticed; they're discarded quickly anyway; each campaign needs its own name).
  • Check: whois example.com | grep -i creation → Creation Date: 1995-08-14.... A WHOIS query doesn't touch the attacker's servers, so it is quieter than a DNS lookup.
  • The "new" threshold (7/30/90 days) is the organisation's choice. Shorter = more precise but misses more.
  • New to us: old on the internet but first seen in our organisation — catches compromised old sites too. Better as a supporting signal than a standalone alert.
  • Bulk processing needs automation (e.g. Mark Baggett's domain_stats; check its current maintenance status).

docs.title: Randomness and length
docs.text:
• DGA: malware computes hundreds of names a day deterministically (often seeded by date); the attacker registers just one. Block one and tomorrow there's another — hard to block.
  • But the footprint is large: random registered domains + NXDOMAIN spikes.
  • How randomness is judged: character-pair frequency (freq.py), entropy, machine learning.
  • Legitimate subdomains are random too (d1a2b3...cloudfront.net, r3---sn-...googlevideo.com) → judge by the registered domain. Abnormally long, random subdomains suggest DNS tunnelling (see DNS abuse).
  • Long domains are suspicious. Exception: llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch.co.uk.
Example Naive randomness check Real judgement d3k9x7qplm2v8.cloudfront.net Fires (subdomain) Registered domain cloudfront.net → normal on randomness. Attackers use CloudFront too, so not a "safe" guarantee xvqkplmzrtb.top Fires The registered domain itself is random + cheap TLD → suspicious. Check NXDOMAIN, age, other hosts xn--80ak6aa92e.com Fires (Punycode) Not random — the encoded form of non-ASCII letters. Decodes to the famous Cyrillic "apple" look-alike → more suspicious (IDN)

docs.title: How domain age is faked, and how to check
docs.text:
WHOIS/RDAP shows one snapshot of the current state; there is no "owner changed on" field. An old creation date doesn't mean "same owner for a long time".

Route Creation date Clue Fully deleted, then registered fresh (drop catch) Reset to the new date → age signal works Recent creation date Bought at an expired-domain auction before deletion Original date kept Recent Updated Date, registrar/NS change Bought from / transferred by the previous owner Original date kept Recent Updated Date, registrar/NS change Bought early and left to age Old No real use for a long time → sudden recent activity
  • Caution: "a re-bought expired domain keeps its original creation date" is only half true. If it was fully deleted and re-registered, the date resets; it is kept only for pre-deletion auctions or direct purchase.
  • More checks: Updated Date, registrar change, NS change history (passive DNS), a gap in A records followed by sudden activity (passive DNS), historical WHOIS services (mostly paid; owner data is redacted since 2018 but dates, registrar and NS are still useful), first certificate issuance (crt.sh), changes in web content (Wayback Machine).

2026 view

  • WHOIS → RDAP: structured (JSON) results. As far as I know ICANN made RDAP the official standard for gTLDs from early 2025. Owner data is mostly REDACTED FOR PRIVACY; creation date is usually visible.
  • "Newly Observed Domain" is now a standard security-product feature.
  • Dictionary DGAs (summerhousetable.com) evade character-pair checks → combine with NXDOMAIN spikes, age, lookup patterns, ML.
  • [Caution] Punycode (xn--) causes randomness false positives and is a look-alike attack vector. Decode it first.

docs.title: ASN and geolocation
docs.text: Add "whose network is this (ASN)" and "which country (geolocation)" to an IP. Both are weak alone; the main use is "does the claim match the source?".

docs.title: ASN
docs.text:
• AS = a network run independently by one organisation; ASN = its number (the entity announcing IP blocks in BGP). E.g. AS15169 Google, AS8075 Microsoft, AS16509 Amazon, AS13335 Cloudflare, AS1221 Telstra.
  • Lookup: whois -h whois.cymru.com " -v 8.8.8.8" → AS, BGP prefix, country, registry, AS name. Web: bgp.he.net, ipinfo.io. A downloaded database (MaxMind etc.) leaves no external trace.
  • Example: ChromeSetup.exe from Google's ASN is natural; from another ASN (e.g. AS4134, which once topped Spamhaus's botnet list) suspect a fake installer.
  • Rule idea: alert on "executable downloaded from a top-10 risky ASN".
  • Limit: attackers rent cloud, so the ASN shows Amazon, Google, DigitalOcean → less useful for inbound attacks, but trends are visible.
  • [Added] The ASN type is more useful than the name: residential / mobile / enterprise / hosting. A human account logging in from a hosting ASN is suspicious.
  • [Caution] Brands also distribute through CDNs (large software vendors on Akamai, etc.). Don't conclude from "ASN isn't the brand name" alone — check whether it is that brand's CDN.

docs.title: Geolocation
docs.text:
• Not much use as a whole: web traffic goes everywhere, and anycast CDNs blur location → split by direction and protocol.
  • Inbound: geo-restrict staff-only services (VPN, portals). A travel/deployment exception process is mandatory.
  • Outbound: ignore web; pay attention to SSH, FTP etc. going to unexpected countries.
  • Rarely a rule on its own — "one more vote" on something already suspicious.
  • Map charts have little technical value but real value for convincing executives and budgets.
  • ASN + location = a concrete picture: "a US data centre" vs "a US home".
Review Q&A
  • AdobeReader_Update.exe + adobe-update-center.top + a small overseas VPS ASN: both the claim (Adobe) and the source mismatch. The registered domain adobe-update-center.top is not Adobe (a brand-stuffed look-alike), cheap TLD; also check age, reputation, new-to-us. Next: did it execute? (Sysmon Event ID 1 process creation, Event ID 11 file creation, Security 4688 new process), search by hash (no upload), isolate if executed, block the domain, check other hosts.
  • "Block all VPN logins from outside Australia": cuts a lot of noise such as brute force from overseas IPs. But it does not block "all malicious attempts from overseas" — attackers route through Australian residential proxies, Australian cloud regions and compromised Australian servers. Other limits: blocks travelling/deployed staff, geo-database errors block legitimate users, false sense of safety.

2026 view

  • Residential proxies: attackers rent home IPs in any country or city, so location and ASN both look normal → pair with phishing-resistant MFA (security keys, passkeys) and managed-device conditions.
  • Key cloud sign-in signals: impossible travel, hosting-ASN logins, never-seen countries. VPNs cause frequent false positives.
  • Bad-ASN rankings change over time. Block whole large-carrier ASNs with care; prefer narrow, conditional rules.
  • [Caution] Geolocation is an estimate. Country level is mostly reliable; city level is a hint. In reports write "the IP is registered to country X".
  • [Added] IP location ≠ attacker location — it is only the last hop. Attribution is a separate job.

docs.title: Eight name-only signals — summary
docs.text:
A well-filtered, well-enriched DNS log catches a lot of evil from the domain name alone — and that many organisations don't collect DNS logs because they wrongly think they are low-value and high-volume.

Signal In one line TLD Heavily abused TLDs like .top; TLDs not on the IANA list (blockchain) Reputation Bad reputation is evidence; good reputation is not a guarantee Age New domains + "new to us", RDAP Randomness DGA. Beware Punycode and CDN false positives Length Long subdomains = tunnelling; long registered domains = phishing Rank [Added] Not on a popularity list (Tranco etc.) → look closer. On the list ≠ safe IP reputation Response IP's ASN, residential proxies, shared hosting IDN xn--, mixed scripts + brand comparison

docs.title: Rank [Added]
docs.text:
• A top-sites list: on it = a common name, not on it = a rare name.
  • [Changed] Alexa Top 1M shut down in May 2022 → Tranco (combines several lists to resist manipulation), Cisco Umbrella Popularity List, Cloudflare Radar.
  • In a SOC it's mostly used to filter (lower the score).
  • [Caution] A high rank isn't safety: popular platforms (drive.google.com, github.com, *.workers.dev) are attacker favourites → look at them by subdomain or URL. Rank lists can be manipulated with bot lookups.

docs.title: Walking one log line through the signals [Added]
docs.text:
ts=2026-10-19T02:14:07Z  id.orig_h=10.20.4.57  query=a8f3k2.x7qpz9wm.top  qtype_name=A  rcode_name=NOERROR  answers=185.199.xx.xx  TTLs=60
  1. TLD: .top → score up (never decisive alone)
  2. Registered domain / randomness: by Public Suffix List, x7qpz9wm.top — unreadable = DGA-shaped
  3. Length: long, ever-changing subdomains → tunnelling; a long registered domain → phishing
  4. Age: RDAP creation date, and "first time seen in our organisation"
  5. Rank: not on any popularity list
