  6. Reputation: bad = evidence; nothing at all may just mean nobody has reported it yet
  7. IP reputation: ASN type of the response IP; TTLs=60 (CDNs use it too, but it also fits fast flux)
  8. IDN: no xn--

Signals only give you a reason to look further; the verdict comes after you add who (which host, which process) and what next (the actual connection, bytes, regular intervals).

docs.title: Encrypted DNS — DoT, DoH, DoQ, DNSSEC and Collection Strategy
Encrypted DNS — DoT, DoH, DoQ, DNSSEC and Collection Strategy
docs.text:
What this page covers

What DoT, DoH and DNSSEC each protect, how DoH blinds the blue team and the four ways to respond, DoH as seen in Wireshark, and where to collect DNS logs in 2026 now that encryption is the default.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview and the triage sheet.

docs.title: The future of DNS: DoT, DoH, DNSSEC
docs.text:
The three protect different things. DoT and DoH give confidentiality (no eavesdropping); DNSSEC gives authenticity and integrity (no forgery). They protect users — and block the blue team's view.

DoT DoH DNSSEC How DNS wrapped in TLS DNS inside HTTPS Digital signature on answers Port TCP 853 TCP 443 (UDP 443 over HTTP/3) 53 (ordinary DNS) Protects Confidentiality Confidentiality Authenticity, integrity Blue-team view Content hidden; easy to identify and block by port Hard to tell from ordinary web traffic (only SNI and destination IP as clues) Fully visible Analogy An envelope A letter inside a parcel A notarised seal

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• DoT: a dedicated port, so "easy to block". Android "Private DNS" is DoT → 853 traffic is common on corporate Wi-Fi; control it with MDM.
  • DoH: you can't block 443, so it's the standard that "wins". [Correction] The common claim that DoH is "JSON encoded" is inaccurate — standard DoH (RFC 8484) carries binary DNS as application/dns-message; JSON (application/dns-json) is a non-standard Google/Cloudflare API.
  • DoH encrypts only the PC ↔ recursive resolver leg. Recursive → authoritative is usually plaintext, and the DoH provider sees everything → external DoH = the company can't see, the external provider can.
  • DNSSEC chain of trust: root key (anchor) → the parent's DS (vouches for the child's key) → the domain's DNSKEY (public key) → the answer's RRSIG (signature). In dig +dnssec output the ad flag = validated; a signature mismatch → SERVFAIL.
  • DNSSEC limits: usually validated only up to the recursive resolver (the PC trusts ad), doesn't stop account takeover or record swaps (signed with the real key), many domains are unsigned, and an attacker's own domain validates as "genuine" too (authenticity ≠ good intent).
Review Q&A
  • What's wrong with "we'll turn on DNSSEC for our domain to stop eavesdropping on staff lookups and hijacking": ① DNSSEC doesn't encrypt, so it can't stop eavesdropping, and signing our domain only prevents forgery when others look up our domain — it has nothing to do with staff looking up other sites ② compromise the registrar account and the attacker changes DS/NS or turns DNSSEC off, so it doesn't stop hijacking (MFA, Registry Lock and change monitoring do).
  • → 9.9.9.9:853 = Quad9 DoT, identified and blocked by port / → 104.16.248.249:443 SNI cloudflare-dns.com = Cloudflare DoH, blends with web traffic (a known provider, so SNI/IP still catch it; a self-hosted DoH server or ECH wouldn't be caught).
  • "With external DoH nobody knows" is wrong: the DoH provider sees all of it; recursive → authoritative is plaintext (though the authoritative server only sees the resolver's IP); the PC itself (EDR, browser logs) sees it; and when the site is then visited, SNI and destination IP reveal it (ECH hides SNI too).

2026 view

  • Added more recently: DoQ (RFC 9250, UDP 853) and DoH over HTTP/3 (UDP 443).
  • DDR (RFC 9462): the PC discovers that its current resolver supports encryption and upgrades to an encrypted connection to the same server → if company DNS supports DoH you get "encrypted, but the company keeps the logs" (check per-product support).
  • ODoH (RFC 9230): hides who asked even from the DoH provider.
  • OS-level DoH in Windows 11 (the long-promised "soon" has arrived).
  • [Caution] Detection or proxy rules that look only for the JSON format miss standard DoH. "DNSSEC = the DNS security solution" is a misconception.

docs.title: Responding to DoH, and DoH in Wireshark
docs.text: With DoH, DNS becomes HTTP: ① the questions vanish from view and ② it is effectively an unauthorised external resolver. The overall direction: block external DoH; provide internal DoH or turn it off.

docs.title: Four responses
docs.text: Response What it does What it covers Limits ① Decryption (the traditional best answer) Company proxy decrypts TLS (company cert installed on PCs) Known and self-hosted DoH alike Cost/performance, pinned apps break, privacy/legal burden, managed PCs only ② Canary domain Company DNS returns NXDOMAIN for use-application-dns.net Firefox automatic DoH only Useless against manual settings, Chrome, Edge, OS DoH, malware ③ Internal DoH server The company runs a DoH server What comes to the company server (encrypted + company logging/blocking) External DoH still needs blocking ④ Client logging Firefox MOZ_LOG=nsHostResolver:5 + MOZ_LOG_FILE, about:networking That PC, that app Hard to run permanently; for investigations

docs.title: Wireshark
docs.text:
• Encrypted: just Application Data. Clues are the destination IP (104.16.248.249 = Cloudflare) and SNI. With an attacker-run DoH server you can't tell it's DNS, let alone which name.
  • Decrypted: TLS → HTTP/2 → DNS, POST /dns-query, content-type: application/dns-message, and the query name is visible.
  • Transaction ID 0x0000: the DoH standard (RFC 8484) recommends 0 for HTTP-cache friendliness → pair queries and answers by TCP connection + HTTP/2 Stream ID. HTTP/2 sends HEADERS and DATA frames separately.
  • Home-lab exercise: set the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable → point Wireshark's TLS settings at the key-log file → filter dns or http2.header.value == "application/dns-message". Delete the file and unset the variable afterwards. A work PC with SSLKEYLOGFILE set is worth investigating.
  • Exercise: find 443 traffic to 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9. Zeek: cat ssl.log | zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h server_name.
Review Q&A
  • The canary domain stops Firefox's default (automatic) DoH. It doesn't stop: Firefox manual DoH, Chrome and Edge (they ignore the canary), Windows 11 / macOS / iOS OS-level DoH, malware or other apps with their own DoH, DoT (853).
  • Why the DoH Transaction ID is 0: so HTTP caches see identical questions as identical requests. Pair by TCP connection + HTTP/2 Stream ID.
  • In EDR, firefox.exe → cloudflare-dns.com:443 vs Temp\svchelper.exe → dns.google:443 — the second first: not a browser, running from Temp, named to look like a system file → suspected malware doing DoH C2 lookups (Sysmon 1 and 22, parent process, subsequent connections, consider isolation). The first is a policy-violation check.

2026 view

  • Priorities ahead of decryption: ① pin DoH to the company server or turn it off by policy (Chrome/Edge DnsOverHttpsMode / DnsOverHttpsTemplates, Firefox DNSOverHTTPS, Windows Group Policy) ② internal DoH and DDR ③ block public DoH and 853 ④ use EDR to detect non-browser processes connecting to DoH ⑤ selective decryption.
  • [Caution] The canary domain is a helper, not "DoH is blocked".

docs.title: DNS Summary — where to collect DNS logs
docs.text: Conclusion: filter and enrich DNS logs well and you can catch evil from the domain name alone. The eight-signal summary lives on the domain signals page.

docs.title: Collection considerations
docs.text:
• DNS is proxied → depending on where you collect, "who asked" disappears (a sensor outside the forwarder sees only the server IP).
  • Network extraction (Zeek etc.) is the easiest method "for now".
  • As encrypted DNS spreads → you must move to DNS server and endpoint logs.

2026 view

  • [Changed] What was called "the future" a few years ago is here: DoH, DoT, DoQ + ECH (hides SNI too) → on the network, little more than the destination IP remains.
  • Collection priority: ① company DNS server logs (Windows DNS Analytical log 256/257/258 and 260/261, BIND/Unbound query logs) ② endpoint logs (Sysmon 22 = per-process DNS, EDR) ③ Protective DNS (blocking and logging together) ④ network extraction as a supplement.
  • [Changed] Popularity lists: Alexa Top 1M shut down in 2022 → Tranco, Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Radar.
  • [Caution] Never conclude from one signal. Stack signals and add context (who · what · where · what next).
Review Q&A
  • Excluding the top 100,000 by popularity from alerts: upside — a big drop in alert noise. Risk — you lose abuse of popular platforms (Google Drive, GitHub, *.workers.dev, Discord CDN, dynamic DNS…), compromised popular domains and rank manipulation wholesale. Adjust: keep collecting logs and reduce only alerts; lower the score rather than exclude; take user-content platforms off the list and look at them by subdomain; look at non-browser lookups regardless of rank.
  • C2 traffic is in the firewall, but there is no DNS server event 256 for it: ① hard-coded IP (no DNS) ② the malware's own DoH (policy only covers browsers) ③ direct external 53 or 853 ④ hosts file ⑤ looked up under another name (CNAME or a different domain) ⑥ another internal DNS server that isn't logging ⑦ the lookup is outside the search window (PC cache) ⑧ Analytical log loss. Check: Sysmon 22, 3 and 11, EDR, firewall for 53/853/DoH servers, ipconfig /displaydns, other DNS servers' logs, widen the time range.
  • Combining DNS server 256 with Sysmon 22: the server log = which host IP asked what (for scoping across the company); Sysmon 22 = which program asked. Together: C:\ProgramData\Intel\igfxsvc.exe (Intel imitation in a non-standard location) looked up a never-seen .top domain → suspected malware. Next: hash, parent process, persistence; firewall connection to the response IP; search DNS server logs for other hosts that asked the same name (scoping).

docs.title: 2026 collection priority in detail [Added]
docs.text:
① Company DNS server logs — the Windows DNS Server Analytical log (Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Analytical, off by default)

Event ID Meaning When it fires 256 Query received (QUERY_RECEIVED) Every time a PC asks the DNS server 257 Response success (RESPONSE_SUCCESS) An answer was returned 258 Response failure (RESPONSE_FAILURE) NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, … 260 Recursive query out (RECURSE_QUERY_OUT) Not in cache, asking outside 261 Recursive response in (RECURSE_RESPONSE_IN) The outside answer arrived 
Event ID: 256
QUERY_RECEIVED: TCP=0; InterfaceIP=10.20.0.10; Source=10.20.4.57; RD=1; QNAME=x7qpz9wm.top.; QTYPE=1; XID=41377; Port=52114; Flags=256; PacketData=...

TCP=0 arrived over UDP · InterfaceIP the DNS server IP that received it · Source the client IP that asked · RD=1 recursion desired · QNAME the name asked (trailing dot = root) · QTYPE=1 A record · XID transaction ID · Port the client's source port. Every query that passed through company DNS (tunnelling included) is here; queries that never touched company DNS are not.

② Endpoint logs — Sysmon Event ID 22 (DNSEvent): which program asked

Event ID: 22
UtcTime: 2026-10-19 02:14:07.311
ProcessId: 7412
QueryName: x7qpz9wm.top
QueryStatus: 0
QueryResults: ::ffff:185.199.xx.xx;
Image: C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\svchelper.exe

QueryStatus: 0 success (otherwise a Windows error code, e.g. 9003 = name does not exist) · QueryResults the returned addresses (::ffff: is IPv4 written in IPv6 form) · Image the path of the program that asked. Limit: it only captures lookups that go through the Windows DNS client, so a program's own DoH may not appear → supplement with Sysmon 3 (network connection) and EDR.

③ Protective DNS — resolve through a DNS service with threat intel that blocks and logs. Recommended by CISA and NSA in the US; in Australia, ASD reportedly runs a service for government entities.

④ Network extraction (Zeek dns.log) — a supplement for plaintext DNS through company resolvers and outbound-53 attempts. Field details: Zeek dns.log.

docs.title: Suspicious DNS Triage Sheet · Corrections · Common Confusions
Suspicious DNS Triage Sheet · Corrections · Common Confusions
docs.text:
What this page covers

A practical reference for what to check, in what order, when you are handed one DNS log line; things that are commonly stated wrongly or have changed recently; and the points that actually caused confusion during review.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = changed recently / risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview for the full reading order.

docs.title: 0. Before judging: can you trust the log?
docs.text:
• Is the client the real PC? (If the sensor is only above company DNS, every client is the DNS server IP)
  • Are response IPs logged?
  • Are the TTL and response-code fields intact?
  • Can you see company-DNS bypass (direct external 53, DoH)?
  • Is retention long enough for past incidents?

docs.title: 1. Principles
docs.text:
1. One strong signal, or several weak ones
  2. A bad verdict is evidence; a good verdict is not
  3. Does the claim match the source?
  4. Read domains from the right; judge ownership by registered domain
  5. Compare with baseline
  6. Judge by "then", not "now"

docs.title: 2. Field by field
docs.text:
A. The name asked (domain)

Signal Strength Tips / common false positives Exact threat-intel match Strong A match settles it / shared domains wrongly listed Registered domain itself random Strong–medium Suspect DGA / decode Punycode first Only the subdomain random Usually benign Re-judge on the registered domain / CDN, cloud. But on DDNS and hosting platforms (duckdns.org, pages.dev …) each subdomain has its own owner, so the subdomain is the registration unit → random = suspicious Abnormally long, random subdomain Medium Suspect tunnelling. Check the registered domain first (AV lookups like sophosxl.net are benign). Detect at the company DNS server, then block the registered domain Brand name stuffed in Strong–medium The registered domain isn't the brand's Punycode (xn--) Decode to know Strong if it imitates a famous brand / legitimate non-English domains Recently registered (7/30/90 days) Weak–medium New legitimate businesses Old but recently woken up Medium Updated Date, registrar or NS change, passive-DNS gap then activity, recent first certificate First time seen in our organisation Weak Supporting signal / new business services Cheap TLD, .zip / .mov Weak Split with the Public Suffix List Subdomain on free hosting Weak–medium Judge per subdomain Reputation malicious / medium risk or above Strong Quick verdict Reputation uncategorised Weak New or rarely visited Reputation safe Not evidence Flip, compromise, platform, expired re-buy, cloaking Abnormally long name Weak Exceptions exist (the Welsh village)

A additions: a lookup of a TLD not on the IANA list (.bazar, .emc, .lib, .eth …) is a strong signal — even NXDOMAIN proves malware on the host. Exceptions: internal names (.local, .corp, .lan), typos, dot-less single words. Blockchain gateway domains (eth.limo, ipfs.io, dweb.link …) are on official TLDs, so watch or block them from a separate list. E addition: a host or program with no business reason querying blockchain node APIs, then connecting to an IP with no DNS = suspect EtherHiding.

A additions: any label starting xn-- is an IDN → always decode it. Mixed scripts (Latin + Cyrillic, Greek, Cherokee …) = strong signal; decoded name resembling a famous brand or our domain = strong signal (same-script letters like ɡ, ḟ exist, so brand comparison is mandatory). Compare the Punycode second part with the brand: the missing letter = the swapped position. A natural single-script name (한국.kr) is usually fine.

B. Query type (record type)

Pattern Suspect Benign when High TXT share from an ordinary PC Command receipt, tunnelling Mail servers Mass MX lookups from an ordinary PC Spambot Mail servers SRV (_ldap, _kerberos, _gc) in a burst Internal recon A few at boot/logon; MFP address-book LDAP Sequential PTR over an IP range Internal scan (nmap) — Direct CNAME-type query A human using a lookup tool Admin work A/AAAA pairs, HTTPS (65) / SVCB (64) Normal Parsers that don't know 65 cause false positives

B additions: NULL (10) is almost never used by legitimate software, so its appearance alone is a strong tunnelling signal (iodine's default). Judge tunnelling by unique subdomain count and volume per "one source × one registered domain", accumulated over days to weeks. False positives: AV lookups (sophosxl.net), DNSBLs (zen.spamhaus.org), CDNs, Chrome's hijacking test (random dot-less single word + NXDOMAIN).

C. Response content

Pattern Suspect Tips NXDOMAIN spike (mostly different domains) DGA With random names, nearly conclusive. Dictionary DGAs leave this trace too 127.0.0.1 / 0.0.0.0 Dormant C2, sinkhole Not harmless. A host still asking = still infected Short TTL + constantly changing IPs Fast flux Short TTL alone can't be told from a CDN Several answer IPs Can be normal Record and investigate all; firewall shows which was used CNAME chain Can be normal Follow to the end; judge the final destination

D. Response IP

Add Tips Caution Threat intel Strong if listed as C2 On a shared IP, IP reputation weakens ASN name Claim vs source (the brand, or the brand's CDN) Big companies distribute via CDNs ASN type A human account logging in from hosting ASN = suspicious Residential proxies disguise it Shared IP? If shared, no IP blocking or IP pivot. "How many behind this IP?" is a reverse IP lookup (passive DNS), not PTR. Small hosting ASN → IP block possible after checking logs; CDN/cloud → never Work at domain level Location Split by direction and protocol (ignore web; watch SSH, FTP) An estimate. IP location ≠ attacker location

E. The asking host and context

Look at Tips Host role Does the lookup fit the role? DHCP mapping at incident time Program Sysmon Event ID 22. chrome.exe vs Temp\update.exe Time of day Office hours vs 3 a.m. Preceding seconds Was there an originating site? Derived from an ad? Number of other hosts Only one = targeted / infected; dozens = possibly a normal service What next Actual connection, duration, bytes Against baseline Same time every day may be a scheduled task

F. The path

Pattern Meaning Ordinary PC sends 53 straight to an external resolver (found via destination IP) Bypassing logging and blocking. Policy breach, misconfiguration or malware. Suspicious even with an ordinary name (connectivity check) External DNS lookup of Google/Microsoft, then a lookup/connection elsewhere Malware connectivity check → the next one is the real destination Firewall deny on outbound 53, host-firewall Event ID 5157 Blocked, but that host and program still need investigating Outbound 853 (TCP DoT / UDP DoQ) Bypass via encrypted DNS 443 to a known public DoH server DoH bypass. A browser = policy breach; a non-browser process (confirm in EDR) = strong malware suspicion. A work PC with SSLKEYLOGFILE set is also worth investigating Company DNS queries stop but web browsing continues Possibly DoH DNS-shaped traffic on a non-53 port Bypass attempt PC DNS-server setting (registry NameServer) changed — Sysmon Event ID 13 Caught before any traffic. Every program now uses the attacker's DNS hosts file changed — Sysmon Event ID 11 / FIM No DNS query is made, so nothing in network or DNS logs Internal domain names going to external DNS Internal information leak, misconfiguration Our resolver's query source port is fixed Vulnerable to cache poisoning

Caution: list legitimate exceptions (IoT and streaming devices with hard-coded DNS, some VPN and dev tools) during a log-only period. Blocking outbound 53 still doesn't stop tunnelling that goes through company DNS normally (detect with the A and B patterns). For remote workers, consider home-router DNS hijacking.

docs.title: 3. Anomalies in our own domain (regular checks, change monitoring)
docs.text:
Anomaly Meaning Response NS changed Full domain takeover Recover → lock down → ride out the TTL → check rogue certificates and intercepted mail → notify MX changed Mail interception Revert immediately, review the account External CNAME target returns NXDOMAIN Subdomain takeover imminent Delete the CNAME, audit them all Verification TXT for services no longer used SaaS exposure Clean up

Addition: anomalies when the DNS admin account is compromised

Anomaly Meaning Response New subdomain under our domain that isn't in our inventory Domain shadowing (riding our reputation) Maintain a record inventory + alert on new records, review the account A record for one of our services (VPN etc.) points at an unfamiliar IP Record swap (cloned login page steals passwords) Revert immediately, account MFA and session revocation crt.sh shows a certificate for our domain we never issued DNS control → TXT ownership proof → genuine certificate Revoke, investigate records and account Unfamiliar logins or config-change alerts on the DNS admin account The starting point of every tampering MFA, Registry Lock

docs.title: 4. Triage workflow
docs.text:
1. Check log quality
  2. Split into fields (time, host, domain, type, response, IP, TTL)
  3. Strong signals first (threat intel, malicious reputation)
  4. Enrich: who · what · where · why / what next
  5. How many weak signals stack up?
  6. Compare with common false positives
  7. Confirm in OPSEC order: our logs → external passive DNS → fresh lookup from a non-attributable environment
  8. Verdict and response: state what is certain as certain, and what is unknown as unknown

Common false positives: random CDN subdomains, A/AAAA pairs, dozens of lookups for one web page, HTTPS (65) queries, short TTLs, legitimate Punycode, MFP LDAP, TXT and MX from mail servers, impossible travel caused by VPN, the company DNS server appearing in alerts.

Don't: nslookup a suspicious domain from a corporate PC, treat PTR as proof of ownership, search in-addr.arpa without reversing it, block shared IPs, upload suspicious files to VirusTotal, publicly scan phishing URLs, believe "blocking overseas = blocking overseas attacks".

docs.title: 5. What makes triage harder in 2026
docs.text: Change Effect Response DoH by default Invisible to company DNS logs and port-53 monitoring Browser policy ECH Site name (SNI) hidden DNS and endpoint logs gain value HTTPS record ipv4hint Connections without an A lookup Revisit "connection without DNS" rules Dictionary DGAs Pass randomness checks Combine with NXDOMAIN, age, lookup patterns Free hosting platforms Top-tier parent reputation Judge per subdomain Cloaking Reputation services see a clean page Mail context first Aged / expired re-buys Evade the age signal Check recent changes, NS, reactivation Residential proxies Location and ASN look normal Phishing-resistant MFA, managed-device conditions Endpoint logs matter more More is invisible to the network Sysmon 22, EDR (browser-native DoH may not show in Sysmon 22)

docs.title: Common misstatements and 2026 updates
docs.text:
None of the DNS principles are out of date. Below are only the places that are often explained wrongly or where the environment has changed.

Kind Common claim / older situation 2026 Correction "Linux does not cache answers by default" systemd-resolved caches (resolvectl show-cache). macOS caches too. All three major OSes cache Correction "SPF TXT records start with spf=" They start with v=spf1 Correction TXT "255-character limit" Per character-string; several strings are concatenated Correction MX rules cite RFC 974 Superseded by RFC 5321 (same rule) Correction PTR of 8.8.4.4 = google-public-dns-b.google.com As far as I know now dns.google (a live example of PTRs changing) Correction DoH "JSON encoded" Standard DoH is application/dns-message; JSON is a non-standard API New Only the classic record types matter HTTPS (65) and SVCB (64), RFC 9460 (Nov 2023). Very common now New SNI reveals the site name ECH (RFC 9848 and 9849, March 2026). Name encrypted → DNS logs gain value Changed DoH is still rare Close to a browser default. Watching port 53 alone misses it Changed SPF + DKIM SPF + DKIM + DMARC required (Google and Yahoo 2024, Microsoft 2025) Changed Warning about the shared-IP accident CDN growth makes IP blocking less and less suitable for web threats. Domain blocking is the default Changed Alexa Top 1M Shut down 2022 → Tranco, Cisco Umbrella, Cloudflare Radar Changed OpenNIC resolves EmerDNS Reportedly dropped around 2019 Changed Free TLDs .tk / .ml Freenom stopped new registrations in 2023 Added — Subdomain takeover (dangling CNAME) Added — Domain/NS hijacking, orphaned DNS-provider accounts (Sitting Ducks, 2024) Added — Attacks using legitimate services (Living off Trusted Sites) Added DNS collection = server logs + network extraction Endpoint logs (Sysmon, EDR) rising as a third pillar

Still valid as written: the hierarchy, delegation, caching and TTL, record meanings, many-to-many mapping, "don't trust PTR", "check before you block".

docs.title: Common confusions
docs.text:
Mix-ups that actually came up while working through review questions. Getting the terms right in exams and reports keeps an investigation pointed the right way.

Confusion Correct understanding A record vs PTR record Give it a name → A; give it an IP → PTR. A domain changed to point at 127.0.0.1 means the domain owner (attacker) changed its A record How to verify a PTR result Not another reverse lookup — look the name up forward (A) and see whether the original IP comes back (FCrDNS). In reports write "FCrDNS confirmed" Canonical name Not the name you asked — the name in the answer Reversing PTR Reverse by octet; digits inside an octet stay put. Only IPv6 reverses per character SPF/DKIM pass = genuine mail? Check which domain passed, alignment with the visible From (DMARC), and possible account compromise. Authenticated ≠ benign First action on NS hijack After an incident, first restore NS (recover). MFA belongs to the next, lock-down step. The target is the registrar account, not the DNS server Lots of queries = infected? Dozens per web page is normal. Judge by content, pattern, process and time, not count Judging the past with today's lookup Don't. Use records from that time (our DNS logs, passive DNS) 127.0.0.1 answer = harmless? It may be dormant. A host still asking = a host still infected A forwarder's destination IP = the server that knew the answer? No — it may have asked someone else behind it. Capture location decides what you see

Further confusions from the detection and attacks part:

Confusion Correct understanding An egress sensor shows the client? Only if it sits inside the NAT; outside, everything collapses into the company public IP Blocking outbound 53 ends bypass DNS? DoH (443) bypasses both sensor and block. Stop it with browser policy Pivot window = a few seconds after the lookup? Thanks to caching, other hosts can connect with no DNS query for the whole TTL. Widen the window by the TTL to find hidden infected hosts The only problem with direct lookups is being noticed? Noticed + today's answer ≠ the answer then + polluting our own logs — three problems What to add when enriching Who (host) · what (domain) · where (IP) · why / what next (context) Reading the registered domain From the right, up to the label just before the public suffix. The rest is decoration "Probably" vs "certainly" What follows from domain structure is fact — state it. Only unverified things are "probably" Reputation "safe" = false positive? Good reputation isn't evidence: flip, compromise, platform, expired domain, cloaking A domain with an old creation date has had the same owner? WHOIS/RDAP is a snapshot. Look at Updated Date, registrar/NS changes, passive-DNS gaps NXDOMAIN for .bazar = failed, so nothing happened? The lookup itself proves malware on the host; it may have retried another way "Block every xn--" Blocks legitimate multilingual sites. Mixed scripts + brand comparison instead DNSSEC stops eavesdropping and hijacking? It doesn't encrypt, and registrar compromise defeats it

docs.title: Understanding DNS — Structure and Records
docs.text:
What this page covers

The four DNS server roles and the recursive lookup path, TTL and caching, record types (A, AAAA, PTR, TXT, CNAME, MX, SRV, NS, HTTPS), the security risk attached to each (subdomain takeover, domain hijacking), and how to read DNS packets in Wireshark.

Conventions

[Added] = practical must-knows, [Correction] = a commonly repeated mistake, [Changed] / [Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. See the DNS overview for the whole path and the triage sheet for the per-log-line checklist.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. DNS only hands out the address. The real connection happens afterwards, so read DNS logs together with connection (firewall) logs.
  2. Behind a forwarding server the original client IP disappears. Sensor placement decides visibility.
  3. Answers are found root → TLD → authoritative server, and cached for the TTL at every step.
  4. One domain can resolve to several IPs. Record all of them, investigate all of them.
  5. PTR queries are written backwards in in-addr.arpa form. Always reverse them before reading.
  6. The IP owner can put any name in a PTR. It is a hint, not evidence.
  7. Domains and IPs are many-to-many and change at any time. Never judge a past incident by today's answer.
  8. Before blocking a malicious domain's IP, count how many internal hosts talk to that IP. If it is shared, block the domain.
  9. The canonical name in a CNAME is the name in the answer. An orphaned CNAME leads to subdomain takeover.
  10. Lose your NS and you lose the whole domain — web, mail and certificates.

docs.title: DNS basics — four server roles and the lookup path
docs.text: DNS turns names into IPs, and in almost every investigation you end up recording "the IP + the domain that pointed to it".

docs.title: The four roles
docs.text:
Role Where / example What it does Caches? Stub resolver Your PC (Windows DNS Client) Answers from its cache, otherwise passes the question to its configured server Yes Forwarding server Corporate domain controller, home router Passes unknown questions upward; never walks the tree itself Yes Recursive (caching) server 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9, ISP DNS, Pi-hole Walks the tree from the root itself Yes Authoritative name server ns1.google.com Holds the master copy of its own zone No

The single most important point: a forwarding server does not pass the question along — it builds a new question from its own IP. Any log collected above the forwarder shows every client as that one server IP.

docs.title: The recursive path
docs.text:
1. PC → corporate forwarder → recursive server
  2. Recursive → root ("."): "Don't know — ask the .com servers"
  3. Recursive → .com: "Don't know — ask ns1.google.com"
  4. Recursive → authoritative: the real IP
  5. The answer travels back down and is cached by the recursive server, the forwarder and the PC

The recursive server does all of steps 2–4. Each server only needs to know the layer below it. If another PC in the company asks the same name within the TTL, the forwarder answers from cache and nothing goes outside — so an outside sensor sees only the first lookup.

docs.title: TTL
docs.text:
TTL is "how many seconds you may trust this answer", set by the domain owner. Higher layers are long (root NS: 6 days); real service IPs are short (google.com A: 300 s).

  • Short TTLs (≤ 60 s) are common for CDNs and cloud. Attacker fast flux looks the same, so TTL only means something combined with other signals.
  • The remaining TTL in ipconfig /displaydns lets you back-calculate when the lookup happened: original 300, remaining 187 → looked up about 113 s ago.

docs.title: Commands to see it yourself
docs.text:
• Windows cache: ipconfig /displaydns, Get-DnsClientCache (Record Type 1 = A, 5 = CNAME)
  • Linux cache: resolvectl show-cache, resolvectl statistics
  • Lookup path: dig +trace google.com A

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: Default is UDP 53; if the answer is too big the TC flag is set and the client retries over TCP 53. Today there is also DoH (TCP 443), DoT (TCP 853), DoQ (UDP 853) and DoH over HTTP/3 (UDP 443), so watching port 53 alone misses things. There are 13 root server names but, thanks to anycast, thousands of physical machines worldwide.

docs.title: Record types and A/AAAA
docs.text: The record type is "the kind of question you ask DNS". Ask the same name for A and you get an IP; ask for MX and you get mail servers.

docs.title: Type numbers
docs.text:
Type No. Asks for Note A 1 Name → IPv4 Most common AAAA 28 Name → IPv6 Usually paired with A NS 2 Name of the authoritative server CNAME 5 Alias → canonical name SOA 6 Zone metadata PTR 12 IP → name MX 15 Mail server TXT 16 Arbitrary text SRV 33 Service location + port SVCB 64 Service binding info Relatively recent (RFC 9460, 2023) HTTPS 65 HTTPS connection info Relatively recent; now very common

Some logs store only the number, so know 1, 28, 5, 12, 16 and 65 by number too.

docs.title: Five things to take from an A/AAAA exchange
docs.text:
• Question — the name asked. Repeated in the response packet for matching.
  • Answer — the IP(s). There can be several. Record only the first and you may miss the IP actually connected to.
  • Transaction ID — 16-bit ticket that pairs question and answer.
  • TTL — cache lifetime in seconds.
  • Source/Destination IP — the destination server did not necessarily know the answer; above a forwarder, the source may not be the real client.

docs.title: Practical points
docs.text:
• One page visit triggers dozens to hundreds of lookups (e.g. one visit to a large portal → 60 A + 95 AAAA). When one lookup looks suspicious, lay out the same PC's lookups a few seconds either side to find where it started.
  • "40 lookups a second" alone does not mean infection. Random-string names + NXDOMAIN spikes + no originating site + 3 a.m. + an odd process, together, look like DGA.
  • A and AAAA in pairs are normal.
  • Cache-poisoning defence is Transaction ID plus source-port randomisation. A resolver with a fixed source port is a vulnerability.

docs.title: [2026] What the HTTPS record (65) changed
docs.text:
Example: dig -t HTTPS cloudflare.com +short → 1 . alpn="h3,h2" ipv4hint=104.16.132.229 ech=...

  • alpn="h3" lets the browser go straight to HTTP/3 (UDP 443). Watching TCP 443 only misses it.
  • ipv4hint means a connection can happen with no A lookup at all — the "connection without DNS = suspicious" rule weakens.
  • ech= is the ECH public key. With ECH the site name (SNI) disappears from the wire, which makes DNS logs more valuable.

docs.title: PTR — reverse lookups
docs.text: PTR asks IP → name (a reverse phone-book lookup). Two traps: the address is written backwards, and the result cannot be trusted.

docs.title: Trap 1: it is written backwards
docs.text:
nslookup 8.8.4.4 actually sends a query for 4.4.8.8.in-addr.arpa.

  • Why: DNS names get bigger to the right (www.google.com), IPs get bigger to the left (8.8.4.4), so the IP is reversed to match.
  • in-addr.arpa is the zone reserved for reverse lookups.
  • How to read it: drop the suffix and reverse the order of the four octets. Do not reverse digits inside an octet.
  • Example: 36.129.85.203.in-addr.arpa → 203.85.129.36
  • Common mistake: pasting it unreversed into a threat-intel site, getting a clean result for the wrong IP, and closing the case.
  • IPv6 uses ip6.arpa and reverses each hex nibble. Don't do it by hand — use dig -x <IP>.

docs.title: Trap 2: don't trust it
docs.text:
Conclusion: don't rely on what a PTR record says.

  • The domain owner sets A; the IP owner sets PTR. They can be different people.
  • The IP owner can put someone else's domain in the PTR.
  • Even with thousands of sites behind one IP, the PTR returns the one name the IP owner chose.
  • Even Google doesn't match: google.com → 142.250.6.206 → PTR lga25s72-in-f14.1e100.net
  • Cloud PTRs (ec2-...amazonaws.com) only tell you "somewhere in the cloud".

docs.title: FCrDNS (Forward-Confirmed reverse DNS)
docs.text:
1. PTR lookup on the IP → get a name
  2. Forward (A) lookup on that name → does it return the original IP?

If it does, the domain owner has also claimed that IP — an attacker cannot change someone else's A record. Mail servers use this for spam scoring. Passing proves "same owner", not "safe".

docs.title: How to use PTR
docs.text:
• As a hint only: residential line? cloud? Tor? Internal PTRs are relatively trustworthy.
  • Decide with WHOIS/RDAP (registered owner), ASN (network operator) and passive DNS (domains that IP has served).
  • [Caution] A PTR lookup on an attacker IP goes to the attacker's DNS server and leaves a trace. Check tools for automatic reverse resolution too.
  • [Caution] An internal PC doing PTR lookups in sequence (1.5.0.10, 2.5.0.10, …) is internal scanning; nmap does PTR lookups by default.
  • The old 8.8.4.4 → google-public-dns-b.google.com has, as far as I know, since become dns.google — a live example of PTRs changing.

docs.title: Many-to-many mapping and the IP-block accident
docs.text: Domains and IPs are two separate maps kept by different people, and each changes independently at any time.

docs.title: Four rules
docs.text:
1. One domain → many IPs, or none. A domain owner can point at someone else's IP without permission.
  2. Many domains → the same IP, or none. CDNs and shared hosting put thousands of sites behind one IP (one apartment block, hundreds of flats).
  3. IP → any name (PTR is up to the IP owner).
  4. All of the above can change at any time.

docs.title: The classic accident
docs.text:
c703[.]info (malicious) points at a Google IP → the analyst blocks that IP at the firewall → the whole company loses Google. The intel wasn't wrong; the mistake was assuming "that IP belongs only to that domain". The fix: before you block an IP or domain, check your logs first.

  • [.] is the "defang" convention so nobody clicks by accident — use it when writing malicious domains in reports.
  • A malicious domain pointing at 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0 is not harmless — it may be parked (dormant) or sinkholed. An internal PC still looking it up is still infected.
  • Investigate past incidents with records from that time (our DNS logs, passive DNS), not today's answer. Write "this IP as of HH:MM" in your notes.

docs.title: Checklist before blocking an IP
docs.text:
• How many internal hosts talk to this IP? (1–2: consider; hundreds: don't)
  • Per WHOIS/ASN, is it shared infrastructure — Cloudflare, AWS, Google, Microsoft, Akamai?
  • Do our DNS logs / passive DNS show other (legitimate) domains on the same IP?
  • If there were several answer IPs, did you check them all — and which one was actually connected to?
  • Would a domain block (DNS sinkhole / DNS firewall) be enough?
  • If you block, did you set an expiry (30–90 days) and record the reason (case number, date, owner)?

2026 view

  • CDN growth means a malicious domain is far more likely to sit on a shared IP. For web threats, IP blocking fits less and less; domain blocking is the default.
  • With ECH, network devices struggle to tell sites on the same IP apart by name. The reliable enforcement points are the DNS layer and the endpoint (EDR).
  • Attackers use legitimate services (GitHub, Google Drive, Telegram) for C2 — Living off Trusted Sites. Domain and IP are both genuine, so detect on behaviour.
  • An IP block with no expiry breaks things six months later when the IP is reassigned to a partner.
  • Before feed-driven auto-blocking (SOAR), add an allow list of major cloud/CDN ranges and an automatic "how many internal hosts talk to this" check.

docs.title: TXT — a box for text
docs.text: TXT attaches arbitrary text to a domain. It is central to mail anti-spoofing and domain-ownership proof — and also a covert channel for attackers.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Any printable ASCII; binary is base64-encoded first.
  • A name can have several TXT records.
  • [Correction] The "255-character limit" applies to each quoted string. A record can hold several strings that are concatenated — that is how 400+ character DKIM keys fit.

docs.title: The three mail-authentication records
docs.text:
Name Where What it checks Example SPF TXT on the domain May this server send mail as this domain? v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ip4:203.0.113.10 -all DKIM TXT at <selector>._domainkey.<domain> Has the content been tampered with? (signature) v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIB... DMARC TXT at _dmarc.<domain> Policy on failure + alignment with the visible From v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:...
  • SPF terminators: -all reject, ~all soft-fail, ?all neutral, +all anyone (worst).
  • DMARC policy: none report only, quarantine spam folder, reject reject. rua reports show who is spoofing your domain.
  • [Correction] "SPF records start with spf=" is a common mistake — SPF starts with v=spf1.
  • [Added] DMARC is just as essential. In February 2024 Google and Yahoo made SPF + DKIM + DMARC mandatory for bulk senders, and Microsoft followed for Outlook.com in 2025.

docs.title: Reading an SPF/DKIM pass
docs.text:
• What it means: sent from an authorised server (SPF), content unchanged (DKIM).
  • Trap 1: pass for which domain? The attacker's micros0ft-billing.com passes for itself.
  • Trap 2: SPF checks the envelope sender (Return-Path), which can differ from the visible From — DMARC alignment closes that gap.
  • Trap 3: a compromised genuine account (BEC) passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
  • Bottom line: authentication confirms identity, not intent.

docs.title: Domain-ownership proof
docs.text: Services hand you a string to publish as TXT (facebook-domain-verification=..., MS=..., google-site-verification=...). [Added] These records reveal which SaaS the company uses — useful recon for tailored phishing. Remove them for services you no longer use.

docs.title: Why attackers abuse it
docs.text: It can hold anything, DNS is almost always open, and mail servers make TXT lookups common enough not to stand out. An infected PC asks for the TXT of cmd.evil-c2.xyz and gets a base64 command back. Many TXT lookups from an ordinary (non-mail) PC are suspicious — detection is covered in DNS abuse.

docs.title: CNAME and subdomain takeover
docs.text: CNAME says "this name is an alias — go and ask that name instead". Neglect it and an attacker can take over a company address.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Ask for A and you get the CNAME plus the canonical name's A (CNAME chasing).
  • Canonical name = the name in the answer. The name you asked is the alias. This is the most-missed exam point.
  • Uses: pointing several names at one server, and today mostly handing off to external services (shop.mycompany.com → mycompany.myshopify.com).
  • CNAMEs pointing at each other loop forever. In practice CDNs create 3–4-step chains, so read the whole response chain to see the final destination.
  • Ordinary PCs rarely query type CNAME directly (they ask for A and get the CNAME as a bonus).

docs.title: Dangling CNAME → subdomain takeover
docs.text:
1. promo.mycompany.com CNAME mycompany-event.herokuapp.com hosts an event page.
  2. After the event the Heroku app is deleted, but the CNAME stays.
  3. The target now returns NXDOMAIN — "this spot is free, anyone can take it".
  4. The attacker creates an app with the same name → attacker content on the genuine company address (credential phishing, malware, fake notices).

Training users to "check the domain in the address bar" does not help, because the address is genuine.

docs.title: When you find one
docs.text:
• Quickly confirm with the owning team whether the service is still in use (don't let it sit for days)
  • Delete the CNAME (first choice). If still needed, re-create the target name yourself to claim the spot
  • Check whether any other CNAME is already taken over (normal response, content we never made)
  • Audit every CNAME pointing outside: *.azurewebsites.net, *.cloudapp.azure.com, *.herokuapp.com, *.s3.amazonaws.com, *.github.io, *.myshopify.com
  • Process rule: when retiring a service, delete the DNS record first, then the service

Cloud providers have added protections such as TXT-based ownership checks, but I'm not certain they cover every service and setting, so cleaning up on our side is the dependable defence. Products that automate this audit are called EASM (external attack surface management).

2026 view

  • With cloud and SaaS everywhere, subdomain takeover is much more common than a few years ago.
  • CNAME can't be used at the zone apex (mycompany.com); the HTTPS/SVCB record's AliasMode fills that gap.
  • CNAME cloaking: ad/tracking vendors hide behind first-party names like metrics.mycompany.com that CNAME to them. "Company address" may not mean "company server".

docs.title: MX, SRV, NS
docs.text: Simple concepts, each with one security risk attached: MX — mail interception, SRV — internal recon, NS — full domain takeover.

docs.title: MX — mail servers
docs.text:
• Mail delivery in three steps: look up the recipient domain's MX → look up that name's A → SMTP to port 25 on that IP.
  • The number in front is preference — lower goes first; equal numbers load-balance.
  • MX must point at an FQDN with A/AAAA. No bare IPs, no CNAMEs.
  • [Correction] The often-cited RFC 974 is superseded by RFC 5321 (same rule).
  • Security clues: mass MX lookups from an ordinary PC = spambot; a phishing domain's MX shows intent (none = click-only, Gmail/Outlook = wants replies, self-hosted = infrastructure lead); a change to our MX = mail-interception emergency.
  • [Added] For domains that never send mail: Null MX (MX 0 ., RFC 7505) + v=spf1 -all + DMARC p=reject stops spoofing.

docs.title: SRV — service location
docs.text:
• Format _service._proto.name (underscores separate it from host names).
  • Answer: priority weight port target, e.g. 0 100 389 dc01.corp.local. — it even gives you the port.
  • Key AD queries: _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<domain> (domain controllers), _kerberos._tcp.<domain> (authentication), _gc._tcp.<domain> (Global Catalog).
  • SRV lookups should only be visible on the internal network → if they leave, your internal domain name leaks.
  • Recon signals: many SRV types in a short burst, at night, from a device that never does it (printer, server), from an odd process. But an MFP may legitimately use LDAP for scan-to-email address books, so compare to baseline.
  • MFPs and IP cameras patch slowly and have no EDR, making them attacker footholds.

docs.title: NS — the name of the server with the answers
docs.text:
• NS lives in two places: a referral copy at the parent TLD (entered at your registrar) and the master on the authoritative server.
  • Why: you can't ask the authoritative server if you don't know who it is — the parent's copy breaks the chicken-and-egg problem.
  • If the two differ: lame delegation (a cause of intermittent resolution failures).

docs.title: Domain hijacking (NS takeover)
docs.text:
Point NS at an attacker server and the attacker controls A, MX and TXT — and can pass TXT ownership checks to get a genuine HTTPS certificate in the company's name. The main route is not hacking DNS but taking over the registrar account. Real examples: the 2018–2019 Sea Turtle and DNSpionage campaigns against government and telco domains; in 2024 the "Sitting Ducks" pattern (hijacking domains whose DNS-provider account no longer exists) was published.

Response order after an incident:

  1. Recover: restore NS at the registrar. If you can't log in, use the registrar's emergency contact (have it ready beforehand).
  2. Lock down: change passwords, kill all sessions, MFA, Registry Lock, check whether the account's contact email was changed.
  3. Ride out: for the NS TTL (e.g. 172800 s = 2 days) some resolvers still go to the attacker even after recovery.
  4. Find the damage: check crt.sh (Certificate Transparency) for rogue certificates and revoke them; assume mail and password-reset emails during the window were intercepted and review key accounts.
  5. Notify: tell customers, partners and staff to re-verify any requests from that window (especially bank-detail changes).

Prevention: registrar MFA, Registry Lock, change alerts on NS/MX/SPF, DNSSEC (useless on its own if the account is taken). When retiring a service, clean up DNS first. Before an incident the first control is MFA; after an incident the first action is recovery.

docs.title: Reading packets — DNS on the wire
docs.text:
A capture mixing A, CNAME and PTR query/response pairs (client IP and transaction IDs are illustrative).

No. Source         Destination    Info
1   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x1a2b A example.com
2   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x1a2b A example.com A 1.2.3.4 A 162.255.119.240
3   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x3c4d CNAME mail.google.com
4   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x3c4d CNAME mail.google.com CNAME googlemail.l.google.com
5   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x5e6f PTR 27.208.194.173.in-addr.arpa
6   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x5e6f PTR 27.208.194.173.in-addr.arpa PTR ql-in-f27.1e100.net

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• query = question, query response = answer. The answer line repeats the question, then the answers.
  • Same ticket (0x...) = one pair.
  • In a response line, each type label starts one answer (three As on line 2 = the question + two answers).
  • Wireshark filters: dns, dns.flags.response == 0 (questions only), dns.qry.type == 12 (PTR only).

docs.title: Questions and answers
docs.text: Question Answer Point 1. Domain looked up with A example.com Right after the type label in the query 2. Resolved IPs 1.2.3.4, 162.255.119.240 Two — one alone is wrong. 1.2.3.4 is a placeholder → a domain owner can publish any IP 3. Canonical name of Google's mail host googlemail.l.google.com Canonical = the name in the answer 4. IP looked up via PTR 173.194.208.27 Reverse the octets 5. DNS server used 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) The query destination — but the capture only shows the PC ↔ 1.1.1.1 leg 6. (Bonus) Problem if this is a corporate PC Bypassing company DNS to use an external resolver No logs, domain blocking defeated, internal names leak. Block outbound 53 + alert on attempts. With DoH it wouldn't even look like this

docs.title: MX → A → PTR investigation flow
docs.text: The IP in question 4 came from gmail.com MX → gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com → A 173.194.208.27 → PTR ql-in-f27.1e100.net. Forward and reverse names differ — another "don't trust PTR" example. Use the same order (MX → A → compare with the sending IP in the headers) to check whether a phishing email's sending server is genuine.

docs.title: Exam Format & Scoring
docs.text:
Section: OSCP+ · Source: OffSec OSCP+ Exam Guide (checked 2026-10-23) · Last updated: 2026-10-23

In one sentence

23 h 45 m of hands-on hacking in a private VPN, then 24 h to upload the report; 100 points available, 70 to pass, no bonus points since 1 November 2024 — and a flag only counts if the report proves it was taken from an interactive shell.

Rules change — re-read before booking

Everything on this page is summarised from the official OSCP+ Exam Guide. OffSec updates it without notice. Read the live guide again the week before the exam.

docs.title: Exam at a glance
docs.text: Item Value Hands-on window 23 h 45 m (e.g. start 09:00, VPN closes 08:45 next day) Report window 24 h after the hands-on window ends Machines 3 standalone + 1 Active Directory set of 3 machines Points available 100 Pass mark 70 Bonus points None (removed 1 Nov 2024) Connection Kali Linux + OpenVPN (OffSec only supports this setup) Proctoring Webcam + screen sharing for the whole hands-on window Results By email within 10 business days of submitting the report

docs.title: Where the points come from
docs.text:
Target Points How Standalone 1 / 2 / 3 20 each 10 for local.txt (low-privilege user) + 10 for proof.txt (root / Administrator) AD machine #1 10 Full compromise of the first host AD machine #2 10 Full compromise of the second host AD machine #3 (Domain Controller) 20 Domain compromise

For the AD set you are given a username and password at the start, simulating a user whose account has already been phished ("assumed breach"). The exact objectives for each machine are shown in the exam control panel — read them at the start.

docs.title: What makes a flag count
docs.text:
Getting the flag is not enough. Each one must meet all of these, or the target can score zero:

  1. Interactive shell. Read the flag with cat (Linux) or type (Windows) from an interactive shell on the target. Web shells are not valid — a flag read through a web shell earns zero points for that target.
  2. Original location. Read it where it lives — don't copy or move it first.
  3. Screenshot with the IP. The same screenshot must show the flag contents and the target's IP address (ip addr, ifconfig or ipconfig).
  4. Right privilege for proof.txt. Linux: a root shell. Windows: a shell as SYSTEM, Administrator, or a user in the local Administrators group.
  5. Submitted in the control panel before the exam ends. The panel does not tell you whether the flag is correct.
  6. Documented in the report well enough that a technically competent reader can repeat every step.

A proof screenshot that satisfies rules 1–4 in one frame:

LinuxWindows 
hostname; whoami; ip addr show | grep 'inet '; cat /root/proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
web01
root
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
    inet 192.168.120.45/24 brd 192.168.120.255 scope global ens160
3f1c0e9b6a2d47c58e1f0a9d2b7c4e61

hostname & whoami & ipconfig | findstr IPv4 & type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
MS01
nt authority\system
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.120.141
9a4e2c71d0b84f6e93c5a1f7e2d6b083

Grading order

OffSec grades machines in the order they appear in your report. Put each target in its own clearly labelled section.

docs.title: Passing combinations
docs.text:
From the official guide — each line is exactly 70 points:

  • 40 AD + 3 × local.txt
  • 40 AD + 2 × local.txt + 1 × proof.txt
  • 20 AD + 3 × local.txt + 2 × proof.txt
  • 10 AD + 3 fully completed standalones

Reading the list the other way round shows why everyone says "get the AD set":

AD points Standalone points needed What that means 40 30 Three footholds, or one full box + one foothold 20 50 Five of the six standalone flags 10 60 Every standalone flag — no mistakes allowed 0 — Cannot pass (standalones max out at 60)

docs.title: What changed in November 2024
docs.text:
Before 1 Nov 2024 OSCP+ exam now AD set start Had to find the initial foothold yourself — no foothold, no AD points Assumed breach: domain credentials given at the start AD scoring All-or-nothing 40 Points per machine: 10 / 10 / 20 Bonus points Up to 10 for lab reports and exercises None Buffer overflow The dedicated 25-point BOF machine already ended in 2022 Still not guaranteed — at most one step of a machine Certification OSCP (lifetime) OSCP (lifetime) and OSCP+ (3 years)

OSCP+ is kept current by passing the OSCP+ recertification exam in the six months before it expires, passing another qualifying OffSec certification, or through OffSec's CPE programme. The plain OSCP never expires.

docs.title: Restricted tools and techniques
docs.text:
The guide lists these as not allowed (quoted):

Spoofing (IP, ARP, DNS, NBNS, etc)

Commercial tools or services (Metasploit Pro, Burp Pro, etc.)

Automatic exploitation tools (e.g. db_autopwn, browser_autopwn, SQLmap, SQLninja etc.)

Mass vulnerability scanners (e.g. Nessus, NeXpose, OpenVAS, Canvas, Core Impact, SAINT, etc.)

AI Chatbots (OffSec KAI, ChatGPT, YouChat, etc.)

Features in other tools that utilize either forbidden or restricted exam limitations

Tools that do the same job as anything on the list are also out. What this means in practice:

Want to… Not allowed Use instead Capture NetNTLMv2 hashes LLMNR / NBNS poisoning with Responder (spoofing) Make the target connect to you — impacket-smbserver, a UNC path in a file or input field Exploit SQL injection sqlmap Manual injection → Web & initial access Intercept web traffic Burp Pro Burp Suite Community, browser dev tools Get help ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, OffSec KAI, other people Your notes, HackTricks, GTFOBins, LOLBAS, man pages, search engines

Explicitly allowed examples from the guide: Nmap (including NSE), Nikto, Burp Free, DirBuster. Searching the internet and Discord is fine; asking anyone for help is not.

docs.title: Metasploit — one target only
docs.text:
• Metasploit modules (auxiliary, exploit, post) or a Meterpreter payload may be used against one target of your choice.
  • Once used on a target, the choice is locked — even if it fails, you cannot move Metasploit to another machine.
  • Running check (or anything else) against several machines to "pick" one is not allowed.
  • No Metasploit pivoting (that would touch more than one target).
  • Always allowed on every target: msfvenom and exploit/multi/handler (with a non-Meterpreter payload).
  • The same limits apply to anything built on Metasploit (Armitage, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit Community).

docs.title: Exploit code in the report
docs.text:
• Unmodified public exploit: give the URL only — don't paste the code.
  • Modified exploit: include the modified code, the original URL, the shellcode / msfvenom command if any, and highlight and explain every change.

docs.title: Other rules
docs.text:
• Don't download files from the exam network unless you need them to compromise a target, and delete them afterwards.
  • Machine reverts are limited (the count is in the control panel). A revert wipes everything on that machine, including your shells.
  • The 23 h 45 m includes all breaks, meals and sleep — there is no pause button. Tell the proctor in chat before stepping away.
  • Have a backup plan for your own failures: second internet connection (phone hotspot), a spare Kali VM snapshot.

docs.title: Ways to lose a target's points
docs.text:
From the guide, you get zero points for a target if you:

  • use a restricted tool or technique on it;
  • use Metasploit modules or Meterpreter on more than one machine;
  • don't provide local.txt / proof.txt both in the control panel and in an interactive-shell screenshot;
  • don't document it well enough to reproduce.

docs.title: Report submission (summary)
docs.text:
Details and checklist on the Reporting page.

Item Requirement Format One PDF, inside a .7z archive; scripts / PoCs as text inside the PDF Names (case-sensitive) OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf and OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z (your OSID) Password None on the PDF or the archive Size Max 200 MB Where / when https://upload.offsec.com, within 24 h of the hands-on window ending Check Compare the MD5 shown after upload with your local file, then click Submit File

docs.title: Scoring strategy
docs.text:
Primary plan: 40 AD + 30 standalone = 70, then build a buffer.

  1. Warm up on one standalone (time-box about 2–3 h). The aim is to get into a working rhythm and, ideally, bank 10–20 points.
  2. Move to the AD set while still fresh. It is the largest single block of points and it is chained — every credential found matters for the next machine.
  3. Go back to the remaining standalones with the AD points banked. Each foothold is another 10.
  4. Aim for 80, not 70. A buffer protects against a flag that the report fails to prove.

Fallback: if the AD set stalls. With 20 AD points (two machines) you need 50 from standalones; with 10 you need all 60. If the AD set has stalled for a long time (several hours with no new information), switch to the standalones, bank everything you can, then return to AD with fresh eyes.

Situation at about hour 12 Points so far Next move AD 40, one standalone foothold 50 Two more footholds, or finish one box AD 20, nothing standalone 20 Standalones now; return to AD later AD 0, two full standalones 40 AD — 30 more points must come from the set

docs.title: Collection order (when time is short)
docs.text:
1. Memory (if the box is live and you can) — then everything else.
  2. $MFT, $UsnJrnl:$J, $LogFile — cheap, huge payoff.
  3. Registry hives + transaction logs (SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY, every NTUSER.DAT + UsrClass.dat), Amcache.hve.
  4. C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx.
  5. C:\Windows\Prefetch\, C:\Windows\System32\sru\, users' Recent\ (LNK + Jump Lists), PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt.
  6. Browser data, Tasks\, Startup folders, Temp directories, setupapi.dev.log.

docs.title: Amcache
docs.text:
Category: Evidence of execution / program inventory · OS: Windows 7 (with update) → 11 · Last updated: 2026-09-16

In one sentence

Amcache.hve is a registry hive that inventories executables, drivers and installed programs the system has seen — most valuable because it stores the SHA-1 hash of the file, so you can identify a renamed or deleted tool with certainty.

docs.title: What it tells you
docs.text:
• Full path, file size, publisher, product/version metadata (from the PE version resource), compile (link) time, and SHA-1 of the first 31,457,280 bytes (30 MB) of the file.
  • The first time Windows became aware of the binary (the key's last-write time) — often, but not always, the first execution.
  • Installed programs (from MSI/uninstall data), drivers, shortcuts, device PnP info.

Execution is inferred, not proven

Entries are created by the Application Experience / Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task (\Microsoft\Windows\Application Experience\Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser) and by the shim engine when a process launches. A file can appear because it was scanned (e.g. sitting in Program Files) rather than executed. Treat Amcache as "this binary existed here, this is its hash", and use Prefetch / 4688 / Sysmon 1 to prove execution.

docs.title: Location
docs.text: Item Path Hive C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve (+ .LOG1, .LOG2 transaction logs — collect them too) Predecessor (XP/7) C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\RecentFileCache.bcf — path only, no hash Locked while running Yes — use raw copy (KAPE, FTK Imager, esentutl-style volume shadow)

docs.title: Structure (Windows 10 1709+ format)
docs.text:
Key What it inventories Key fields Root\InventoryApplicationFile Executables seen (one subkey per file, named <lowercase path>|<hash>) LowerCaseLongPath, Name, Size, FileId (0000 + SHA-1), Publisher, ProductName, ProductVersion, BinFileVersion, LinkDate, BinaryType, ProgramId, IsOsComponent, IsPeFile Root\InventoryApplication Installed programs (MSI, uninstall entries, Store apps) Name, Publisher, Version, InstallDate, RootDirPath, Source (Msi/AddRemoveProgram/…), UninstallString, ProgramId Root\InventoryApplicationShortcut .lnk shortcuts in Start menu / desktop ShortcutPath, ShortcutTargetPath Root\InventoryDriverBinary Drivers (.sys) DriverName, DriverId (SHA-1), DriverSigned, DriverCompany, DriverLastWriteTime Root\InventoryDevicePnp PnP devices Class, manufacturer, driver, InstallDate Root\InventoryDeviceContainer Device containers (USB devices, etc.) FriendlyName, Manufacturer, ModelName

Older format (Win 8 – 10 1607) used Root\File\<VolumeGUID>\<FileRef> with numbered values: 15 = full path, 101 = SHA-1, 17 = last modified, 0F = link date, 11 = created, 100 = program ID.

Which timestamp is which

The key LastWrite time on an InventoryApplicationFile entry = when the appraiser wrote/updated the entry (≈ first-seen, and may be refreshed). LinkDate = PE compile time from the header (attacker-controllable). There is no reliable "last executed" timestamp in Amcache.

docs.title: How to collect
docs.text:
KAPEVelociraptorLive copy 
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest C:\Case\out --target Amcache --mdest C:\Case\mod --module AmcacheParser

Windows.System.Amcache — parses the live hive via raw NTFS read.

# Locked — use a shadow copy or a raw-reading tool.  RawCopy example:
RawCopy.exe /FileNamePath:C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve /OutputPath:C:\Case

docs.title: How to parse
docs.text:
AmcacheParser (Eric Zimmerman)RegRipperPlaso 
# Full parse → several CSVs (UnassociatedFileEntries, AssociatedFileEntries, Programs, Drivers, Shortcuts, Devices…)
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out

# Only files NOT tied to an installed program (where attacker tools live) + include Windows OS files
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out -i

# Whitelist known-good hashes to shrink output
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out -w C:\Case\known_good_sha1.txt

The most useful output is *_UnassociatedFileEntries.csv: binaries that are not part of any installed product. Sort by FileKeyLastWriteTimestamp.

rip.pl -r Amcache.hve -p amcache

log2timeline.py --parsers amcache out.plaso Amcache.hve

docs.title: Analysis tips
docs.text:
Hash first, name second

Take every SHA-1 from UnassociatedFileEntries, drop the leading 0000, and check against VirusTotal / your threat-intel. A file called svchost.exe whose SHA-1 is Mimikatz ends the argument.

  • Renamed tools: Amcache keeps the on-disk name and the PE resource ProductName/OriginalFileName-derived fields. Name = update.exe, ProductName = "mimikatz" happens more often than you'd think.
  • Deleted binaries: Amcache entries survive deletion of the file. Pair with $MFT/USN to reconstruct when it was dropped and removed.
  • Unsigned / no publisher binaries in Users\*, ProgramData, Windows\Temp, Users\Public in the incident window are the first things to pull.
  • LinkDate sanity: a compile time in the future or 1970/2000-ish suggests a packed or forged header.
  • Drivers: InventoryDriverBinary with DriverSigned = 0 or an unusual DriverCompany → BYOVD (bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver) attacks and rootkits.
  • Don't over-read the timestamp — the appraiser task runs roughly daily; an entry's last-write may be hours after actual first execution, or refreshed later.

docs.title: Timeline / correlation
docs.text: Question Cross-check with Did it actually run, and when? Prefetch, Security 4688, Sysmon 1, BAM/DAM Does this hash match a known tool? VirusTotal, MISP, internal hash sets Where did it come from? USN journal FILE_CREATE, Zone.Identifier ADS ($MFT), browser history, 4663 Same tool on other hosts? Fleet-wide Velociraptor hunt on the SHA-1 Program installed vs. dropped? InventoryApplication vs UnassociatedFileEntries

docs.title: Identifying Artefacts by Scenario
docs.text:
Category: Triage methodology · OS: Windows · Last updated: 2026-10-09

A single artefact rarely proves anything on its own. The same trace can be routine or malicious depending on who, when, where and how. This page gives a repeatable way to judge an artefact, decide what context you need, and pick the next artefact that confirms or rules it out.

docs.title: The three-step method
docs.text:
1. Classify — is it likely normal, possibly suspicious or definitely suspicious?
  2. Ask for context — the question that decides whether the behaviour is expected. Is this a known admin task? Is remote access expected for this user?
  3. Find the next artefact — the evidence that answers that question. 4624 logons, VPN logs, Prefetch, USBSTOR.

Rule of thumb

Context is the question. The next artefact is the evidence that answers it.

When a baseline exists, sort every deviation into one of three buckets: normal variation (documented reason, no security impact), potential misconfiguration (security weakened, no attack evidence yet) or suspicious/malicious (matches a known attack pattern).

docs.title: Six-question checklist
docs.text:
Question Leans normal Leans suspicious When? Business hours, scheduled maintenance (e.g. AV scan at 02:00) Overnight, weekends, leave, off-pattern times Where from? Internal IP, corporate VPN, usual location New external IP, overseas, hosting/VPS ranges Who? Account fits the job; admin doing admin work Intern or standard user on sensitive data; service account logging on interactively Which path? C:\Program Files, C:\Windows\System32 %Temp%, %AppData%, Downloads, C:\Users\Public, C:\ProgramData What does it look like? Signed binary, recognisable name Double extension (invoice.doc.exe), random name, Base64/obfuscation, look-alike names (svch0st.exe) What changed? Documented change with a change request New autorun, weakened security settings, cleared logs, AV stopped

One hit → possibly suspicious. Two or three together → definitely suspicious. "03:00 + %Temp% + obfuscated PowerShell" is three hits.

These are definitely suspicious on their own:

  • An autorun location (Run/RunOnce, scheduled task, service) pointing at a random name or a temp path
  • Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell (-enc, FromBase64String, IEX)
  • Security or antivirus logs cleared manually
  • An executable with a double extension

docs.title: 1. Logons and remote access
docs.text:
• Normal: internal IP during business hours.
  • Suspicious: overnight logons, external IPs, impossible travel, failures followed by success.
  • Context: external IP → approved IP list, user role, login history. Internal movement (RDP, SMB) → is remote access expected for that user/system?
  • Next artefact: Security 4624/4625/4634/4647/4648, logon type (3 network, 10 RDP), VPN logs, RDP logs (TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager 21/24/25, RemoteConnectionManager 1149).

docs.title: 2. PowerShell and scripts
docs.text:
• Normal: an admin running a signed script from a known location.
  • Suspicious: execution from %Temp%, -enc / -w hidden / -nop, FromBase64String, IEX, DownloadString.
  • Context: is it a known admin task? What does the script contain? What is the parent process?
  • Next artefact: PowerShell 4104 (script block — the decoded code), 4103 (module logging), 4688 / Sysmon 1 (process and command line), ConsoleHost_history.txt, process tree.

docs.title: 3. Persistence
docs.text:
• Normal: documented entries such as antivirus or updater services.
  • Suspicious: random names under Run/RunOnce, tasks on short intervals (e.g. every 30 minutes), services pointing at temp folders.
  • Context: was it in the baseline? Who created it and when? What file does it launch?
  • Next artefact: HKCU/HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Run and RunOnce, C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\, 4698 (task created), 7045 (service installed), binary path/hash/signature, Autoruns.

docs.title: 4. DNS and network
docs.text:
• Normal: microsoft.com, internal *.local names.
  • Suspicious: random-looking domains (possible DGA, e.g. xf21zy.biz), newly registered domains, external 443 from a host that should only reach an internal database, regular beaconing.
  • Context: domain age, WHOIS, threat-intel reputation, does this host normally talk to the internet?
  • Next artefact: DNS, firewall and proxy logs, PCAP, Zeek conn.log / dns.log / ssl.log, Sysmon 3 and 22, the process that opened the connection.

docs.title: 5. Files and executables
docs.text:
• Normal: signed installer from an official source.
  • Suspicious: double extensions, update.exe run from Downloads, unsigned binaries, name impersonation.
  • Context: where did the file come from? Did the user knowingly download it? Is it a legitimate update?
  • Next artefact: hash + VirusTotal, digital signature, Zone.Identifier (source URL), Prefetch (execution and count), Amcache, Shimcache, browser download history.

docs.title: 6. USB and data exfiltration
docs.text:
• Normal: approved device during work hours.
  • Suspicious: device connected overnight on a no-USB host, bulk file access right after connection, uploads to external FTP or cloud storage.
  • Context: work schedule, USB policy, sensitivity of files touched.
  • Next artefact: USBSTOR, MountedDevices, setupapi.dev.log (first connection), Partition/Diagnostic 1006, LNK and Jump Lists (files opened from the device), Shellbags.

docs.title: 7. Browser extensions
docs.text:
• Normal: extensions on the allow list.
  • Judgement: not on the list but no malicious evidence → start at policy violation / misconfiguration. Excessive permissions (read all sites, cookies), outbound data or sideloading → malicious.
  • Context: source (store or sideloaded), requested permissions, who installed it.
  • Next artefact: ...\User Data\Default\Extensions\<ID>\manifest.json, Preferences / Secure Preferences, extension ID reputation, proxy logs.

docs.title: 8. Log clearing and defence evasion
docs.text:
• Normal: retention-based log rollover.
  • Suspicious: manual clearing, AV disabled, new AV exclusions, audit policy changes.
  • Context: who cleared them? Was there a recent malware detection?
  • Next artefact: 1102 (Security log cleared), 104 (System log cleared), 4719 (audit policy changed), Defender 5001/5007, last scan results, copies in the SIEM.

docs.title: 9. Privilege and policy changes
docs.text:
• Normal: admin change backed by a change request.
  • Judgement: weakening security (e.g. password complexity disabled) → potential misconfiguration until proven otherwise. A standard user modifying a logon script → suspicious.
  • Context: group policy permissions, user privileges, change records.
  • Next artefact: 5136 (directory object changed), 4728/4732 (member added to group), 4670 (permissions changed), GPO version history, SYSVOL timestamps, registry changes.

docs.title: 10. Sensitive file access
docs.text:
• Normal: a user whose role fits, during work hours (HR staff opening the HR share at 13:00).
  • Suspicious: an intern opening payroll.xlsx, many files touched in a short time.
  • Context: job role, access rights, group membership.
  • Next artefact: 4663 (object access), 5140/5145 (share access), ACLs, access timestamps, group info, LNK and Jump Lists.

docs.title: Comparing against a baseline
docs.text:
Bucket Test Example Next step Normal variation Reason recorded, no security impact AV update moved 02:00 → 07:00 due to network latency No action if logs and policy agree Potential misconfiguration Security weakened, no attack evidence yet Password complexity disabled; unlisted browser extension Check change history; accidental or deliberate? Suspicious/malicious Matches a known technique 03:14 logon, new Run key, .ps1 task every 30 min, DGA domain, 01:12 USB, AV process missing Pull related artefacts and build a timeline

Order of review:

  1. What disappeared — a missing AV process matters more than a new one.
  2. What appeared — autoruns, tasks, services, extensions, accounts.
  3. What changed — policies, permissions, times, destinations.
  4. Put the times on one line — 01:12 USB → 03:14 logon → PowerShell → external 443. Weak signals alone become a clear story together.

No baseline? Compare with another host in the same role.

docs.title: 2026 trends that change what you look for
docs.text: Attackers increasingly use the user's own hands and legitimate tools instead of custom malware. Look for normal tools used abnormally.

docs.title: ClickFix variants — RunMRU is no longer enough
docs.text:
ClickFix tricks users into pasting and running a command from a fake CAPTCHA or error. The classic Win+R version leaves the command in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU. Early-2026 variants use Win+X → I to open Windows Terminal instead, so RunMRU stays empty (trackr.live).

  • Check: explorer.exe, a browser or wt.exe spawning powershell/cmd/mshta/regsvr32/rundll32 (Sysmon 1, 4688 with command-line auditing), -w hidden / -enc / IEX, a first-seen domain right after, 4104, ConsoleHost_history.txt.
  • Note: RunMRU shows a command was entered, not that it succeeded. Padding with spaces can hide the real command.

docs.title: CrashFix — a browser extension as the lure
docs.text:
In January 2026 Huntress described CrashFix: a fake extension (NexShield, posing as uBlock Origin Lite) deliberately crashes the browser, then a fake "stopped abnormally" warning gets the user to paste a PowerShell command already on the clipboard. It waits an hour after install so the user doesn't connect the two (Cyber Security News).

  • Lesson: an unlisted extension starts as a policy issue, but extension install → browser crash → RunMRU/PowerShell on one timeline is malicious.

docs.title: RMM abuse — legitimate tools as C2
docs.text:
Huntress's 2026 Cyber Threat Report found RMM abuse up 277% year on year, while traditional hacking tools fell 53%. ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, Atera, NetSupport, PDQ Connect and Splashtop all feature (Dark Reading).

  • Judgement: is this RMM actually approved here? Even an approved product is suspicious if it connects to an unfamiliar tenant, account or relay.
  • Check: 7045, install path and signature, first execution in Prefetch/Amcache, the RMM's own connection logs (often under ProgramData), external relay domains.

docs.title: BYOVD and EDR killers
docs.text:
ESET's June 2026 analysis of GentleKiller (The Gentlemen ransomware) shows it loading a vulnerable or malicious kernel driver to kill 400+ processes from 48 security products, disguised with vendor-like names, fake version info and copied signatures (Security Affairs).

  • Judgement: a security process that vanished is a strong signal on its own.
  • Check: Sysmon 6 (driver loaded), 7045/4697, .sys files outside C:\Windows\System32\drivers, Defender 5001, driver hashes against LOLDrivers.

docs.title: Native Sysmon in Windows 11
docs.text:
In February 2026 Microsoft began shipping Sysmon as a built-in optional feature in Windows 11 Insider builds. It is off by default; enable the feature, then run sysmon -i, and events go to the Windows Event Log (BleepingComputer).

  • Meaning: more hosts will have Sysmon 1/3/6/13/22. At the start of an investigation, check whether Sysmon was on and which config it used — some public configs don't log per-user Explorer keys such as RunMRU.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Full lists: Windows event IDs · Registry keys · Event logs
